knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition of the scaled projected-gradient direction for a strictly feasible standard-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\max\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), at a strictly feasible point \(x^0\). Let \(X^0=\operatorname{Diag}(x^0)\) and \(D=(X^0)^2\). The scaling \(x=X^0\xi\) maps \(x^0\) to \(e\). Projecting the scaled objective gradient onto \(\ker(AX^0)\) and transforming it back gives the primal affine-scaling step direction
\[
\Delta x=X^0\left(I-X^0A^T\bigl(A(X^0)^2A^T\bigr)^{-1}AX^0\right)X^0c
=\left(D-DA^T(ADA^T)^{-1}AD\right)c.
\]
This direction satisfies \(A\Delta x=0\). Consequently, \(x^0+\alpha\Delta x\) remains equality-feasible for every \(\alpha\), and it remains strictly feasible whenever \(x^0+\alpha\Delta x>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a strictly positive feasible point of a standard-form linear program, scale each variable by its current value so that the current point becomes the all-ones vector. Project the objective gradient onto the equality-feasible directions in the scaled coordinates and transform the result back. This gives the primal affine-scaling step direction. It preserves the equality constraints, while the step length must keep every component positive to preserve strict feasibility.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\quad c,x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n
Ax^0=b
X^0=\operatorname{Diag}(x^0)
ADA^T\text{ is nonsingular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta x=\left(D-DA^T(ADA^T)^{-1}AD\right)c,\qquad A\Delta x=0,\qquad x^0+\alpha\Delta x>0\Longrightarrow x^0+\alpha\Delta x\text{ is strictly feasible}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given LP data \((A,b,c)\), a primal-feasible \(x^0>0\), \(\epsilon>0\), and \(0<\beta<1\), set \(k=0\). At iteration \(k\), define \(X_k=\operatorname{diag}(x^k)\), \(p^k=(AX_k^2A^\top)^{-1}AX_k^2c\), and \(r^k=c-A^\top p^k\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled feasible affine-scaling direction obtained by linearizing complementarity at zero target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\), form \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) and \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\). Compute the affine direction from \(A\Delta x=0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0\), and \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=-XSe\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-Scaling Convergence and Its Parameter Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-sequence convergence guarantees and a failure boundary for the affine-scaling algorithm, depending on the parameter and degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the affine-scaling algorithm with parameter \(r\): (a) if the problem and its dual are nondegenerate, then for every \(r<1\), the generated sequence converges to the optimal solution; (b) for every \(r\le 2/3\), the generated sequence converges to an optimal solution regardless of degeneracy; and (c) there exist a problem instance and an associated \(r<1\) for which the generated sequence converges to a nonoptimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the affine-scaling algorithm, if the problem and its dual are nondegenerate, the sequence converges to the optimal solution for every parameter r below 1. Regardless of degeneracy, it converges to an optimal solution whenever r is at most 2/3. However, an instance and a parameter r below 1 exist for which the sequence converges to a nonoptimal solution.
assumptions_latex: \text{The sequence is generated by the affine-scaling algorithm with parameter }r.
\text{Clause (a) assumes that the problem and its dual are nondegenerate.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(a) If both problems are nondegenerate, then }\forall r<1,\ x^k\to x^*\text{, where }x^*\text{ is optimal};\quad \text{(b) }\forall r\le 2/3,\ x^k\to \bar x\text{ for some optimal }\bar x\text{, regardless of degeneracy};\quad \text{(c) }\exists\text{ an instance and }\exists r<1\text{ such that }x^k\to \hat x\text{ with }\hat x\text{ nonoptimal}.

knowledge_statements.title: Nondegenerate Affine-Scaling Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical convergence under boundedness and a unique nondegenerate optimal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the primal affine-scaling iteration for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), with a strictly feasible initial point and fixed step fraction \(\beta\in(0,2/3]\). Suppose the feasible set is bounded, \(A\) has full row rank, and the linear program has a unique optimal vertex \(x^*\) whose positive-coordinate columns form a nonsingular basis and whose nonbasic reduced costs are strictly positive. Then the affine-scaling iterates are well defined, remain strictly feasible, their objective values decrease, and \(x^k\to x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a bounded feasible set and a unique nondegenerate strictly complementary optimum, classical short-step affine scaling converges from a strictly feasible point to that optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank and the feasible set is bounded.
\(x^*\) is the unique nondegenerate optimum with strictly positive nonbasic reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^k\to x^*\quad\text{and}\quad c^{\mathsf T}x^k\downarrow c^{\mathsf T}x^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Affine-Scaling Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of scaled first-order information at a degenerate boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible sequence \(x^k>0\) converging to \(\bar x\geq0\), let \(D_k=\operatorname{Diag}(x^k)\) and \(P_k=I-D_kA^{\mathsf T}(AD_k^2A^{\mathsf T})^{-1}AD_k\). The affine direction is \(d^k=-D_kP_kD_kc\). If \(\bar x\) is degenerate, then \(D_k\to\bar D\) with \(\bar D\) singular, so \(d^k\to0\) may result from vanishing diagonal factors rather than satisfaction of the unscaled KKT conditions. Consequently, convergence of scaled directions alone does not certify optimality at a degenerate limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Scaling Stalling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonoptimal stagnation caused by summably small affine-scaling steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k\) be strictly feasible affine-scaling iterates. Stalling occurs if some subsequence remains in a compact neighborhood containing no optimal point while \(\alpha_k\lVert d^k\rVert_2\to0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x^k\) converges to a value strictly above the optimum. A sufficient displacement mechanism is \(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_k\lVert d^k\rVert_2<\infty\): then \(x^k\) is Cauchy, and if its limit is nonoptimal, the method has stalled despite nonzero unscaled descent information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine scaling stalls when accepted displacements become summably small and the iterates converge before attaining the optimal objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k\) and \(Ax^k=b\), \(x^k>0\).
\(\sum_k\alpha_k\lVert d^k\rVert_2<\infty\).
The resulting limit \(\bar x\) is feasible but nonoptimal.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonoptimal Affine-Scaling Limit Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaled stationarity at the boundary does not by itself certify LP optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Karmarkar Projective Algorithm with Exact Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projective-scaling iteration and exact optimal-solution recovery for the normalized Karmarkar LP; tolerance-based practical termination does not provide the stated exact certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(r=[n(n-1)]^{-1/2}\), \(L=\lceil1+\log(1+|c_{j\max}|)+\log|\det_{\max}|\rceil\), \(\alpha=(n-1)/(3n)\), \(\mathbf x_0=(1/n,\ldots,1/n)^T\), and \(k=0\). If \(\mathbf c\mathbf x_k<2^{-L}\), use the purification routine to obtain an extreme point \(\bar{\mathbf x}\) with \(\mathbf c\bar{\mathbf x}\leq\mathbf c\mathbf x_k<2^{-L}\) and return it as optimal. Otherwise, define \(D_k=\operatorname{diag}(x_{k1},\ldots,x_{kn})\), \(\mathbf y_0=(1/n,\ldots,1/n)^T\), \(P=\begin{bmatrix}AD_k\\\mathbf1\end{bmatrix}\), \(\bar{\mathbf c}=\mathbf cD_k\), and \(\mathbf c_p=[I-P^T(PP^T)^{-1}P]\bar{\mathbf c}^{\,T}\). Set \(\mathbf y_{\mathrm{new}}=\mathbf y_0-\alpha r\,\mathbf c_p/\|\mathbf c_p\|\) and \(\mathbf x_{k+1}=D_k\mathbf y_{\mathrm{new}}/(\mathbf1D_k\mathbf y_{\mathrm{new}})\), increment \(k\), and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from the uniform feasible point, project the scaled objective onto the null space of the scaled equality system, move in the negative projected-objective direction, and map back projectively. When the objective falls below 2^{-L}, purification returns an optimal extreme point. Stopping instead at a larger practical tolerance is only approximate termination and does not invoke this exact optimality guarantee.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) be the all-ones vector and define \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n_+:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\). The normalized Karmarkar format is
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=0,\ x\in\Delta_n\}.\]
Its canonical initial point is \(q:=e/n\), and the condition \(Aq=0\) is equivalent to \(Ae=0\). In the normalized decision version whose optimal value is known to be \(0\), the inequality \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le\varepsilon\), for \(\varepsilon>0\), is the corresponding additive stopping condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Karmarkar's normalized problem minimizes a linear objective over the intersection of a homogeneous linear subspace with the unit simplex and uses the simplex center as its initial point. In the version with known optimal value zero, an objective value at most epsilon gives an additive stopping condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A linear program is in Karmarkar canonical form when it is written as
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} c^\top x
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
Ax=0,\qquad e^\top x=1,\qquad x\ge 0.
\]
Thus its feasible set is the intersection of \(\ker A\) with the standard simplex. In the stated development, the entries of \(A\) and \(c\) are assumed to be integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Karmarkar canonical form minimizes cᵀx over the intersection of the nullspace of A and the standard simplex. In the stated development, A and c have integer entries.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathbb R^n
A\text{ and }c\text{ have integer entries in the stated development}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{c^\top x:Ax=0,\ e^\top x=1,\ x\ge0\}\text{ is in Karmarkar canonical form.}

children.top_down_role: Homogeneous presentations supporting projective normalization.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(n\ge2\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projective representation of a homogeneous nonnegative cone by a simplex cross-section.

source_refs.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) be the all-ones vector, \(K:=\{z\in\mathbb R^n_+:Az=0\}\), and \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n_+:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\). For nonzero vectors in \(K\), define \(z\sim z'\) if and only if \(z'=\lambda z\) for some \(\lambda>0\). Every nonzero \(z\in K\) has the unique normalized representative
\[x:=\frac{z}{e^{\mathsf T}z}\in K\cap\Delta_n.\]
Conversely, each \(x\in K\cap\Delta_n\) represents the positive ray \(\{\lambda x:\lambda>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative homogeneous feasible cone has a bounded projective representation obtained by selecting the unique point of each positive ray that lies in the unit simplex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact Polyhedral Cross-Section and Positive-Point Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic geometry of the unit-simplex cross-section of a nonnegative homogeneous linear cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{z\in\mathbb R^n_+:Az=0\}\) and \(\Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n_+:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\). If \(K\) contains a nonzero vector, then \(K\cap\Delta_n\) is a nonempty compact polytope. Moreover, \(K\cap\Delta_n\) contains a coordinatewise strictly positive point if and only if \(K\) contains a vector \(z>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simplex section of a nontrivial nonnegative homogeneous linear cone is a nonempty compact polytope and contains a strictly positive point exactly when the cone contains a strictly positive ray.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.
K=\{z\in\mathbb R^n_+:Az=0\}\text{ contains a nonzero vector}.
\Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n_+:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}.

children.title: General-LP Projective Format
children.top_down_role: Representations extending projective scaling to general linear programs.

assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(P:=\{u\in\mathbb R^k_+:Bu=b\}\).
A homogenizing coordinate \(t\ge0\) is introduced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The affine feasible set is recovered from the \(t>0\) part of the homogeneous cone, while its nonzero rays admit simplex normalization and its \(t=0\) points represent recession directions.

notation.meaning: All-ones vector of the required dimension.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous-coordinate representation; it does not by itself produce an equivalent Karmarkar decision instance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P:=\{u\in\mathbb R^k_+:Bu=b\}\), introduce \(t\ge0\) and define the homogeneous cone
\[K:=\{(u,t)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}_+:Bu-bt=0\}.\]
Every \(u\in P\) embeds as \((u,1)\in K\). Conversely, every \((u,t)\in K\) with \(t>0\) determines the feasible point \(u/t\in P\). If \(e\in\mathbb R^{k+1}\) is the all-ones vector, each nonzero \((u,t)\in K\) has the simplex representative
\[\frac{(u,t)}{e^{\mathsf T}(u,t)}.\]
The points \((u,0)\in K\) satisfy \(Bu=0\) and represent recession directions rather than finite feasible points in the affine chart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general standard-form feasible set embeds into a homogeneous cone. Positive homogenizing coordinates recover ordinary feasible points, nonzero rays can be normalized into a simplex, and zero homogenizing coordinates represent recession directions.
knowledge_statements.title: General-LP Projective Format

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degree-Zero Objective on the Finite Projective Chart
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective representation on the t>0 chart of the general-LP homogeneous cone; it does not supply the additional normalized-format data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}v:Bv=b,\ v\ge0\}\) and \(K=\{(u,t)\ge0:Bu-bt=0\}\), define \(F(u,t)=c^{\mathsf T}u/t\) on \(K\cap\{t>0\}\). Then \(F(\lambda u,\lambda t)=F(u,t)\) for every \(\lambda>0\), and, for \(v=u/t\), \(F(u,t)=c^{\mathsf T}v\). Thus the original objective is well defined on finite projective classes, whereas \(c^{\mathsf T}u\) alone is not ray invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the positive homogenizing chart, the original objective is the ray-invariant ratio cᵀu/t; its numerator alone changes under ray scaling.
assumptions_latex: B\in\mathbb R^{m\times k},\quad b\in\mathbb R^m,\quad c\in\mathbb R^k.
K=\{(u,t)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}_+:Bu-bt=0\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(u,t)=c^{\mathsf T}u/t\text{ is constant on positive rays and equals }c^{\mathsf T}(u/t).
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Zero Objective on the Finite Projective Chart

children.title: General-LP Normalization Conversions
children.top_down_role: Transformations connecting general LP instances to normalized projective presentations.

assumptions_latex: The original linear program is converted to an equality system \(Bu=b\), \(u\in\mathbb R^k_+\), using variable splitting and nonnegative slack variables.
A homogenizing coordinate \(t\ge0\) is introduced, and dehomogenization is restricted to \(t>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Variable splitting, slack introduction, homogenization, and ray normalization preserve the finite feasible points under the stated correspondences; a normalized Karmarkar instance additionally requires centering, objective, and projective-boundary data.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative positive and negative parts of a free component.
All-ones vector of the required dimension.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary conversion chain from a general LP toward a homogeneous simplex representation.

source_refs.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replace each free component \(x_j\) by \(x_j^+-x_j^-\), where \(x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0\), and replace each inequality by an equality with a nonnegative slack variable. Write the resulting equality standard form as \(Bu=b\), \(u\in\mathbb R^k_+\). Its homogenization is
\[Bu-bt=0,\qquad (u,t)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}_+.\]
On the chart \(t>0\), dehomogenization maps \((u,t)\) to \(u/t\), and normalization by \(e^{\mathsf T}(u,t)\), where \(e\in\mathbb R^{k+1}\) is the all-ones vector, selects one simplex point from each nonzero positive ray. Variable splitting and slack introduction preserve the corresponding finite feasible points and their original objective values; homogenization preserves those values after dehomogenization. A normalized Karmarkar decision instance additionally requires suitable centering, objective-target, and \(t=0\)-boundary data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable splitting and slacks produce equality standard form, after which homogenization and ray normalization give a projective simplex representation. Equivalence of objectives is interpreted after dehomogenization, and a Karmarkar decision instance still needs centering, target-value, and boundary safeguards.
knowledge_statements.title: General-LP Normalization Conversions

children.title: Format-Preservation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation changes that alter interiority, conditioning, or recoverability.

assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(K:=\{(u,t)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}_+:Bu-bt=0\}\).
Projective normalization identifies nonzero positive scalar multiples.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original finite feasible set corresponds to the \(t>0\) projective classes; classes with \(t=0\) and the absence of a strictly positive normalized point delimit direct use of normalized Karmarkar format.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of interpreting a general-LP homogenization as a normalized Karmarkar instance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[K:=\{(u,t)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}_+:Bu-bt=0\}\]
and let \(\Delta_{k+1}:=\{z\in\mathbb R^{k+1}_+:e^{\mathsf T}z=1\}\), where \(e\) is the all-ones vector. Dehomogenization \((u,t)\mapsto u/t\) gives a correspondence between the projective classes in \(K\cap\{t>0\}\) and the finite feasible points \(\{v\in\mathbb R^k_+:Bv=b\}\). A normalized point in \(K\cap\Delta_{k+1}\) with \(t=0\) represents a recession direction rather than a finite point. If \(K\cap\Delta_{k+1}\) has no strictly positive point, its simplex center is not a feasible interior start. Thus homogenization and simplex normalization alone do not guarantee the finite-chart, strict-interior, or objective-target conditions required by normalized Karmarkar format.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projective normalization represents the original finite feasible points only through classes with positive homogenizing coordinate. Classes at zero homogenizing coordinate and the absence of a strictly positive normalized point prevent direct use of normalized Karmarkar format.
knowledge_statements.title: Format-Preservation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Positivity Does Not Imply Center Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Centering boundary for the homogenized cone before applying normalized Karmarkar format.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{(u,t)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}_+:Bu-bt=0\}\), \(\Delta_{k+1}=\{z\ge0:e^{\mathsf T}z=1\}\), and \(q=e/(k+1)\). The section \(K\cap\Delta_{k+1}\) may contain a point \(z>0\) even though \(q\notin K\). In fact, \(q\in K\) if and only if \(B\mathbf 1_k=b\). Thus existence of a strictly positive normalized feasible point is necessary for an interior projective recentering, but does not by itself make the untransformed simplex center feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous simplex section can have strictly positive feasible points without containing the uniform center. The untransformed center is feasible exactly when B1=b, so a separate recentering transformation may be required.
assumptions_latex: B\in\mathbb R^{m\times k},\quad b\in\mathbb R^m.
K=\{(u,t)\in\mathbb R^{k+1}_+:Bu-bt=0\}.

children.title: Projective Recentering Transformations
children.top_down_role: Projective coordinate changes that relocate the current interior point.

assumptions_latex: \(a\in\operatorname{int}\Delta_n\), so every component of \(a\) is positive.
\(D_a:=\operatorname{diag}(a)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_a\) is a projective automorphism of the simplex interior satisfying \(T_a(a)=e/n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal projective automorphism that moves a chosen interior simplex point to the center.

source_refs.locator: Moving to a Solution from an Interior Point p. 55

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) be the all-ones vector, let \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n_+:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\), and let \(a\in\operatorname{int}\Delta_n\). With \(D_a:=\operatorname{diag}(a)\), define
\[T_a(x):=\frac{D_a^{-1}x}{e^{\mathsf T}D_a^{-1}x},\qquad x\in\operatorname{int}\Delta_n.\]
Then \(T_a\) maps \(\operatorname{int}\Delta_n\) bijectively to itself, satisfies \(T_a(a)=e/n\), and has inverse
\[T_a^{-1}(y)=\frac{D_a y}{e^{\mathsf T}D_a y}.\]
Both formulas extend continuously to \(\Delta_n\), preserve each coordinate face, and preserve projective incidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal scaling followed by normalization is a projective simplex automorphism that maps any selected interior point to the uniform center and has an explicit inverse of the same form.
knowledge_statements.title: Projective Recentering Transformations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composition Law for Simplex Recentering Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Group structure of normalized positive-diagonal projective transformations of the simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_n^\circ:=\{x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\), and define \(T_a(x):=D_a^{-1}x/(e^{\mathsf T}D_a^{-1}x)\). For \(a,b\in\Delta_n^\circ\), set \[a\star b:=\frac{a\circ b}{e^{\mathsf T}(a\circ b)}.\] Then \[T_b\circ T_a=T_{a\star b}.\] The parameter \(q=e/n\) gives the identity map, and \[a^{\star-1}:=\frac{(a_1^{-1},\ldots,a_n^{-1})}{\sum_i a_i^{-1}}\] satisfies \(T_{a^{\star-1}}=T_a^{-1}\). Thus these transformations form an abelian group under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recentering maps compose by normalized componentwise multiplication; the uniform center is the identity parameter and normalized componentwise reciprocals parameterize inverses.
assumptions_latex: \(a,b,x\in\Delta_n^\circ\), so every normalization denominator is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_b\circ T_a=T_{a\star b}\), with identity \(T_{e/n}\) and inverse parameter proportional to the componentwise reciprocal of \(a\).
knowledge_statements.title: Composition Law for Simplex Recentering Maps

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the diagonal projective normalization used in Karmarkar's method and records its inverse on the normalized simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), let \(D=\operatorname{Diag}(d)\). The projective transformation \(T_d:\mathbb R_+^n\setminus\{0\}\to\Sigma_n\) is defined by \[T_d(x)=\frac{nDx}{d^Tx}=\frac{nDx}{e^TDx}.\] It is the composition of the coordinate scaling \(x\mapsto Dx\) and the normalization \(u\mapsto nu/(e^Tu)\), and is nonlinear. It maps \(\Sigma_n\) onto itself, where its inverse is \(T_{d^{-1}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly positive vector d defines a projective map that scales coordinates by d and normalizes their sum to n. The map is nonlinear and restricts to a bijection of the normalized simplex whose inverse uses reciprocal coordinate scaling.
assumptions_latex: d\in\mathbb R_{++}^n
D=\operatorname{Diag}(d)
x\in\mathbb R_+^n\setminus\{0\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_d(x)=\frac{nDx}{d^Tx},\qquad T_d(\Sigma_n)=\Sigma_n,\qquad (T_d|_{\Sigma_n})^{-1}=T_{d^{-1}}|_{\Sigma_n}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) be the all-ones vector, \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n_+:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\), and \(q:=e/n\). Each facet is \(F_i:=\{x\in\Delta_n:x_i=0\}\). The distance within \(H:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\) from \(q\) to every \(F_i\) is
\[r_n:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n(n-1)}}.\]
The largest Euclidean ball in \(H\) centered at \(q\) and contained in \(\Delta_n\) is
\[\{q+d:e^{\mathsf T}d=0,\ \lVert d\rVert_2\le r_n\}.\]
This ball is tangent to each facet at that facet's barycenter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uniform center of the normalized simplex has distance 1/square-root-of-n-times-(n-minus-one) from every facet, and this distance is the radius of its largest centered inscribed ball.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) be the all-ones vector, \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n_+:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\), and \(q:=e/n\). Every vertex \(e_i\) satisfies
\[\lVert e_i-q\rVert_2=R_n,\qquad R_n:=\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n}}.\]
The smallest Euclidean ball in the affine hull \(H:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\), centered at \(q\), and containing \(\Delta_n\) is
\[\{q+d:e^{\mathsf T}d=0,\ \lVert d\rVert_2\le R_n\}.\]
For the inradius \(r_n:=1/\sqrt{n(n-1)}\), the radius ratio is \(R_n/r_n=n-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All vertices of the normalized simplex lie at distance square root of (n-minus-one)/n from the uniform center. This is the radius of the smallest centered ball containing the simplex, and its ratio to the inradius is n minus one.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) be the all-ones vector and \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n_+:e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\). For \(a\in\operatorname{int}\Delta_n\), define \(D_a:=\operatorname{diag}(a)\) and
\[T_a(x):=\frac{D_a^{-1}x}{e^{\mathsf T}D_a^{-1}x}.\]
For every \(x\in\Delta_n\),
\[(T_a(x))_i=\frac{x_i/a_i}{\sum_{j=1}^n x_j/a_j}.\]
Hence \((T_a(x))_i=0\) if and only if \(x_i=0\), so each coordinate face is preserved. For \(x_i,x_j>0\),
\[\frac{(T_a(x))_i}{(T_a(x))_j}\frac{x_j}{x_i}=\frac{a_j}{a_i}.\]
As \(a_{\min}:=\min_i a_i\) approaches \(0\), these coordinate-ratio factors can be arbitrarily large. Therefore no coordinate-ratio distortion bound is uniform over all \(a\in\operatorname{int}\Delta_n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projective recentering preserves every coordinate face, but its rescaling of coordinate ratios can become arbitrarily large as the recentering point approaches the simplex boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Projective Boundary Distortion

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(q:=e/n\) is strictly feasible for \(Ay=0\), \(e^{\mathsf T}y=1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) be the all-ones vector, let \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and define
\[M:=\begin{bmatrix}A\\e^{\mathsf T}\end{bmatrix},\qquad P:=I-M^{\mathsf T}(MM^{\mathsf T})^{-1}M.\]
If the rows of \(M\) are linearly independent, then \(P\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\ker M\). For the linear objective \(g^{\mathsf T}y\), feasible first-order displacements at \(q:=e/n\) satisfy \(Md=0\). If \(Pg\ne0\), the unit feasible direction of greatest instantaneous decrease is
\[d_*:=-\frac{Pg}{\lVert Pg\rVert_2}.\]
The step \(y^+:=q+\alpha d_*\) remains nonnegative for
\[0\le\alpha\le\min_{i:(d_*)_i<0}\frac{q_i}{-(d_*)_i}.\]
If \(Pg=0\), the objective derivative is zero along every feasible first-order direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the recentered simplex point, the objective gradient is orthogonally projected onto the nullspace of the equality and simplex constraints. The negative normalized projection is the steepest feasible unit descent direction, with the step length limited by nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Search-Direction View

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) be arbitrary and define \[P:=I-M^{\mathsf T}(MM^{\mathsf T})^{\dagger}M.\] Then \(P\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\ker M\), including when \(M\) is row-rank deficient. For \(Pg\ne0\), \[d_*=-\frac{Pg}{\lVert Pg\rVert_2}\] uniquely minimizes \(g^{\mathsf T}d\) over \(\{d:Md=0,\ \lVert d\rVert_2=1\}\). If \(Pg=0\), every feasible direction has zero first-order objective derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant transformed constraints can be handled with a pseudoinverse projector; the normalized negative projection remains the steepest feasible descent direction.
assumptions_latex: M\in\mathbb R^{r\times n} may have dependent rows.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational LP data, determinant bounds imply that distinct basic feasible objective values, when finite, are separated by at least \(2^{-p(n,L)}\) for some polynomial \(p\) determined by the encoding convention. Thus an interior method must ordinarily reduce its optimization or certification error to \[\varepsilon\le 2^{-p(n,L)}\] before exact rational recovery is justified. knowledge_statements.title: Polynomiality Interpretation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates iteration, arithmetic, bit, weak-polynomial, and strong-polynomial assertions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An iteration count polynomial in \(n\) and \(L\), or in \(n\) and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), establishes weak polynomiality only after the stopping tolerance is tied to rational input encoding. A unit-cost arithmetic bound does not establish polynomial Turing complexity unless operand bit lengths are controlled. Moreover, a complexity analysis whose operation bound explicitly depends on \(L\) does not by itself establish strong polynomiality: a strongly polynomial analysis requires an arithmetic-operation bound polynomial in the combinatorial dimensions and independent of the numerical magnitudes of the input data, together with polynomial control of intermediate encoding sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical encoding-dependent analysis establishes weak polynomiality, not strong polynomiality; iteration counts, unit-cost arithmetic, and bit complexity remain distinct claims.

Arithmetic precision and exact recovery are included when bit complexity is claimed.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Scaling Reinterpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal feasible affine-scaling reinterpretation of the local scaled projection underlying projective methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal LP \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x>0\}\), let \(x\) be strictly feasible and scale displacements by \(d=Xu\). Feasibility becomes \(AXu=0\), and minimizing the objective derivative over \(\lVert u\rVert_2\le1\) gives the ray \[d_{\mathrm{AS}}=-XP_{AX}Xc.\] It satisfies \(Ad_{\mathrm{AS}}=0\) and is the steepest feasible descent direction for the local norm \(\lVert d\rVert_x=\lVert X^{-1}d\rVert_2\). This supplies a local affine-scaling reinterpretation of the scaled projected geometry used by the projective construction, without asserting equality of finite-step normalizations or trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Locally, the projective construction and affine scaling share a diagonally scaled feasible projection of the cost, without implying identical finite steps or trajectories.

\(A\) has full row rank and \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Scaling Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural commonality of local metrics and projections, without claiming identical algorithms or iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Affine scaling uses the local metric \(X^{-2}\); the logarithmic barrier has Hessian \(\mu X^{-2}\); and primal-dual elimination produces metrics involving \(X^{-1}S\) or its inverse. Each is positive definite when \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), weights coordinates according to their boundary-related scaling, and can become increasingly ill-conditioned when those coordinate scales separate. Each is combined with \(A\) or \(A^T\) to enforce linear feasibility. Therefore these interpretations share a diagonal boundary-sensitive scaling structure followed by projection or Newton correction, although their residuals, centering terms, step lengths, and global trajectories need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine scaling, barrier Newton steps, and primal-dual steps all use positive diagonal boundary-sensitive metrics with linear-constraint projection or correction, though their residuals and trajectories differ.
assumptions_latex: The current primal and dual variables satisfy \(x>0\) and \(s>0\).
Search directions are obtained from a feasible projection or Newton linearization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All three interpretations use positive diagonal boundary scaling followed by enforcement of the linear constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common Local Direction Does Not Determine a Finite Simplex Iterate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary finite-step counterexample to inferring iterate identity from shared projected geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\Delta_3\), let \(q=(1/3,1/3,1/3)\) and \(d=(-1,1,0)/\sqrt2\), so \(e^{\mathsf T}d=0\). Both \(q+(1/12)d\) and \(q+(1/6)d\) lie in \(\operatorname{relint}(\Delta_3)\), use the same feasible tangent direction, and are unequal. Therefore agreement of the local projected direction does not determine the finite iterate unless the step-length and coordinate-mapping rules also agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two methods can use the same feasible simplex direction yet produce different interior iterates through different admissible step lengths.
assumptions_latex: The comparison is made in the normalized simplex with Euclidean tangent geometry.
The two step rules choose the displayed positive step lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q+\tfrac1{12}d\ne q+\tfrac1{6}d,\qquad q+\tfrac1{12}d,q+\tfrac1{6}d\in\operatorname{relint}(\Delta_3).
review_flags: Shows insufficiency of a shared direction, not a complete comparison of named implementations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iterate Equivalence as Conjugacy of Update Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact criterion distinguishing structural reinterpretation from iterate-by-iterate identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:Z\to Z\) and \(G:W\to W\) be deterministic update maps on invariant domains, and let \(\phi:Z\to W\) be a bijective coordinate identification. For initial states \(w_0=\phi(z_0)\), the iterates satisfy \(w_k=\phi(z_k)\) for every \(k\) if and only if \(G(\phi(z))=\phi(F(z))\) for every state \(z\) reachable from \(z_0\). Thus an iterate-equivalence claim must include commuting normalization, objective transformation, metric, step selection, and inverse coordinate mapping; agreement of only a direction or local linear system is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two deterministic algorithms have identical mapped iterates exactly when their update maps commute with the declared coordinate identification on all reachable states.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(G\) are deterministic single-step maps on invariant domains.
\(\phi\) is a bijection between the compared state representations.
The initial states satisfy \(w_0=\phi(z_0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall k,\ w_k=\phi(z_k)\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall z\in\mathcal R(z_0),\ G\circ\phi(z)=\phi\circ F(z)\bigr).

notation.meaning: single-step update maps of the compared algorithms
states reachable from the initial state

Reinterpretation Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on identifying Karmarkar’s projective iteration with later interior-point formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An iterate-by-iterate equivalence between Karmarkar’s projective algorithm and an affine-scaling, logarithmic-barrier, or primal-dual method is valid only after specifying a projective chart, normalization, transformed objective, scaling metric, and step rule. Agreement of search-direction structure or polynomial complexity alone does not imply equality of iterates. In particular, changing the normalization or mapping a projective step back to the original coordinates can change both its direction and length; consequently, an unspecified “reinterpretation” establishes a structural relationship, not an identity of algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projective, affine-scaling, barrier, and primal-dual algorithms may share structure, but their iterates coincide only under an explicit coordinate transformation, normalization, metric, and step rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Structural similarity does not by itself imply iterate-by-iterate algorithmic equivalence.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Barrier Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal logarithmic-barrier path following for equality-form linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linear program \(\min\{c^{T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\), choose \(x^{0}>0\) with \(Ax^{0}=b\), parameters \(\mu_{k}\downarrow0\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At iteration \(k\), compute or approximately track the minimizer \[x(\mu_k)\in\arg\min_{Ax=b,\,x>0}\left(c^{T}x-\mu_k\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log x_i\right).\] Update \(\mu_k\) while retaining strict primal feasibility. For an exact minimizer, there exist \(y(\mu_k)\) and \(s(\mu_k)>0\) satisfying \(A^{T}y+s=c\) and \(X s=\mu_k e\). Stop when \(n\mu_k\le\varepsilon\), and output \(x(\mu_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal barrier method follows minimizers of the logarithmically penalized primal objective through strictly feasible points until the associated duality gap is sufficiently small.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank and the primal feasible region has a strictly feasible point.
The barrier subproblems attain their minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At an exact barrier minimizer, \(x^{T}s=n\mu_k\), so \(n\mu_k\le\varepsilon\) gives an \(\varepsilon\)-duality-gap stopping certificate.

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrix formed from the primal variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Barrier Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual logarithmic-barrier path following for equality-form primal linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the dual program \(\max\{b^{T}y:A^{T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), choose \((y^{0},s^{0})\) with \(A^{T}y^{0}+s^{0}=c\) and \(s^{0}>0\), parameters \(\mu_k\downarrow0\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). At iteration \(k\), compute or track a maximizer \[(y(\mu_k),s(\mu_k))\in\arg\max_{A^{T}y+s=c,\,s>0}\left(b^{T}y+\mu_k\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log s_i\right).\] Retain strict dual feasibility as \(\mu_k\) decreases. The stationarity equations induce \(x(\mu_k)>0\) satisfying \(Ax=b\) and \(X s=\mu_k e\). Stop when \(n\mu_k\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual barrier method follows maximizers of the logarithmically regularized dual objective while maintaining strict dual feasibility and reducing the barrier parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank and the dual feasible region has a strictly feasible point.
The dual barrier subproblems attain their maximizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The induced primal-dual pair satisfies \(x^{T}s=n\mu_k\), yielding an \(\varepsilon\)-gap certificate when \(n\mu_k\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Short-Step Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible short-step tracking in a narrow Euclidean central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=x^{T}s/n\) and fix constants \(0<\beta<1\) and \(0<\eta<1\). Starting from a strictly feasible point satisfying \(\|XSe/\mu-e\|_{2}\le\beta\), set \(\mu^{+}=(1-\eta/\sqrt n)\mu\), solve the feasible primal-dual Newton equations with target \(\mu^{+}\), and take the full Newton step whenever it remains in the same neighborhood. Repeat until \(x^{T}s\le\varepsilon\). For standard admissible constants, the neighborhood is invariant and the method requires \(O(\sqrt n\log((x^{0})^{T}s^{0}/\varepsilon))\) Newton iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Short-step path following makes parameter reductions of order one over square root of dimension, preserving a narrow central neighborhood and attaining the standard polynomial bound.
assumptions_latex: A strictly feasible starting point lies in the prescribed narrow neighborhood.
The fixed constants are chosen within the neighborhood-invariance bounds of the short-step analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration count is \(O\!\left(\sqrt n\log\!\left((x^{0})^{T}s^{0}/\varepsilon\right)\right)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Large Barrier-Parameter Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative distinction between short and large reductions of the complementarity target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the current average complementarity be \(\mu>0\), and write the next target as \(\mu^{+}=(1-\theta)\mu\) with \(0<\theta<1\). The update is large relative to the classical short-step scale when \(\theta\sqrt n\) is not bounded by the small neighborhood-dependent constant required for one-step narrow-neighborhood invariance; in particular, a dimension-independent \(\theta\) is a large update. Such an update does not alone guarantee acceptance of a full Newton step: positivity and membership in the selected neighborhood must be checked after recentering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large update reduces the barrier target by more than the narrow-neighborhood short-step scale; full-step feasibility and centrality therefore require separate verification.
assumptions_latex: \(n\) is the number of complementary variable pairs.
The comparison uses a fixed narrow-neighborhood short-step analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dimension-independent reduction fraction \(\theta\) is asymptotically larger than the classical \(O(n^{-1/2})\) short-step fraction.

source_refs.locator: A General Complexity Theorem for Path-Following Methods p. 61

The cited general complexity section must be inspected, or a specialized full-Newton large-update source supplied, before selecting the exact criterion.

children.title: Full-Newton Neighborhood Regimes
children.top_down_role: Central neighborhoods compatible with full recentering steps.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Newton Neighborhood Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhoods characterized by invariance under an undamped primal-dual Newton correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu=x^{T}s/n\), define the Euclidean centrality residual \(r_c=XSe/\mu-e\) and the neighborhood \[\mathcal N_2(\beta)=\{(x,y,s):Ax=b,\ A^{T}y+s=c,\ x>0,\ s>0,\ \|r_c\|_2\le\beta\}.\] A pair \((\beta,\theta)\), with \(0<\beta<1\) and \(0<\theta<1\), defines a full-Newton neighborhood regime if every point in \(\mathcal N_2(\beta)\), after one full feasible Newton correction to target \((1-\theta)\mu\), remains positive and belongs to \(\mathcal N_2(\beta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-Newton neighborhood regime is a centrality neighborhood and target-reduction pair for which every prescribed undamped Newton correction preserves positivity and neighborhood membership.
assumptions_latex: The feasible primal-dual Newton direction exists uniquely at every point under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full-step invariance means \((x,y,s)\in\mathcal N_2(\beta)\) implies \((x^{+},y^{+},s^{+})\in\mathcal N_2(\beta)\) for the specified target update.

notation.meaning: Euclidean central-path neighborhood of radius beta.
Fractional reduction of the Newton target.

source_refs.locator: The Short-Step Path-Following Algorithm p. 86

children.title: Large-Update Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity architectures associated with substantial barrier-target changes.

assumptions_latex: Every accepted outer update satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-\theta)\mu_k\) for a fixed \(\theta\in(0,1)\).
Each outer update can be recentered within \(r(n,\theta)\) Newton steps while preserving feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first stopping index satisfies \(K\le K_{*}\), and the Newton-step complexity is at most \(r(n,\theta)K_{*}\), where \(K_{*}=\left\lceil\log(n\mu_0/\varepsilon)/[-\log(1-\theta)]\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: First outer-update index at which the target gap condition holds.
Geometric upper bound on the required number of outer updates.
Worst-case Newton recentering steps per outer update.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic outer-update and Newton-work accounting for geometric barrier reductions.

source_refs.locator: A General Complexity Theorem for Path-Following Methods p. 61

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each outer update satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-\theta)\mu_k\), where \(0<\theta<1\), and restoring the prescribed neighborhood requires at most \(r(n,\theta)\) Newton steps. Define \[K_{*}=\left\lceil\frac{\log(n\mu_0/\varepsilon)}{-\log(1-\theta)}\right\rceil.\] Then \(n\mu_{K_{*}}\le\varepsilon\). Consequently, if \(K\) is the first index for which \(n\mu_K\le\varepsilon\), then \(K\le K_{*}\), and the total Newton-step count is at most \(r(n,\theta)K_{*}\). A large update can decrease the number of outer updates, but its overall complexity depends on the recentering cost \(r(n,heta)\); no improved total bound follows from the larger parameter reduction alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric target reductions reach the requested gap after at most a logarithmic number of outer updates, while total work is bounded by this update count times the Newton steps needed to restore centrality after each update.
knowledge_statements.title: Large-Update Complexity Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: A General Complexity Theorem for Path-Following Methods p. 61

children.title: Full-Step Acceptance Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where neighborhood geometry does not support an undamped recentering step.

assumptions_latex: The current vectors satisfy \(x>0\) and \(s>0\).
The Newton direction preserves the linear feasibility equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full-step acceptance is equivalent to \(\alpha_{\mathrm{pos}}>1\) together with satisfaction of the prescribed post-step neighborhood condition.

notation.meaning: Supremal step length allowed by componentwise nonnegativity, without a unit-step cap.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact positivity boundary plus the selected neighborhood test for an undamped Newton step.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a strictly positive primal-dual point and direction \((\Delta x,\Delta s)\), define \[\alpha_{\mathrm{pos}}=\min\left\{\min_{\Delta x_i<0}\frac{-x_i}{\Delta x_i},\min_{\Delta s_i<0}\frac{-s_i}{\Delta s_i}\right\},\] with each empty inner minimum interpreted as \(+\infty\). The undamped step is strictly positive exactly when \(\alpha_{\mathrm{pos}}>1\), equivalently when \(x+\Delta x>0\) and \(s+\Delta s>0\). It is accepted by a neighborhood-based full-step method exactly when these inequalities hold and the updated point satisfies the method's centrality predicate. Equality \(\alpha_{\mathrm{pos}}=1\) is the positivity boundary and does not give a strictly interior full step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full Newton step is acceptable precisely when its uncapped positivity step bound exceeds one and the updated point passes the chosen centrality-neighborhood test.
knowledge_statements.title: Full-Step Acceptance Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

children.title: Adaptive-Update Path Following
children.top_down_role: Methods adapting trajectory progress to observed proximity and local geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Update Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path following with target reduction and step length selected from observed centrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a strictly feasible iterate \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\), compute \(\mu_k=(x^k)^{T}s^k/n\). Choose trial pairs \((\theta,\alpha)\in(0,1)\times(0,1]\), solve the primal-dual Newton equations for target \((1-\theta)\mu_k\), and accept a pair only if the trial point remains positive, satisfies the selected centrality neighborhood, and achieves the required complementarity decrease. Select an accepted pair according to the method’s progress rule, update \((x,y,s)\), and repeat until \(x^{T}s\le\varepsilon\). If no aggressive pair is accepted, reduce \(\theta\) or \(\alpha\); thus progress responds to local geometry rather than a fixed parameter schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive path following chooses target reductions and step lengths from positivity, centrality, and progress tests, retreating to smaller changes when aggressive trials fail.
assumptions_latex: The current iterate is strictly primal-dual feasible.
The trial procedure eventually includes a sufficiently small target reduction and step length that pass the acceptance tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted iterate remains strictly feasible and satisfies the chosen neighborhood condition; termination certifies \(x^{T}s\le\varepsilon\).

source_refs.locator: Path-Following Methods p. 9

children.title: Complexity-Oriented Predictor-Corrector Methods
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood-controlled predictor-corrector families designed for global analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Oriented Predictor-Corrector Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Short-step primal-dual predictor-corrector complexity for feasible standard-form linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal-dual pair
\[\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\},\qquad \max\{b^\top y:A^\top y+s=c,\ s\geq0\}.\]
Let \(n\) be the number of complementary variable pairs and let \(\mu_k=x_k^\top s_k/n\). Suppose a strictly feasible initial iterate with \(\mu_0>0\) is available, every accepted predictor-corrector iterate remains in a fixed short-step neighborhood of the central path, and there is a constant \(\eta\in(0,1)\) such that
\[\mu_{k+1}\leq\left(1-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt n}\right)\mu_k\]
for every accepted iteration. Then, for every \(\varepsilon\in(0,\mu_0)\), an iterate satisfying \(x_k^\top s_k/n\leq\varepsilon\) is obtained in
\[O\!\left(\sqrt n\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\]
iterations. If each iteration uses a constant number of primal-dual Newton solves, the same bound holds for the number of such solves up to a constant factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neighborhood-controlled predictor-corrector method whose accepted iterates reduce average complementarity by a factor of at most 1−η/√n reaches average complementarity ε in O(√n log(μ₀/ε)) iterations; a constant number of Newton solves per iteration gives the same asymptotic solve bound.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, and the primal-dual pair is strictly feasible.
The initial iterate belongs to the prescribed fixed short-step neighborhood and has \(\mu_0>0\).
Every accepted iterate remains in that neighborhood and satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\leq(1-\eta/\sqrt n)\mu_k\) for a fixed \(\eta\in(0,1)\).
Each iteration uses a constant number of primal-dual Newton solves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[N(\varepsilon)=O\!\left(\sqrt n\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right).\]

children.title: Mehrotra Predictor-Corrector Family
children.top_down_role: The practical affine-predictor, centering, and second-order-correction lineage.

knowledge_statements.title: Mehrotra Predictor-Corrector Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-form Mehrotra step with affine prediction, adaptive centering, and second-order correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a strictly feasible iterate \((x,y,s)\), solve the feasible primal-dual Newton equations with complementarity right-hand side \(-XSe\), obtaining \((\Delta x^{\rm aff},\Delta y^{\rm aff},\Delta s^{\rm aff})\). Let \(\alpha_{\rm aff}^{\rm pri}\) and \(\alpha_{\rm aff}^{\rm dual}\) be the largest values in \([0,1]\) for which \(x+\alpha_{\rm aff}^{\rm pri}\Delta x^{\rm aff}\geq0\) and \(s+\alpha_{\rm aff}^{\rm dual}\Delta s^{\rm aff}\geq0\), respectively. Set
\[\mu=\frac{x^\top s}{n},\qquad \mu_{\rm aff}=\frac{(x+\alpha_{\rm aff}^{\rm pri}\Delta x^{\rm aff})^\top(s+\alpha_{\rm aff}^{\rm dual}\Delta s^{\rm aff})}{n},\qquad \sigma=\left(\frac{\mu_{\rm aff}}{\mu}\right)^3.\]
Solve the corrected Newton system with complementarity right-hand side
\[-XSe+\sigma\mu e-\Delta X^{\rm aff}\Delta S^{\rm aff}e.\]
Choose primal and dual fraction-to-the-boundary steps in \((0,1]\) along the corrected direction, update the iterate, and stop when the prescribed primal, dual, and complementarity tolerances hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mehrotra’s method computes an affine-scaling predictor, estimates the attainable complementarity using capped primal and dual boundary steps, chooses centering adaptively, includes a second-order correction, and takes positivity-preserving primal and dual steps.
assumptions_latex: The primal-dual Newton systems are solvable.
A fraction-to-the-boundary parameter in \((0,1)\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next iterate is obtained from the centered, second-order-corrected Newton direction and satisfies \(x^+,s^+>0\).

notation.meaning: capped affine primal and dual boundary steps

children.title: Multiple-Correction Methods
children.top_down_role: Extensions using repeated centrality or complementarity corrections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family-level repeated-correction construction using a componentwise complementarity box and the fixed-iterate Newton matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d^{(0)}=(\Delta x^{(0)},\Delta y^{(0)},\Delta s^{(0)})\) be a predictor-corrector direction at an interior iterate \((x,y,s)\). For an accepted trial length \(\alpha_j>0\), set \(p^{(j)}=(x+\alpha_j\Delta x^{(j)})\circ(s+\alpha_j\Delta s^{(j)})\), \(\bar\mu_j=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}p^{(j)}/n\), and \(q^{(j)}=\Pi_{[\beta_\ell\bar\mu_j,\,\beta_u\bar\mu_j]^n}(p^{(j)})-p^{(j)}\), where \(0<\beta_\ell<1<\beta_u\). Solve \[A\delta x^{(j)}=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\delta y^{(j)}+\delta s^{(j)}=0,\qquad S\delta x^{(j)}+X\delta s^{(j)}=q^{(j)},\] and form \(d^{(j+1)}=d^{(j)}+(\delta x^{(j)},\delta y^{(j)},\delta s^{(j)})\). Retain a correction only when the recomputed trial is strictly positive and improves the prescribed step-length or centrality acceptance test; stop after rejection or a fixed correction limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gondzio-style method repeatedly projects trial complementarity products into a centrality box, solves correction systems with the original Newton matrix, and retains only corrections that improve an interior accepted trial.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
The fixed-iterate primal-dual Newton matrix is solvable.
\(0<\beta_\ell<1<\beta_u\), and a finite correction limit and trial-acceptance test are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each retained outer direction consists of the base predictor-corrector direction plus finitely many feasibility-neutral centrality corrections, and its accepted endpoint remains strictly interior.

notation.meaning: componentwise complementarity products at the j-th trial point
componentwise projection onto a complementarity box
clipped complementarity discrepancy used by correction j
lower and upper relative bounds for the correction box

knowledge_statements.title: Gondzio-Style Multiple Centrality Corrections
Multiple-Correction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predictor-corrector extension applying repeated centrality corrections before accepting one outer iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At an interior primal-dual iterate, compute a predictor direction and a trial step. For \(j=1,\ldots,q\), form the trial complementarity residual
\[r_c^{(j)}=X^{(j)}S^{(j)}e-t^{(j)},\]
where the target \(t^{(j)}>0\) represents the selected centered complementarity products. Solve the primal-dual Newton system with zero primal and dual residual corrections and complementarity right-hand side \(-r_c^{(j)}\); add the resulting correction to the accumulated direction. Accept a fraction-to-the-boundary step only while positivity and the prescribed centrality neighborhood are maintained. Output the accepted iterate, or terminate the correction loop when its residual test, correction limit \(q\), or progress test is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-correction method augments one predictor with several Newton corrections, repeatedly reducing complementarity imbalance while retaining positivity and an accepted centrality neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The current primal and dual variables are strictly positive.
Each correction Newton system is solvable.
The number of corrections \(q\geq1\) and an acceptance neighborhood are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted outer step uses the predictor plus at most \(q\) centrality corrections and remains strictly interior.

children.title: Adaptive Predictor-Corrector Methods
children.top_down_role: Variants with adaptive centering, damping, and target updates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Type-consistent generic predictor-corrector family whose centering, complementarity target, and accepted step lengths depend on current diagnostics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an interior iterate \(z_k=(x_k,y_k,s_k)\), compute an affine predictor \((\Delta x_k^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta y_k^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta s_k^{\mathrm{aff}})\) and diagnostics \(d_k\). An adaptive policy selects a positive target vector \(q_k\in\mathbb R_{++}^{n}\) and trial step controls. Compute a combined predictor-corrector direction satisfying the linearized feasibility equations and \[S_k\Delta x_k+X_k\Delta s_k=q_k-X_kS_ke-\Delta X_k^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta S_k^{\mathrm{aff}}e.\] Choose primal and dual step lengths \(\alpha_k^p,\alpha_k^d\in(0,1]\) from the policy's trial values, shortening them whenever necessary until \(x_k+\alpha_k^p\Delta x_k>0\), \(s_k+\alpha_k^d\Delta s_k>0\), and the prescribed centrality and progress predicates hold. Update the iterate and terminate only when the specified primal-residual, dual-residual, and complementarity tests hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive predictor-corrector method uses affine-predictor diagnostics to choose the complementarity target and step controls, then accepts the corrected direction only after positivity, centrality, and progress tests pass.
assumptions_latex: The predictor and corrector linear systems are solvable.
The adaptive policy includes a safeguarding rule that either finds an accepted positive trial or declares failure without updating the iterate.
The stopping tolerances and centrality and progress predicates are fixed by the particular method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted update is strictly interior and satisfies the method's stated centrality and progress predicates; no convergence rate follows from adaptivity alone.

notation.meaning: Diagnostics computed from the current iterate and affine predictor.
Type-consistent adaptive vector of complementarity targets.
Accepted primal and dual step lengths.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Predictor-Corrector Policy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a diagnostic-dependent parameter policy and a well-defined globally safeguarded predictor-corrector iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Diagnostic-dependent choices of \(q_k\), \(\alpha_k^p\), or \(\alpha_k^d\) do not by themselves imply positivity, neighborhood invariance, complementarity decrease, or convergence. If a trial violates any required endpoint predicate, it must be shortened, recomputed, or rejected. A polynomial iteration bound additionally requires explicit uniform neighborhood and progress invariants of the kind owned by complexity-oriented predictor-corrector methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive parameter selection alone supplies no feasibility, progress, or complexity guarantee; explicit endpoint safeguards and, for complexity, uniform invariants are required.
assumptions_latex: The adaptive policy is otherwise unrestricted beyond producing trial parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without explicit acceptance and progress safeguards, no global convergence or polynomial-complexity conclusion is valid.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptivity Without Safeguards
Adaptive Predictor-Corrector Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic neighborhood-controlled family with iteration-dependent centering, damping, and complementarity targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an interior iterate \(z_k=(x_k,y_k,s_k)\), compute an affine predictor and diagnostics \(d_k\), including predicted boundary step, complementarity reduction, and centrality deviation. A prescribed policy selects \((\sigma_k,\tau_k,t_k)=\Pi(d_k,z_k)\), where \(\sigma_k\in[0,1]\), \(\tau_k\in(0,1)\), and \(t_k>0\). Compute a corrector whose complementarity equation targets \(X_kS_ke=t_k\), combine it with the predictor, and choose the largest step satisfying
\[x_{k+1},s_{k+1}>0,\qquad z_{k+1}\in\mathcal N_k.\]
Apply the damping factor \(\tau_k\), update the policy diagnostics, and stop when primal residual, dual residual, and average complementarity meet their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive predictor-corrector methods choose centering, damping, and complementarity targets from current diagnostics while enforcing positivity and a selected centrality neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The policy \(\Pi\) always returns admissible parameters.
The corrector Newton system is solvable.
The step acceptance rule enforces strict positivity and membership in \(\mathcal N_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is an interior, neighborhood-admissible predictor-corrector step with iteration-dependent parameters.

children.title: Target-Map Representations
children.top_down_role: Mappings that associate current interior states with desired local targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Target-Map Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-feedback representation of complementarity targets in primal-dual target-following methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal Z\) be the set of strictly interior primal-dual states and let \(\mathcal H_k\) contain the information available through iteration \(k\). A target-following rule has a target-map representation if maps
\[T_k:\mathcal H_k\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R_{++}^n\]
are specified and the complementarity target used at iteration \(k\) is
\[t_k=T_k(h_k,z_k).\]
The associated Newton correction replaces the complementarity equation \(X_kS_ke=0\) by its linearization toward \(t_k\). A stationary Markov target map is the special case \(T_k(h,z)=T(z)\), while a scalar central target has \(T_k(h,z)=\mu_k^{\rm tar}e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target-map representation generates each positive complementarity target from the current interior state and optionally the iteration history.
assumptions_latex: \(z_k\in\mathcal Z\) is strictly interior.
Each map \(T_k\) takes values in \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t_k=T_k(h_k,z_k)\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) is the iteration-k complementarity target.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, and the construction is internally plausible, but no source supports this target-map terminology, its history/state domain, or its asserted special cases.

children.title: Target-Sequence Representations
children.top_down_role: Ordered target families used to organize successive interior iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Target-Sequence Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open-loop representation of the targets followed by a primal-dual interior-point trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an interior trajectory \((z_k)_{k\geq0}\), a target-sequence representation is a sequence \((t_k)_{k\geq0}\subset\mathbb R_{++}^n\) such that the iteration-\(k\) complementarity correction is computed from the residual
\[r_{c,k}=X_kS_ke-t_k.\]
Equivalently, the target equation being followed at iteration \(k\) is \(X_kS_ke=t_k\). The sequence is scalar-central when \(t_k=\mu_k^{\rm tar}e\) for positive scalars \(\mu_k^{\rm tar}\), and weighted-central when \(t_k=\mu_k^{\rm tar}w_k\) for weights \(w_k\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) normalized by \(e^\top w_k=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target sequence records the positive complementarity vector pursued at each iteration; scalar and weighted central paths are special cases.
assumptions_latex: Every state \(z_k=(x_k,y_k,s_k)\) is strictly interior.
Every target satisfies \(t_k\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trajectory follows the residual sequence \(r_{c,k}=X_kS_ke-t_k\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but no source establishes this target-sequence convention or the scalar-central and normalized weighted-central specializations.

children.title: Map-to-Sequence Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between state-dependent target maps and prescribed target sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Map-to-Sequence Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trajectory-wise equivalence between feedback target maps and their realized target sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((T_k)_{k\geq0}\) be target maps and let an interior trajectory \((h_k,z_k)_{k\geq0}\) be fixed. Evaluation defines the realized target sequence uniquely by
\[t_k=T_k(h_k,z_k),\qquad k\geq0.\]
Conversely, any prescribed sequence \((t_k)_{k\geq0}\subset\mathbb R_{++}^n\) admits an open-loop map representation, for example \(T_k(h,z)=t_k\) for every admissible \((h,z)\). Thus maps and sequences are equivalent along a fixed trajectory, but a realized sequence does not uniquely determine off-trajectory map values or the responses of a feedback rule to other states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluating target maps along a trajectory produces one target sequence; any positive sequence has constant-in-state maps, but it cannot identify off-trajectory feedback behavior.
assumptions_latex: \(T_k:\mathcal H_k\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R_{++}^n\) for every \(k\).
The history-state trajectory \((h_k,z_k)\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((T_k)\mapsto(t_k)\) is well defined along the trajectory and is generally noninjective; every positive sequence has an open-loop preimage.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind is suitable for the correspondence leaf, and the evaluation argument is formally plausible. A source is still required for the intended target-map framework and the claimed scope of trajectory-wise equivalence.

children.title: Adaptive Target Selection
children.top_down_role: Target organizations responsive to current centrality or optimization progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Target Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: History-dependent selection of positive complementarity targets subject to neighborhood acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At iteration \(k\), compute diagnostics \(d_k\) from the current interior state, residuals, and a predictor trial. Choose a candidate target
\[\widehat t_k=T_k(h_k,z_k,d_k)\in\mathbb R_{++}^n.\]
Project or damp it to an admissible set \(\mathcal A_k(z_k)\), obtaining \(t_k\). Solve the complementarity-corrector equation toward \(t_k\), select a positivity-preserving step, and accept the update only if the new state lies in the prescribed neighborhood. If acceptance fails, replace \(t_k\) by a more central target or shorten the step. Stop when feasibility residuals and \(x_k^\top s_k/n\) satisfy their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive selection uses current diagnostics to propose a positive target, enforces admissibility, and retreats toward centrality or shorter steps when acceptance fails.
assumptions_latex: The admissible set \(\mathcal A_k(z_k)\) is nonempty.
The target selection and fallback rules return strictly positive vectors.
The Newton correction is solvable for every accepted target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted target satisfies \(t_k\in\mathcal A_k(z_k)\subseteq\mathbb R_{++}^n\), and the resulting step preserves the required neighborhood.

notation.meaning: admissible target set at the current state

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the proposal, projection, fallback, and acceptance rules describe an unspecialized template rather than a verifiable algorithm. No source defines the admissible set or supports the claimed procedure.

children.title: Target Admissibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Target choices incompatible with interiority, solvability, or intended progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Target Admissibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local positivity and neighborhood conditions delimiting usable complementarity targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an interior state \(z=(x,y,s)\), a centrality neighborhood \(\mathcal N\), and a fraction-to-the-boundary constant \(\tau\in(0,1)
\). A target \(t\in\mathbb R^n\) is locally admissible if \(t>0\) and the Newton direction \(\Delta z(t)\) toward \(XSe=t\) admits some \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) such that
\[x+\alpha\Delta x(t)\geq(1-\tau)x>0,\qquad s+\alpha\Delta s(t)\geq(1-\tau)s>0,\]
\[z+\alpha\Delta z(t)\in\mathcal N.\]
The admissibility boundary consists of targets for which every feasible step reaches equality in at least one positivity or neighborhood constraint; targets beyond it cannot be accepted under this rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A target is admissible when its Newton correction permits a positive step remaining in the required neighborhood; the boundary occurs when a constraint becomes tight.
assumptions_latex: \(x,s>0\) and \(z\in\mathcal N\).
The Newton direction \(\Delta z(t)\) is defined for candidate targets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\) is admissible exactly when the displayed existential step and neighborhood conditions hold.

notation.meaning: Newton direction generated by target t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the leaf, but the proposed boundary is not reliably characterized: admissibility is existential in the step length, while the claim that every feasible step reaches equality does not follow and depends on the topology and defining inequalities of the neighborhood. A precise sourced definition is required.

children.title: Central-Path Weighting Regimes

children.title: Ordinary Central Target Following
children.top_down_role: Target-following organized around the standard central trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Central Target Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted primal-dual central path for a strictly feasible standard-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal-dual pair
\[\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\},\qquad \max\{b^\top y:A^\top y+s=c,\ s\geq0\},\]
the ordinary central target at parameter \(\mu>0\) is \(t(\mu)=\mu e\). Its central point is any solution of
\[Ax=b,\qquad A^\top y+s=c,\qquad x>0,\quad s>0,\qquad XSe=\mu e.\]
Thus every complementary pair has the same product \(x_is_i=\mu\). Ordinary central target following generates interior iterates near these equations while driving \(\mu\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary central following targets equal complementarity products xᵢsᵢ=μ and decreases the common positive parameter toward zero.
assumptions_latex: The primal-dual feasible region contains a strictly feasible point.
\(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordinary target is \(t(\mu)=\mu e\), equivalently \(x_is_i=\mu\) for every \(i\).

children.title: Weighted Central Target Following
children.top_down_role: Target-following organized around weighted complementarity trajectories.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive coordinate-weighted complementarity targets for strictly feasible standard-form primal-dual central equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) satisfy \(e^\top w=n\). For \(\mu>0\), define the weighted central target by \[t_w(\mu)=\mu w.\] A weighted central point satisfies \[Ax=b,\qquad A^\top y+s=c,\qquad x>0,\quad s>0,\qquad XSe=\mu w.\] Hence \(x_i s_i=\mu w_i\), and the normalization implies \(x^\top s/n=\mu\). Weighted target following keeps iterates near these equations while reducing \(\mu\); choosing \(w=e\) recovers ordinary central following.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted central following prescribes positive relative complementarity weights; normalization makes mu the average complementarity, and equal weights recover the ordinary path.
assumptions_latex: The standard-form primal-dual pair has a strictly feasible point.
\(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) and \(e^\top w=n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(XSe=\mu w\), \(x^\top s/n=\mu\), and \(w=e\) gives ordinary centrality.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Central Target Following

children.title: Fixed-Weight Target Regimes
children.top_down_role: Weighted target families retaining a prescribed weight profile.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted central-target regime with one positive normalized weight profile held fixed across iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) with \(e^\top w=n\). A target sequence is in the fixed-weight regime when \(t_k=\mu_k w\) for positive scalars \(\mu_k\). Equivalently, all target ratios are iteration-invariant: \[\frac{(t_k)_i}{(t_k)_j}=\frac{w_i}{w_j}.\] Moreover, \(e^\top t_k/n=\mu_k\), and \(t_k\to0\) if \(\mu_k\to0\). The all-ones profile \(w=e\) recovers ordinary central targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-weight regime scales one positive normalized profile, preserving every target-component ratio; equal weights recover ordinary targets.
assumptions_latex: \(w\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) and \(e^\top w=n\).
\(\mu_k>0\) for every iteration \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ratios \((t_k)_i/(t_k)_j\) are fixed, \(e^\top t_k/n=\mu_k\), and \(w=e\) yields the ordinary regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Weight Target Regimes

children.title: Adaptive-Weight Target Regimes
children.top_down_role: Weighted target families changing the weight profile across iterations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient regime for translating weighted-centrality control into ordinary componentwise complementarity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(0<\underline w\leq w_i^k\leq\overline w<\infty\) for every \(i,k\), and an iterate satisfies \[\left|\frac{x_i^ks_i^k}{\mu_k w_i^k}-1\right|\leq\theta<1\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] Then \[(1-\theta)\underline w\leq\frac{x_i^ks_i^k}{\mu_k}\leq(1+\theta)\overline w\qquad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] Thus uniform positive weight bounds prevent a weighted-neighborhood guarantee from degenerating relative to ordinary componentwise centrality; adaptivity without such bounds gives no weight-independent implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform lower and upper bounds on adaptive weights convert weighted-centrality control into uniform ordinary complementarity bounds; positivity and normalization alone do not.
assumptions_latex: \(w^k\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) and \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}w^k=n\).
\(0<\underline w\leq w_i^k\leq\overline w<\infty\).
\(0\leq\theta<1\) and \(\mu_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weighted proximity is uniformly comparable with ordinary componentwise complementarity proximity under bounded adaptive weights.

notation.meaning: uniform componentwise lower and upper weight bounds
scalar complementarity scale at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformly Nondegenerate Adaptive Weights

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines adaptation of the component weight profile, distinct from adaptation of only the scalar complementarity parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An adaptive-weight target regime is a sequence \(w^k\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) with \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}w^k=n\), where \(w^{k+1}\) is selected from information available through iteration \(k\). Its next complementarity target is \(\widehat\mu_{k+1}w^{k+1}\), and a feasible Newton direction satisfies \[A\Delta x^k=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y^k+\Delta s^k=0,\qquad S^k\Delta x^k+X^k\Delta s^k=\widehat\mu_{k+1}w^{k+1}-X^kS^k\mathbf1.\] A step is accepted only if the resulting primal and slack variables remain positive and satisfy the prescribed weighted-neighborhood test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive-weight regime changes the normalized positive component-weight profile using currently available information, then follows the resulting weighted complementarity target subject to positivity and weighted-centrality acceptance.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax^k=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y^k+s^k=c\), and \(x^k,s^k>0\).
\(w^{k+1}\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}w^{k+1}=n\), and \(\widehat\mu_{k+1}>0\).
The weight and target are selected before the iteration-k direction is computed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target has total complementarity \(n\widehat\mu_{k+1}\) while its component distribution may vary causally between iterations.

selected scalar level for the next weighted target

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
\(w^k\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) satisfies \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}w^k=n\).

A target-following step is computed from \[A\Delta x=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0,\qquad S^k\Delta x+X^k\Delta s=\mu_{k+1}w^{k+1}-X^kS^k\mathbf1,\] with a step length preserving \(x^{k+1},s^{k+1}>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive weights may respond to the current iterate, but normalization, positive component bounds, and controlled variation keep the weighted central targets nondegenerate.
