children.title: Extreme-Weight Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Weighted regimes where highly uneven targets threaten centrality or stability.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Weight Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits loss of uniform ordinary centrality under degenerate normalized weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), define \[w^{\varepsilon}=\left(\varepsilon,\frac{n-\varepsilon}{n-1},\ldots,\frac{n-\varepsilon}{n-1}\right).\] Then \(w^{\varepsilon}>0\) and \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}w^{\varepsilon}=n\). At any exact weighted-central point satisfying \(x_i s_i=\mu w_i^{\varepsilon}\), \[\min_{1\leq i\leq n}\frac{x_i s_i}{\mu}=\varepsilon\longrightarrow0.\] Consequently, no constant \(\beta>0\) independent of \(\varepsilon\) can ensure \[x_i s_i\geq\beta\frac{x^{\mathsf T}s}{n}\qquad\text{for every }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized positive weight can approach zero, forcing one complementarity product arbitrarily below the average and destroying every weight-independent ordinary-centrality lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Weighted centrality is imposed exactly as \(x_i s_i=\mu w_i\), where \(w>0\) and \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}w=n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Normalization alone gives no weight-independent ordinary-centrality bound when \(\min_i w_i\to0\).

children.title: Pure Centering Targets
children.top_down_role: Targets devoted primarily to restoring proximity to a central trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Pure Centering Targets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal-dual pure-centering Newton target at the current duality measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a strictly feasible primal-dual iterate, the pure-centering target keeps the current average complementarity \(\mu=(x^{\mathsf T}s)/n\) and uses the Newton equations \[A\Delta x=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\mu\mathbf1-Xs.\] It directs the componentwise products toward \(\mu\mathbf1\) and prescribes \[s^{\mathsf T}\Delta x+x^{\mathsf T}\Delta s=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure-centering target directs all complementarity products toward their current average while prescribing zero first-order change in total complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
\(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), and \(\mu=(x^{\mathsf T}s)/n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target redistributes complementarity toward \(\mu\mathbf1\) without prescribing first-order reduction of \(x^{\mathsf T}s\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pure Optimization Targets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal-dual affine-scaling target corresponding to zero centering parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pure optimization target sets the linearized complementarity target to zero. Its feasible primal-dual Newton equations are \[A\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}}+\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=0,\qquad S\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}+X\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=-Xs.\] Equivalently, the primal-dual centering parameter is \(\sigma=0\), and the prescribed first-order change is \[s^{\mathsf T}\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}}+x^{\mathsf T}\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}}=-x^{\mathsf T}s.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pure optimization target sets the linearized complementarity vector to zero and prescribes complete first-order reduction of total complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
\(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) and \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Combined Optimization Targets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard feasible primal-dual centering-plus-progress Newton target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\sigma<1\), the combined target is \(\sigma\mu\mathbf1\), where \(\mu=(x^{\mathsf T}s)/n\). The corresponding feasible Newton equations are \[A\Delta x=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0,\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu\mathbf1-Xs.\] The common positive target recenters the componentwise products, while \(\sigma<1\) prescribes a reduction in their average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combined target directs the complementarity products toward a common positive value below their current average, combining centering with optimization progress.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
\(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), \(0<\sigma<1\), and \(\mu=(x^{\mathsf T}s)/n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Centering-Progress Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies the first-order centering-versus-gap-reduction tradeoff through the centering parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the feasible Newton target \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu\mathbf1-Xs\), \[Dg:=s^{\mathsf T}\Delta x+x^{\mathsf T}\Delta s=-(1-\sigma)x^{\mathsf T}s.\] Thus a full linearized step predicts average complementarity \(\sigma\mu\). The endpoint \(\sigma=0\) prescribes complete first-order reduction and targets the boundary; \(\sigma=1\) prescribes no first-order reduction and targets equal positive products. Values \(0<\sigma<1\) interpolate between these objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The centering parameter trades first-order duality-gap reduction against the positive distance of the complementarity target from the boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
The feasible Newton direction satisfies \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu\mathbf1-Xs\), where \(0\leq\sigma\leq1\) and \(\mu=(x^{\mathsf T}s)/n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smaller \(\sigma\) prescribes greater first-order gap reduction, whereas larger \(\sigma\) places the target farther from the complementarity boundary.

children.title: Incompatible Target Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Incompatible Target Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows algebraic incompatibility of simultaneous exact pure-centering and pure-optimization targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(xs=\mu>0\), pure centering requires \[s\Delta x+x\Delta s=\mu-xs=0,\] while pure optimization requires \[s\Delta x+x\Delta s=-xs=-\mu.\] These requirements cannot hold simultaneously. In addition, a direction satisfying the pure-optimization equation can place a full step on the boundary; for example, \(\Delta x=-x\) and \(\Delta s=0\) give \(x+\Delta x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At positive complementarity, pure centering requires zero linearized product change while pure optimization requires complete linearized decrease, so the two exact targets are incompatible.
assumptions_latex: Consider a scalar complementarity pair \(x>0\), \(s>0\), with \(xs=\mu>0\).
One Newton target is required both to preserve \(xs=\mu\) to first order and to drive its linearization to zero in one full step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\mu>0\), pure centering and pure optimization impose inconsistent complementarity right-hand sides and cannot be the same Newton target.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Newton Target Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal-dual Newton method for a general positive complementarity target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a strictly feasible primal-dual point \((x,y,s)\) and a target \(t\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), solve \[\begin{pmatrix}0&A^{\mathsf T}&I\\ A&0&0\\ S&0&X\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\Delta x\\ \Delta y\\ \Delta s\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\t-Xs\end{pmatrix}.\] Choose \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) such that \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\) and \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\), and set \[(x^+,y^+,s^+)=(x+\alpha\Delta x,\ y+\alpha\Delta y,\ s+\alpha\Delta s).\] Common targets include \(t=\sigma\mu\mathbf1\) and positive weighted variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual method solves one coupled Newton system for primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and a prescribed positive complementarity target, followed by a positivity-preserving step.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x,s>0\).
A target \(t\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) is prescribed, and the displayed Newton system is solvable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled Newton direction preserves both linear feasibility equations and targets componentwise complementarity \(t\) to first order.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonsingularity of the Feasible Primal-Dual Target Newton System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and uniqueness of the coupled feasible Newton direction for an arbitrary complementarity right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank and \(x,s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), then \[K=\begin{pmatrix}0&A^{\mathsf T}&I\\A&0&0\\S&0&X\end{pmatrix}\] is nonsingular. Hence, for every \(r\in\mathbb R^n\), the equations \(A\Delta x=0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0\), and \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=r\) have a unique solution.

\(x>0\) and \(s>0\), with \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) and \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Newton Target Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual logarithmic-barrier Newton orientation in the variable y with slack eliminated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize the negative dual barrier function \[\phi_\mu(y)=-b^{\mathsf T}y-\mu\sum_{i=1}^n\log\bigl(c-A^{\mathsf T}y\bigr)_i.\] With \(s=c-A^{\mathsf T}y>0\), solve \[\mu AS^{-2}A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y=b-\mu AS^{-1}\mathbf1,\qquad \Delta s=-A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y.\] Choose \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) satisfying \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\), and set \[y^+=y+\alpha\Delta y,\qquad s^+=s+\alpha\Delta s.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual orientation applies Newton's method to the negative dual logarithmic-barrier objective after expressing the slack as a function of the dual variable.
assumptions_latex: \(s=c-A^{\mathsf T}y>0\) for some \(y\in\mathbb R^m\).
\(\mu>0\), and \(AS^{-2}A^{\mathsf T}\) is nonsingular on the chosen dual-variable space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update is a dual-oriented Newton step toward a stationary point of the dual logarithmic-barrier subproblem at parameter \(\mu\).

knowledge_statements.title: Newton-Orientation Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence at a common barrier parameter under strict primal-dual feasibility and well-defined reduced-system eliminations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a common parameter \(\mu>0\), the primal and dual logarithmic-barrier optimality conditions are the central equations \[Ax=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\qquad Xs=\mu\mathbf1,\qquad x,s>0.\] Linearizing these equations gives the primal-dual Newton system. Under the nonsingularity assumptions required for the relevant eliminations, eliminating the dual increments produces the primal reduced Newton system, while eliminating the primal increment produces the dual reduced Newton system. Thus the three orientations represent Newton linearizations of the same parameterized central equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a common barrier parameter, the primal and dual barrier conditions coincide with the primal-dual central equations, and valid variable elimination yields the corresponding one-sided Newton systems.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(\mu>0\), and strictly feasible primal and dual points exist.
The primal and dual reduced Newton systems satisfy the nonsingularity conditions needed for their stated eliminations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal, dual, and primal-dual Newton orientations represent the same central equations whenever the corresponding reduced-system eliminations are well defined.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Feasibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates domain feasibility of a one-sided Newton system from existence of a finite central target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal barrier requires \(x>0\) with \(Ax=b\), whereas a dual barrier requires \(y,s\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\) and \(s>0\). These are distinct requirements, and one-sided strict feasibility alone does not ensure a finite barrier target. For example, \[\min_{x>0}-x\] is strictly feasible but unbounded below. Its dual slack condition would require \(s=-1\geq0\), which is impossible, and for every \(\mu>0\) its primal barrier objective \(-x-\mu\log x\) is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict feasibility on one side neither supplies feasibility on the opposite side nor guarantees that a finite central target exists.
assumptions_latex: The primal LP is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), with dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\).
A one-sided barrier orientation is formed only on its own strictly feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility on one side alone does not ensure that its barrier target exists or converges to a finite LP optimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a strictly primal-dual feasible point \((x,y,s)\), weak duality gives \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts>0\). The primal-dual potential is \[\Phi_{\rho}^{PD}(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(x_is_i).\] Equivalently, with \(\mu=x^Ts/n\), it is an additive constant plus \((\rho-n)\log\mu-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(x_is_i/\mu)\), separating gap progress from complementarity balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual potential combines logarithmic duality-gap reduction with a barrier term penalizing unequal or vanishing complementarity products.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic AM-GM structure of the standard primal-dual logarithmic potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=x^{\mathsf T}s>0\), \(\mu=g/n\), and \(q_i=x_is_i/\mu\). Then \(\sum_iq_i=n\) and \[\Phi_{\rho}^{PD}(x,s)=(\rho-n)\log g+n\log n+D(q),\qquad D(q)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log q_i.\] Moreover, \(D(q)\geq0\), with equality if and only if \(q_i=1\) for every \(i\). Consequently, \[\Phi_{\rho}^{PD}(x,s)\geq(\rho-n)\log(x^{\mathsf T}s)+n\log n,\] with equality exactly when all complementarity products equal \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual potential is a weighted log-gap plus a nonnegative dispersion term that vanishes exactly at uniform complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \rho>n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(q)\geq0,\qquad D(q)=0\Longleftrightarrow x_is_i=(x^{\mathsf T}s)/n\ \forall i.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual potential function and its domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the logarithmic primal-dual potential on strictly feasible LP primal-dual pairs and relates it to the primal potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\rho>n\), the primal-dual potential function is
\[
\Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i s_i).
\]
Its domain is
\[
\operatorname{dom}(\Phi_\rho)=\{(x,s):\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\text{ such that }(x,\lambda,s)\in\mathcal F^o\}.
\]
For such a primal-dual feasible triple, \(x^Ts=c^Tx-b^T\lambda\); hence the function is related to the primal potential by choosing the dual lower bound \(Z=b^T\lambda\) and including logarithmic barrier terms for the dual slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For rho greater than n, the primal-dual potential equals rho times the logarithm of the duality gap x transpose s, minus the sum of the logarithms of the products x_i s_i. Its domain consists of pairs (x,s) that can be extended by some lambda to a strictly feasible primal-dual triple. The feasible-point identity x transpose s equals c transpose x minus b transpose lambda relates this function to the primal potential, with added barrier terms for the dual slacks.
assumptions_latex: \rho>n
\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\ (x,\lambda,s)\in\mathcal F^o
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i s_i),\qquad \operatorname{dom}(\Phi_\rho)=\{(x,s):\exists\lambda\in\mathbb R^m,\ (x,\lambda,s)\in\mathcal F^o\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-Dual Potential Reduction and Its Convergence Mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded potential properties and conservative parameter regime for feasible primal-dual LP potential-reduction methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x,\lambda,s)\in\mathcal F^o\) and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\). A primal-dual potential \(\Phi\) is required to satisfy \[\Phi\to+\infty\quad\text{if }x_i s_i\to0\text{ for some }i\text{ while }\mu\not\to0,\] and \[\Phi\to-\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (x,\lambda,s)\to\Omega.\] One such logarithmic potential is \[\Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i s_i),\qquad \rho>n.\] Potential-reduction iterations compute primal-dual directions with \(\sigma_k\in(0,1)\) and select an interior step length \(\alpha_k\) to reduce \(\Phi_\rho\). With \(\sigma_k=n/(n+\sqrt n)\) and the corresponding conservative step selection, a fixed positive reduction in \(\Phi_\rho\) is guaranteed at every iteration. Consequently \(\Phi_\rho\to-\infty\) and the iterates approach \(\Omega\). Adaptive or heuristic choices of \(\sigma_k\) and \(\alpha_k\) retain this conclusion if their achieved potential reduction is at least the conservative theoretical reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The potential grows without bound if one complementarity product approaches zero while average complementarity does not, preventing isolated movement toward the orthant boundary. It tends to minus infinity exactly as the iterates approach the solution set. For the displayed potential with rho greater than n, the fixed centering value n divided by n plus square root of n, together with the conservative step selection, guarantees a fixed potential decrease per iteration and hence convergence. Adaptive choices retain the conclusion when they achieve at least the conservative decrease.
assumptions_latex: \((x_k,\lambda_k,s_k)\in\mathcal F^o\) and \(\mu_k=x_k^Ts_k/n\).
The primal-dual direction uses \(\sigma_k\in(0,1)\), and \(\alpha_k\) keeps the accepted iterate in the interior domain of \(\Phi_\rho\).
For the conservative guarantee, \(\sigma_k=n/(n+\sqrt n)\) and the step length realizes the associated theoretical potential reduction.
For adaptive or heuristic parameters, the achieved reduction in \(\Phi_\rho\) is no smaller than the conservative theoretical reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniform positive per-iteration reduction implies \(\Phi_\rho(x_k,s_k)\to-\infty\), and hence \(\operatorname{dist}((x_k,\lambda_k,s_k),\Omega)\to0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Tanabe–Todd–Ye potential and the progress-to-convergence mechanism for strictly feasible primal-dual potential-reduction methods for linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((x,\lambda,s)\in\mathcal F^o\), let \(\mu=x^Ts/n\) and, for \(\rho>n\), define \(\Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^Ts)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_is_i)\). The potential tends to \(+\infty\) if some \(x_is_i\to0\) while \(\mu\neq0\), and tends to \(-\infty\) if and only if \((x,\lambda,s)\) approaches the primal-dual solution set \(\Omega\). Potential-reduction methods compute a primal-dual direction using \(\sigma_k\in(0,1)\) and choose \(\alpha_k\) to approximately minimize \(\Phi_\rho\) along that direction. If the iterates remain in \(\mathcal F^o\) and each iteration achieves a fixed positive reduction in \(\Phi_\rho\), then \(\Phi_\rho\to-\infty\) and the iterates approach \(\Omega\). Adaptive choices have the same conclusion when they achieve at least the reduction guaranteed by the standard choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For strictly feasible primal-dual points, the Tanabe–Todd–Ye potential uses the duality product and the componentwise complementarity products, with rho greater than n. It grows without bound when one complementarity product approaches zero while average complementarity remains nonzero, and it decreases without bound exactly when the iterates approach the primal-dual solution set. The method computes a direction with a centering parameter between zero and one and approximately minimizes the potential along that direction. A fixed positive decrease at every iteration forces convergence to the solution set; adaptive choices retain the guarantee if they produce at least the standard decrease.

Select \(\alpha_k>0\) so that \(x^k+\alpha_k\Delta x^k>0\), \(s^k+\alpha_k\Delta s^k>0\), and \(\Phi(x^k+\alpha_k\Delta x^k,s^k+\alpha_k\Delta s^k)<\Phi(x^k,s^k)\). Set \((x^{k+1},y^{k+1},s^{k+1})=(x^k,y^k,s^k)+\alpha_k(\Delta x^k,\Delta y^k,\Delta s^k)\), and return the first iterate satisfying \((x^k)^Ts^k\leq\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Stopping Certificate for Feasible Potential Reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal or dual update selected by the norm of a projected potential direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with primal- and dual-feasible \(x^0>0\), \(s^0>0\), and \(p^0\). At iteration \(k\), stop if \((s^k)^{\top}x^k<\epsilon\). Otherwise set \[X_k=\operatorname{diag}(x_1^k,\ldots,x_n^k),\qquad \bar A^k=(AX_k)^{\top}(AX_k^2A^{\top})^{-1}AX_k,\] \[u^k=(I-\bar A^k)\left(\frac{q}{(s^k)^{\top}x^k}X_ks^k-e\right),\qquad d^k=-\beta X_ku^k/\lVert u^k\rVert.\] If \(\lVert u^k\rVert\geq\gamma\), set \[x^{k+1}=x^k+d^k,\qquad s^{k+1}=s^k,\qquad p^{k+1}=p^k.\] If \(\lVert u^k\rVert<\gamma\), set \[x^{k+1}=x^k,\qquad s^{k+1}=\frac{(s^k)^{\top}x^k}{q}X_k^{-1}(u^k+e),\] \[p^{k+1}=p^k+(AX_k^2A^{\top})^{-1}AX_k\left(X_ks^k-\frac{(s^k)^{\top}x^k}{q}e\right).\] Increment \(k\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from strictly positive primal- and dual-feasible iterates and stop when the duality gap is below ε. Compute the scaled projected direction u; update only x when its norm is at least γ, and otherwise update the dual multiplier and slack, then repeat.
assumptions_latex: x^0>0\text{ is primal feasible}
(p^0,s^0)\text{ is dual feasible with }s^0>0
\epsilon>0
\text{the displayed inverses and updates are well-defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Use the primal update when }\lVert u^k\rVert\geq\gamma\text{ and the dual update when }\lVert u^k\rVert<\gamma\text{, stopping when }(s^k)^{\top}x^k<\epsilon.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted steps preserve \(x,s>0\) and strictly reduce a merit function that accounts for complementarity, primal infeasibility, and dual infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-augmented potential reduction for infeasible positive iterates.

source_refs.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \((x^0,y^0,s^0)\) with \(x^0,s^0>0\). At iteration \(k\), choose a primal-dual Newton or descent direction for \(M(x,y,s)\), whose terms penalize \((x^Ts)\), \(\|r_p(x)\|\), and \(\|r_d(y,s)\|\). Choose \(\alpha_k>0\) so that \(x^{k+1},s^{k+1}>0\) and \(M(x^{k+1},y^{k+1},s^{k+1})<M(x^k,y^k,s^k)\). Stop when \(x^Ts\leq\varepsilon_c\), \(\|r_p\|\leq\varepsilon_p\), and \(\|r_d\|\leq\varepsilon_d\); output the resulting approximate primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible method keeps primal and dual variables positive while reducing a merit function containing complementarity and both feasibility residuals.
knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible Potential Reduction

children.title: Centrality Regimes in Potential Reduction
children.top_down_role: The distinction between explicit neighborhood control and centrality induced by potential progress.

assumptions_latex: \(n\geq2\), \(x,s\in\mathbb{R}^n_{++}\), and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\).
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define \(t_i=x_is_i/\mu\).
The logarithmic balance term satisfies \(B(x,s)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log t_i\leq K\) for some \(K\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every normalized complementarity product satisfies \(e^{-K}((n-1)/n)^{n-1}\leq t_i<n\), so a uniform bound on \(B\) induces a uniform centrality condition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit centrality obtained from bounded logarithmic complementarity imbalance for LPs with at least two complementarity pairs.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The normalized products satisfy \(t_i>0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n t_i=n\). If \[B(x,s)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log t_i\leq K,\] then, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \[e^{-K}\left(\frac{n-1}{n}\right)^{n-1}\leq t_i<n.\] Thus prescribed central-path neighborhoods impose centrality explicitly, whereas a uniform bound on \(B\) imposes an implicit centrality regime through potential control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit neighborhoods impose centrality directly, while bounded logarithmic imbalance forces every complementarity product to remain uniformly bounded below relative to the average.
knowledge_statements.title: Centrality Regimes in Potential Reduction

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Logarithmic Imbalance Characterizes Exact Complementarity Centrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-centrality equality case in normalized complementarity coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t_i=x_is_i/\mu>0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n t_i=n\), let \(B=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log t_i\). Then \[B\geq0,\qquad B=0\iff t_1=\cdots=t_n=1\iff x_is_i=\mu\ \text{for every }i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logarithmic complementarity imbalance is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when all complementarity products equal their mean.
assumptions_latex: \(x,s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(\mu=x^Ts/n\), and \(t_i=x_is_i/\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\geq0,\qquad B=0\iff x_is_i=\mu\ \text{for every }i.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Logarithmic Imbalance Characterizes Exact Complementarity Centrality

children.title: Potential-Reduction Analysis Architecture
children.top_down_role: The source-supported progression from local potential models to uniform progress and polynomial complexity.

children.title: Local Potential Models
children.top_down_role: Local approximation families used to assess potential progress.

assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) is open and convex, \(z\in U\), and \(\Phi:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable.
The Hessian is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(U\) in the Euclidean operator norm: \(\|\nabla^2\Phi(u)-\nabla^2\Phi(v)\|_2\leq L\|u-v\|_2\) for all \(u,v\in U\).
The direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and step \(\alpha\geq0\) satisfy \(z+t d\in U\) for every \(t\in[0,\alpha]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quadratic model \(m_z(\alpha d)\) approximates \(\Phi(z+\alpha d)\) with absolute error at most \(L\alpha^3\|d\|_2^3/6\).

notation.meaning: quadratic local potential model at z

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order local representation of potential change with a Euclidean cubic remainder allowance.

source_refs.locator: Moving to a Solution from an Interior Point p. 55

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h\in\mathbb{R}^p\), define \[m_z(h)=\Phi(z)+\nabla\Phi(z)^Th+\frac12h^T\nabla^2\Phi(z)h.\] For every admissible \(d\) and \(\alpha\), \[\left|\Phi(z+\alpha d)-m_z(\alpha d)\right|\leq\frac{L\alpha^3}{6}\|d\|_2^3.\] This remainder allowance can be combined with predicted model decrease when testing a potential-reduction step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic Taylor model evaluated at the trial displacement estimates potential change, and a cubic remainder bound controls its error.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Potential Models

source_witnesses.locator: Moving to a Solution from an Interior Point p. 55

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local certificate converting predicted quadratic-model decrease into verified potential decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the accepted local-model assumptions, let \(r(\alpha,d)=L\alpha^3\|d\|_2^3/6\). If \[\nabla\Phi(z)^{\mathsf T}(\alpha d)+\frac12(\alpha d)^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2\Phi(z)(\alpha d)+r(\alpha,d)\le-\delta,\] then \(\Phi(z+\alpha d)\le\Phi(z)-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trial step is certified to decrease the potential by at least delta when its predicted quadratic change plus the cubic error allowance is at most minus delta.
assumptions_latex: The Hessian is L-Lipschitz on the trial segment.
The entire segment from z to z+alpha d lies in the potential domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta m_z(\alpha d)+\frac{L\alpha^3}{6}\|d\|_2^3\le-\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\Phi(z+\alpha d)\le\Phi(z)-\delta.
knowledge_statements.title: Cubic-Remainder Sufficient-Decrease Test

children.title: Uniform Potential-Progress Results
children.top_down_role: Result families establishing iteration-independent potential decrease.

assumptions_latex: A potential-reduction method generates iterates \(z^k\) and values \(\Phi_k=\Phi(z^k)\).
There is a constant \(\delta>0\), independent of \(k\), such that every nonterminal iteration satisfies \(\Phi_{k+1}\leq\Phi_k-\delta\).
The method terminates whenever \(\Phi_k\leq\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number \(N\) of nonterminal iterations is at most \(\max\{0,\lceil(\Phi_0-\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}})/\delta\rceil\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration bound obtained from an iteration-independent potential decrease.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\Phi_k=\Phi(z^k)\) and every nonterminal iteration satisfies \(\Phi_{k+1}\leq\Phi_k-\delta\) for a constant \(\delta>0\) independent of \(k\). If the method terminates whenever \(\Phi_k\leq\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}\), then its number \(N\) of nonterminal iterations satisfies \[N\leq\max\left\{0,\left\lceil\frac{\Phi_0-\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}}{\delta}\right\rceil\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform positive potential decrease bounds the number of nonterminal iterations by the nonnegative ceiling of the initial potential range divided by the per-step decrease.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Potential-Progress Results

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

children.title: Potential Parameter-Step Compatibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Parameter regimes controlling convergence, centrality, and complexity.

children.title: Fixed Potential-Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Potential-reduction families using a fixed parameter choice.

assumptions_latex: \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) is the potential domain, \(\mathcal P\) is the parameter set, and \(\Phi_\rho:Z\to\mathbb{R}\) is defined for every \(\rho\in\mathcal P\).

For \(z\in Z\) and \(\rho\in\mathcal P\), \(\mathcal D(z,\rho)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) is the set of admissible directions and \(\mathcal A(z,d,\rho)\subseteq(0,\infty)\) is the set of admissible step lengths.
A parameter \(\bar\rho\in\mathcal P\) is selected before the first iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is fixed-parameter exactly when \(\rho_k=\bar\rho\) for every iteration \(k\); directions and steps may vary while the potential parameter does not.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential parameter held constant while admissible directions and step lengths may vary.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method is in a fixed potential-parameter regime if \(\rho_k=\bar\rho\) for every iteration \(k\). At iteration \(k\), it may select \(d^k\in\mathcal D(z^k,\bar\rho)\) and \(\alpha_k\in\mathcal A(z^k,d^k,\bar\rho)\), set \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\alpha_kd^k\in Z\), and require \(\Phi_{\bar\rho}(z^{k+1})\leq\Phi_{\bar\rho}(z^k)-\delta_k\) for a prescribed or computed \(\delta_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed regime uses one potential parameter at every iteration while allowing the direction, step length, and achieved decrease to vary.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Potential-Parameter Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

children.title: Adaptive Potential-Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Potential-reduction families changing parameters in response to current state.

assumptions_latex: \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) is the potential domain, \(\mathcal P\) is the parameter set, and \(\Phi_\rho:Z\to\mathbb{R}\) is defined for every \(\rho\in\mathcal P\).
At iteration \(k\), \(\mathcal H_k\) denotes the information available through that iteration, and \(R_k\) maps \(\mathcal H_k\) into \(\mathcal P\).
For each selected parameter, the method chooses an update that remains in \(Z\) and satisfies its stated progress test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is adaptive when \(\rho_k=R_k(\mathcal H_k)\) may vary with \(k\); decrease for \(\Phi_{\rho_k}\) within iteration \(k\) does not by itself imply monotonicity across different parameter values.

notation.meaning: potential parameter selected at iteration k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential parameter selected online, with progress assessed using the potential chosen for the current iteration.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method is in an adaptive potential-parameter regime if \(\rho_k=R_k(\mathcal H_k)\in\mathcal P\), where \(R_k\) uses only information in \(\mathcal H_k\). After selecting \(\rho_k\), the method chooses \(d^k\in\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(\alpha_k>0\) so that \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\alpha_kd^k\in Z\) and \[\Phi_{\rho_k}(z^{k+1})\leq\Phi_{\rho_k}(z^k)-\delta_k\] for the required \(\delta_k>0\). If \(\rho_{k+1}\neq\rho_k\), this inequality alone makes no comparison between \(\Phi_{\rho_{k+1}}(z^{k+1})\) and \(\Phi_{\rho_k}(z^k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive regime selects the current potential parameter from available history and tests progress using that parameter; changing parameters requires a separate cross-iteration comparison.
knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Potential-Parameter Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact accounting needed to compare progress when the potential parameter changes between iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\Phi_{\rho_k}(z^{k+1})\le\Phi_{\rho_k}(z^k)-\delta_k\), and define \[J_k=\Phi_{\rho_{k+1}}(z^{k+1})-\Phi_{\rho_k}(z^{k+1}).\] Then \[\Phi_{\rho_{k+1}}(z^{k+1})-\Phi_{\rho_k}(z^k)\le-\delta_k+J_k.\] Consequently, a bound \(J_k\le\eta_k\) yields corrected decrease at least \(\delta_k-\eta_k\); without control of \(J_k\), within-parameter decrease cannot be telescoped across iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the potential parameter introduces a jump term that must be bounded before within-iteration decreases can be combined globally.
assumptions_latex: Both potentials in the definition of J_k are finite at z^{k+1}.
The selected step satisfies the within-parameter decrease test with \(\delta_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi_{\rho_{k+1}}(z^{k+1})-\Phi_{\rho_k}(z^k)\le-\delta_k+J_k.

notation.meaning: potential-value jump caused solely by changing the parameter at z^{k+1}
an upper bound on the cross-parameter jump

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Parameter Jump Accounting

children.title: Short-Step Potential Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conservative steps emphasizing uniform centrality or progress control.

assumptions_latex: \(n\geq1\), \(x,s\in\mathbb{R}^n_{++}\), \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(e\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is the all-ones vector, and \(\mu=x^Ts/n\).
A radius \(\theta\in(0,1)\) is fixed independently of the iteration.
Each accepted update is required to remain positive and to satisfy the prescribed potential-decrease test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A short-step potential regime maintains \(\|Xs/\mu-e\|_2\leq\theta\) at every iterate and accepts only steps certified to preserve this fixed narrow neighborhood and decrease the potential.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Narrow-neighborhood potential regime whose accepted steps preserve a fixed Euclidean complementarity neighborhood.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\theta\in(0,1)\). A primal-dual potential method operates in this short-step regime when every iterate satisfies \[\left\|\frac{Xs}{\mu}-e\right\|_2\leq\theta,\qquad \mu=\frac{x^Ts}{n},\] and each accepted step preserves positivity, the same inequality, and the required potential decrease. The exact numerical step bound is method-dependent and is not part of this regime definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A short-step potential regime keeps normalized complementarity in a fixed narrow Euclidean neighborhood and accepts only steps that preserve that neighborhood, positivity, and potential decrease.
knowledge_statements.title: Short-Step Potential Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

children.title: Long-Step Potential Regimes
children.top_down_role: More aggressive steps permitted by broader potential-based safeguards.

assumptions_latex: At iteration \(k\), \(x^k,s^k\in\mathbb{R}^n_{++}\) and \((\Delta x^k,\Delta s^k)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\) are given.
The positivity limit is \(\alpha_{\max}^k=\sup\{\alpha>0:x^k+\alpha\Delta x^k>0,\ s^k+\alpha\Delta s^k>0\}\), and \(0<\alpha_{\max}^k<\infty\).
A specified wide-centrality condition and a sufficient-potential-decrease test are imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A long-step regime allows steps up to a fixed fraction \(\tau\in(0,1)\) of \(\alpha_{[1;1Hmax}^k\), subject to positivity, the specified wide-centrality condition, and sufficient potential decrease.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wide-centrality regime allowing aggressive fraction-to-boundary steps, with the exact wide condition supplied by the particular method.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\tau\in(0,1)\). A potential method operates in this long-step regime when it imposes a specified wide-centrality condition rather than a fixed narrow neighborhood and chooses \[0<\alpha_k\leq\tau\alpha_{\max}^k.\] An accepted step must preserve positivity and the wide-centrality condition and must satisfy the method's sufficient-potential-decrease test. Choosing \(\tau\) close to \(1\) permits an aggressive fixed fraction of the positivity-limiting step but does not make \(\alpha_k\) equal to \(\alpha_{[1;1Hmax}^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A long-step regime permits an aggressive fixed fraction of the positivity-limiting step while enforcing a specified wide-centrality condition and sufficient potential decrease.
knowledge_statements.title: Long-Step Potential Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Potential-Reduction Algorithm p. 67

children.title: Parameter-Step Compatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Combinations of potential parameters or step sizes that lose guaranteed progress.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is a potential-parameter set, \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) is open, and \(\Phi_\rho:Z\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable for every \(\rho\in P\).
At \(z\in Z\), a direction \(d\in\mathbb{R}^p\) is fixed, and \(\alpha_{\max}>0\) is such that \(z+td\in Z\) for all \(t\in[0,\alpha_{\max})\).
For each \(\rho\in P\), the Hessian of \(\Phi_\rho\) is \(L_\rho\)-Lipschitz along the trial segment in the Euclidean operator norm.
A target decrease \(\delta>0\) and an admissible centrality set \(C\subseteq Z\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certification boundary is the relative boundary in \(P\) of the parameter set for which at least one positive domain-preserving and centrality-preserving step satisfies the cubic sufficient-decrease test.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cubic-Certificate Failure Does Not Imply Failure of Actual Decrease
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp logical boundary of the local cubic sufficient-decrease certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z=(-2,2)\), \(z=0\), \(d=1\), \(C=Z\), \(\alpha_{\max}=1\), and \(\Phi_\rho(t)=-t^4\). On \([0,1]\), take the valid Hessian Lipschitz constant \(L_\rho=24\). For \(0<\delta<1\), the seed's cubic test has left side \(4\alpha^3>0\), so \(S(\rho)=\varnothing\); nevertheless, every \(\alpha\in[\delta^{1/4},1)\) satisfies \(\Phi_\rho(z+\alpha d)-\Phi_\rho(z)=-\alpha^4\leq-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conservative cubic certificate can reject every step even though actual trial steps attain the target decrease; this is a certification boundary, not an impossibility boundary.

children.title: Potential-Reduction Complexity Results
children.top_down_role: Dimension-, encoding-, and accuracy-sensitive polynomial guarantee families.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Reduction Complexity Results
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration bound for the standard primal-dual logarithmic potential with parameter \(\rho=n+\sqrt n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For strictly feasible primal-dual iterates define \(g_k=x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k\) and \(\Phi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^{\mathsf T}s)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i s_i)\), where \(\rho=n+\sqrt n\). If every iteration satisfies \(\Phi_\rho(x_{k+1},s_{k+1})\leq\Phi_\rho(x_k,s_k)-\delta\) for a constant \(\delta>0\), then \(g_K\leq\varepsilon\) after at most
\[
K=\left\lceil\frac{\max\{0,\Phi_\rho(x_0,s_0)-n\log n-\sqrt n\log\varepsilon\}}{\delta}\right\rceil
\]
iterations. Consequently, if rational input has encoding length \(L\) and \(\Phi_\rho(x_0,s_0)-n\log n=O(\sqrt nL)\), the iteration count is \(O(\sqrt n(L+\log(1/\varepsilon)))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform decrease of the standard potential gives a square-root-dimension polynomial iteration bound, with explicit dependence on input encoding and target duality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k>0,\ s_k>0\) are primal-dual feasible for every \(k\).
\(0<\varepsilon<1\) and \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K=O(\sqrt n(L+\log(1/\varepsilon)))\) under the stated encoding bound.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the rational LP data

\text{condition (4.8) holds for some }\delta>0
\epsilon\in(0,1)
\mu_k=\frac{(x^k)^Ts^k}{n}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K=\left\lbrack\frac{\Phi_\rho(x^0,s^0)}{\delta}+\frac{\rho-n}{\delta}|\log\epsilon|\right\rbrack\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mu_k\leq\epsilon\ \text{for all }k\geq K.

children.title: Potential-Path-Following Correspondence
children.top_down_role: The overlap and separation between potential-based progress and neighborhood-based trajectory control.

children.title: Implicit Path Control by Potentials
children.top_down_role: Path-adjacent behavior induced without explicit neighborhood maintenance.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Path Control by Potentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate centrality control induced by the product-dispersion term of a primal-dual potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g=x^{\mathsf T}s\), \(\mu=g/n\), and \(q_i=x_i s_i/\mu\), so that \(q_i>0\) and \(\sum_iq_i=n\). Define the dispersion term
\[
D(x,s)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log q_i=n\log(g/n)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i s_i).
\]
If \(D(x,s)\leq\beta\), then \(\prod_iq_i\geq e^{-\beta}\) and, because every \(q_j\leq n\),
\[
q_i\geq e^{-\beta}n^{-(n-1)}\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).
\]
Thus a bounded potential-dispersion term prevents any complementarity product from vanishing relative to \(\mu\), without explicitly imposing a central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded potential-dispersion term supplies aggregate, dimension-sensitive control of all complementarity products without explicitly maintaining a neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(D(x,s)\leq\beta<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i s_i/\mu\geq e^{-\beta}n^{-(n-1)}\) for every \(i\).

source_refs.locator: 4 Potential-Reduction Methods p. 65

source_witnesses.locator: 4 Potential-Reduction Methods p. 65

children.title: Potential Versus Neighborhood Analysis
children.top_down_role: Comparison of the principal global-analysis frameworks.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential Versus Neighborhood Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact comparison between logarithmic dispersion and the usual infinity-norm central-path neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q_i=x_i s_i/\mu\), \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\), define \(D=-\sum_i\log q_i\) and
\[
\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)=\{(x,s)>0:|q_i-1|\leq\theta\text{ for all }i\},\qquad 0\leq\theta<1.
\]
Membership in \(\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)\) implies \(D\leq-n\log(1-\theta)\). Conversely, \(D\leq\beta\) implies only \(q_i\geq e^{-\beta}n^{-(n-1)}\). Hence neighborhood analysis gives componentwise centrality directly, whereas a potential bound gives weaker aggregate control whose conversion to componentwise control deteriorates with dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A central-path neighborhood bounds the potential dispersion, but a potential bound yields only weaker dimension-dependent componentwise centrality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,s)\in\mathcal N_\infty(\theta)\Rightarrow D\leq-n\log(1-\theta)\), while \(D\leq\beta\Rightarrow q_i\geq e^{-\beta}n^{-(n-1)}\).

children.title: Feasible-Start Constructions
children.top_down_role: Conceptual and practical routes to primal, dual, or jointly strictly feasible starting points.

children.title: One-Sided Interior Starts
children.top_down_role: Initialization when strict interiority is available only on the primal or dual side.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Interior Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization requiring strict feasibility on one designated side of a standard-form primal-dual pair, without requiring affine feasibility on the other side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal-dual pair
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\},\qquad
\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\geq0\},
\]
a primal-sided interior start is a triple \((x^0,y^0,s^0)\) satisfying \(Ax^0=b\), \(x^0>0\), and \(s^0>0\), without requiring \(A^{\mathsf T}y^0+s^0=c\). Dually, a dual-sided interior start satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y^0+s^0=c\), \(s^0>0\), and \(x^0>0\), without requiring \(Ax^0=b\). In either case, the affine equation on the opposite side may nevertheless hold accidentally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-sided interior start is strictly positive and feasible on one designated side, while feasibility of the opposite affine equation is not required.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least the designated affine equation is satisfied, with \(x^0>0\) and \(s^0>0\); the opposite affine equation is unrestricted.

children.title: Joint Primal-Dual Interior Starts
children.top_down_role: Initialization when both primal and dual strict interiors are available.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Primal-Dual Interior Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly feasible initialization for both members of a standard-form primal-dual LP pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\},\qquad
\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\geq0\},
\]
a joint primal-dual interior start is a triple \((x^0,y^0,s^0)\) satisfying
\[
Ax^0=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y^0+s^0=c,\qquad x^0>0,\qquad s^0>0.
\]
Its initial complementarity is \(\mu_0=(x^0)^{\mathsf T}s^0/n>0\). Thus both linear residuals vanish initially, and a feasible primal-dual interior-point method need only reduce complementarity while preserving the two affine equations and positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint interior start is strictly primal and dual feasible, so subsequent feasible iterations only need to reduce complementarity.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\).

children.title: Artificial-Start Construction Family

children.title: Primal Artificial-Variable Constructions
children.top_down_role: Augmented primal formulations introducing variables to manufacture an interior start.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Artificial-Variable Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar residual embedding that manufactures a strictly feasible point for the primal affine equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(A\), \(b\), and any \(\bar x>0\), set \(r_p=b-A\bar x\) and introduce \(\tau\geq0\). Replace the primal affine equation by
\[
Ax+r_p\tau=b,\qquad x\geq0,\quad \tau\geq0.
\]
Initialize with \((x^0,\tau^0)=(\bar x,1)\), which satisfies the augmented equation and is strictly positive. Apply an interior-point method to drive \(\tau\) toward zero, optionally using a positive penalty on \(\tau\). Stop with an original primal point only when \(\tau=0\); then the augmented equation reduces exactly to \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar artificial variable multiplies the initial primal residual, making any positive trial vector feasible for an augmented system.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(\bar x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,1)\) is strictly feasible for the augmented equation, and \(\tau=0\) recovers \(Ax=b\).

source_refs.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual identity is algebraically correct, but the cited general background page has not been shown to support this scalar Phase-I construction or the claim that an interior-point procedure can drive the artificial variable to zero. A source for the complete augmented formulation and recovery mechanism is required.

children.title: Dual Artificial-Variable Constructions
children.top_down_role: Augmented dual formulations introducing variables to manufacture an interior start.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Artificial-Variable Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar residual embedding that manufactures strict feasibility for the dual affine equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(A\), \(c\), any \(\bar y\in\mathbb R^m\), and any \(\bar s>0\), set \(r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}\bar y-\bar s\) and introduce \(\tau\geq0\). Replace the dual affine equation by
\[
A^{\mathsf T}y+s+r_d\tau=c,\qquad s\geq0,\quad\tau\geq0.
\]
Initialize with \((y^0,s^0,\tau^0)=(\bar y,\bar s,1)\). Apply an interior-point method that reduces the artificial coordinate, optionally penalizing \(\tau\). Accept an original dual point only at \(\tau=0\), when the augmented equation becomes \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar artificial coordinate multiplies the initial dual residual and creates an explicitly known strictly interior augmented dual point.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\bar s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar y,\bar s,1)\) satisfies the augmented dual equation, and \(\tau=0\) recovers dual feasibility.

source_refs.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

children.title: Joint Artificial-Variable Constructions
children.top_down_role: Coupled augmentations designed to produce a primal-dual interior regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Artificial-Variable Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-parameter embedding of both primal and dual residuals around an arbitrary positive trial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(\bar x>0\), \(\bar s>0\), and \(\bar y\), and define \(r_p=b-A\bar x\) and \(r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}\bar y-\bar s\). Introduce \(\tau\geq0\) and solve within the augmented system
\[
Ax+r_p\tau=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s+r_d\tau=c,
\qquad x>0,\ s>0,\ \tau>0.
\]
Initialize at \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar s,1)\), reduce complementarity and \(\tau\), and stop with an original primal-dual feasible point only if \(\tau=0\). At that boundary both artificial residual terms vanish simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One artificial parameter embeds both affine residuals and provides a known positive starting point for the augmented primal-dual equations.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(\bar s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), and \(\bar y\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar s,1)\) satisfies both augmented equations; \(\tau=0\) recovers both original equations.

children.title: Big-Start Constructions
children.top_down_role: Starting formulations based on deliberately oversized positive components or residual allowances.

knowledge_statements.title: Big-Start Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Data-independent positive trial vectors scaled by a large parameter and made feasible through residual embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Choose \(R>0\), let \(e\) be the all-ones vector, and set \(\bar x=Re\), \(\bar y=0\), and \(\bar s=Re\). Form
\[
r_p=b-A\bar x,\qquad r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}\bar y-\bar s,
\]
and introduce \(\tau\geq0\) through
\[
Ax+r_p\tau=b,
\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s+r_d\tau=c.
\]
Initialize at \((x,y,s,\tau)=(Re,0,Re,1)\). The scale \(R\) supplies explicit positivity but does not itself prove recoverability; the algorithm must reduce \(\tau\) to zero and control the augmented objective before reporting a solution of the original LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large uniform primal and slack vectors give positivity immediately; residual embedding then makes the enlarged equations feasible at the chosen start.
assumptions_latex: \(R>0\) and the dimensions of the two all-ones vectors match \(x\) and \(s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((Re,0,Re,1)\) is strictly feasible for the residual-embedded affine equations.

children.title: Artificial-Start Recovery Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where augmented starting solutions do not transfer cleanly to the original LP.

knowledge_statements.title: Artificial-Start Recovery Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which feasibility or optimality of an artificial embedding does not recover the original LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an embedding whose original affine equations are recovered exactly at \(\tau=0\). If the original primal or dual system is infeasible, no augmented feasible point with \(\tau=0\) exists. Even when the original system is feasible, convergence to an augmented optimum does not imply \(\tau=0\) unless the formulation supplies an exact Phase-I objective, a valid sufficiently large penalty, or another argument excluding optimal points with \(\tau>0\). Therefore recovery is certified only by an attained zero artificial variable together with the original residual and sign tests; small positive \(\tau\) alone gives merely approximate residual control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Artificial feasibility is not original feasibility: recovery requires zero artificial variables and direct verification of the original residual and sign conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau\geq0\) is the artificial coordinate and setting \(\tau=0\) restores the original equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Original recovery requires \(\tau=0\) and direct satisfaction of the original feasibility conditions.

children.title: One-Sided Infeasible-Start Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods maintaining feasibility on one side while reducing residuals on the other.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Infeasible-Start Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-feasible Newton variant that contracts the dual residual while targeting reduced complementarity; the dual-feasible variant is symmetric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Start with \(x>0\), \(s>0\), \(Ax=b\), and dual residual \(r_d=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\), which may be nonzero. At each iteration choose \(\sigma\in[0,1)\) and \(\eta\in(0,1]\), set \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\), and solve
\[
A\Delta x=0,
\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=-\eta r_d,
\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-XSe.
\]
Choose \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) such that \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\) and \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\), then update all variables. The new primal residual remains zero and \(r_d^+=(1-\alpha\eta)r_d\). The third equation supplies a centered complementarity target, but decrease of the actual complementarity additionally requires the method's step-acceptance or neighborhood conditions. Stop when the dual residual and complementarity satisfy prescribed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Newton step preserves primal feasibility, contracts the dual residual, and targets reduced complementarity; actual complementarity decrease requires an appropriate step-acceptance or neighborhood condition.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax=b\), \(x>0\), and \(s>0\) initially.
The displayed Newton system is solvable and a positive step length is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax^+=b\) and \(r_d^+=(1-\alpha\eta)r_d\); the displayed equations alone do not guarantee \((x^+)^{\mathsf T}s^+<x^{\mathsf T}s\).

notation.meaning: diagonal matrices formed from x and s

children.title: Fully Infeasible Primal-Dual Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods jointly reducing primal residuals, dual residuals, and complementarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Infeasible Primal-Dual Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual Newton iteration contracting both affine residuals while driving complementarity toward zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Start from arbitrary \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and \(y\), with \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_d=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\), and \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). Choose \(\sigma\in[0,1)\) and \(\eta\in(0,1]\), and solve
\[
A\Delta x=-\eta r_p,
\qquad A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=-\eta r_d,
\qquad S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-XSe.
\]
Select \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) preserving strict positivity, update \((x,y,s)\), and repeat. Then \(r_p^+=(1-\alpha\eta)r_p\) and \(r_d^+=(1-\alpha\eta)r_d\). Stop only when both residual norms and complementarity meet their stated tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fully infeasible primal-dual step contracts both linear residuals and targets smaller complementarity while maintaining positive primal variables and slacks.
assumptions_latex: \(x>0\) and \(s>0\) initially.
The Newton system is solvable and the chosen step preserves positivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_p^+=(1-\alpha\eta)r_p\) and \(r_d^+=(1-\alpha\eta)r_d\), with \(x^+>0\) and \(s^+>0\).

source_refs.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact complementarity change for the fully infeasible centered Newton step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-XSe and \mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n, then for x^+=x+\alpha\Delta x and s^+=s+\alpha\Delta s,
\[(x^+)^{\mathsf T}s^+=\bigl(1-\alpha(1-\sigma)\bigr)x^{\mathsf T}s+\alpha^2\Delta x^{\mathsf T}\Delta s.\]
Thus the centered linearized target alone does not ensure actual complementarity decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Actual complementarity equals its predicted linear decrease plus a quadratic direction term, so positivity and the Newton equations alone do not guarantee decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(S\Delta x+X\Delta s=\sigma\mu e-XSe\).
\(x^+=x+\alpha\Delta x\) and \(s^+=s+\alpha\Delta s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^+)^{\mathsf T}s^+=\bigl(1-\alpha(1-\sigma)\bigr)x^{\mathsf T}s+\alpha^2\Delta x^{\mathsf T}\Delta s\).

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrices formed from the current primal variables and dual slacks.

children.title: Infeasible-Method Convergence Framework
children.top_down_role: Residual-scaling, direction-control, step-control, and limit-point result families.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible-Method Convergence Framework
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional convergence framework for infeasible-start primal-dual iterations in standard-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) define the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\). For iterates \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\), define \(r_p^k=Ax^k-b\), \(r_d^k=A^{\mathsf T}y^k+s^k-c\), and \(\mu_k=(x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k/n\). Suppose \(x^k>0\), \(s^k>0\), \(\|(r_p^k,r_d^k)\|\le C\mu_k\), and \(\mu_{k+1}\le\rho\mu_k\) for constants \(C<\infty\) and \(0<\rho<1\). Then \(r_p^k\to0\), \(r_d^k\to0\), and \((x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k\to0\). Every finite accumulation point of \(\{(x^k,y^k,s^k)\}\) is primal feasible, dual feasible, complementary, and optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If primal and dual residuals are bounded by a constant times complementarity and complementarity decreases geometrically, both residuals and the duality gap converge to zero; every finite accumulation point of the primal-dual iterates is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(x^k>0\) and \(s^k>0\) for every \(k\).
\(\|(r_p^k,r_d^k)\|\le C\mu_k\) for some \(C<\infty\).
\(\mu_{k+1}\le\rho\mu_k\) for some \(0<\rho<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_p^k\to0\), \(r_d^k\to0\), \(\mu_k\to0\), and every finite accumulation point of \(\{(x^k,y^k,s^k)\}\) is primal-dual optimal.

notation.meaning: Primal and dual residuals at iteration k.

source_refs.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complementarity Decay Alone Does Not Imply Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of infeasible-method convergence when residual control is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A=[1], b=0, c=0 and x^k=1, s^k=1/k, y^k=-1/k. Then x^k>0, s^k>0, \mu_k=x^ks^k=1/k\to0, and r_d^k=A^{\mathsf T}y^k+s^k-c=0, but r_p^k=Ax^k-b=1 for every k. Thus vanishing complementarity, even with exact dual feasibility, does not imply primal feasibility or primal-dual optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive sequence can have vanishing complementarity and exact dual feasibility while its primal residual remains nonzero.
assumptions_latex: Residuals are defined by \(r_p=Ax-b\) and \(r_d=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_k\to0\) and \(r_d^k=0\) do not imply \(r_p^k\to0\).

children.title: Self-Dual Embedding Families
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations providing initialization and unified optimization or status outcomes.

children.title: Canonical Self-Dual Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Self-dual formulations for canonical LP and known-interior regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Self-Dual Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-augmented self-dual embedding initialized from a prescribed positive primal-dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), choose \(x^0>0\), \(s^0>0\), \(y^0\), and \(\kappa^0>0\). Define \(r_p=b-Ax^0\), \(r_d=c-A^{\mathsf T}y^0-s^0\), and \(r_g=c^{\mathsf T}x^0-b^{\mathsf T}y^0-\kappa^0\). A canonical residual embedding is
\[Ax-b\tau+r_p\theta=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\tau+r_d\theta=0,\]
\[-c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+\kappa+r_g\theta=0,\qquad (x,s,\tau,\kappa,\theta)\ge0.\]
The point \((x^0,y^0,s^0,1,\kappa^0,1)\) satisfies the equalities, while the face \(\theta=0\) is the homogeneous primal-dual embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual variables place a chosen positive point in an augmented self-dual system whose zero-residual face represents the original primal-dual problem.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^0,y^0,s^0,1,\kappa^0,1)\) is feasible for the embedded equalities, and setting \(\theta=0\) yields the homogeneous embedding.

notation.meaning: Residual vectors and scalar chosen to install the initial point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed system installs the stated initial point algebraically, but its sign on the certificate variable produces the opposite certificate orientation from the later homogeneous-embedding outcomes. An embedding-specific source is required before selecting a corrected convention.

children.title: General-LP Self-Dual Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Alternative embeddings covering general feasibility regimes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General-LP Reduction to a Homogeneous Self-Dual Embedding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact standard-form reduction of a finite general-form LP followed by the homogeneous embedding used for status determination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite linear program with mixed row senses, free or signed variables, and finite bounds can be converted to
\[\min\{q^{\mathsf T}z:Bz=d,\ z\ge0\}\]
by translating finite lower bounds, representing remaining upper bounds as inequalities, adding nonnegative slacks, and splitting each free variable into a difference of nonnegative variables. For the transformed problem use
\[Bz-d\tau=0,\qquad B^{\mathsf T}w+t-q\tau=0,\qquad d^{\mathsf T}w-q^{\mathsf T}z-\kappa=0,\]
with \(z,t,\tau,\kappa\ge0\) and \(w\) free. Original variables and certificates are recovered by reversing the recorded affine translations, slack introductions, and variable splittings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact general-form transformations reduce a finite LP to nonnegative equality standard form, after which a correctly signed homogeneous embedding can be applied and decoded through the inverse transformation.
assumptions_latex: All variables and constraints are finite-dimensional and linear.
Every finite bound and row sense is retained explicitly in the standard-form transformation.
The transformation map and its inverse are recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformed LP admits the displayed homogeneous embedding, and decoded solutions or certificates map back through the inverse standard-form transformation.

knowledge_statements.title: General-LP Reduction to a Homogeneous Self-Dual Embedding
General-LP Self-Dual Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form reduction followed by a homogeneous primal-dual embedding for arbitrary finite linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Convert a finite linear program with equalities, inequalities, bounded variables, and free variables to \(\min\{q^{\mathsf T}z:Bz=d,\ z\ge0\}\) by adding slacks, translating finite bounds, and writing each free variable as a difference of two nonnegative variables. Its self-dual homogeneous system is
\[Bz-d\tau=0,\qquad B^{\mathsf T}w+t-q\tau=0,\qquad -q^{\mathsf T}z+d^{\mathsf T}w+\kappa=0,\]
with \(z,t,\tau,\kappa\ge0\) and \(w\) free. Thus every general finite LP admits an embedding of this form after an explicit standard-form transformation; recovered original variables are obtained by reversing that transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slack, bound-shift, and variable-splitting transformations reduce a general LP to standard form, after which one homogeneous self-dual system covers it.
assumptions_latex: All variables and constraints are finite-dimensional and linear.
Every finite lower or upper bound is represented explicitly in the standard-form conversion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformed LP has the displayed homogeneous primal-dual embedding, and its original variables are recovered by reversing the standard-form map.

notation.meaning: Constraint matrix, right-hand side, and cost after standard-form conversion.
Transformed primal variable, free dual multiplier, and dual slack.

children.title: Homogeneous Self-Dual Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous formulations combining optimization, infeasibility detection, and unboundedness detection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal-solution, infeasibility, improving-ray, and indeterminate branches of the correctly signed homogeneous embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonzero solution of the homogeneous embedding: if \(\tau>0\), then weak duality and \(\kappa=b^{\mathsf T}y-c^{\mathsf T}x\ge0\) force \(\kappa=0\); division by \(\tau\) gives primal-dual feasible points with equal objectives. If \(\tau=0\) and \(\kappa>0\), then
\[Ax=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}(-y)=s\ge0,\qquad \kappa=b^{\mathsf T}y-c^{\mathsf T}x>0.\]
Hence either \(b^{\mathsf T}y>0\), in which case \(-y\) is a strict primal-infeasibility certificate, or \(c^{\mathsf T}x<0\), in which case \(x\) is a primal improving recession direction and certifies dual infeasibility; both may occur. The branch \(\tau=\kappa=0\) supplies neither conclusion without additional nondegeneracy or normalization information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive scale recovers an optimal primal-dual pair; zero scale with positive certificate yields primal infeasibility or a primal improving ray, while the zero-zero branch is indeterminate.
assumptions_latex: The variables satisfy the correctly signed homogeneous embedding.
The embedded solution is nonzero.
\(x,s,\tau,\kappa\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau>0\Rightarrow\kappa=0\) and scaled optimal recovery; \(\tau=0,\kappa>0\Rightarrow b^{\mathsf T}y>0\) or \(c^{\mathsf T}x<0\); \(\tau=\kappa=0\) is not by itself a status certificate.

notation.meaning: Candidate Farkas multiplier for primal infeasibility.
Candidate primal improving recession direction on the zero-scale branch.

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Embedding Outcome Branches

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous feasibility system for an equality-form primal minimization LP and its standard dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\qquad \max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\},\]
the homogeneous embedding is
\[Ax-b\tau=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\tau=0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y-c^{\mathsf T}x-\kappa=0,\]
where \(x,s,\tau,\kappa\ge0\) and \(y\) is free. Every nonnegative scalar multiple of an embedded solution is again an embedded solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The correctly signed homogeneous system combines primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and the certificate scalar in one scale-invariant formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The primal is a minimization problem in equality standard form with the displayed dual convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The embedded feasible set is homogeneous, with certificate equation \(\kappa=b^{\mathsf T}y-c^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Correctly Signed Homogeneous Primal-Dual Embedding
Homogeneous Self-Dual Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous embedding for optimization and strong primal or dual infeasibility outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), consider
\[Ax-b\tau=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\tau=0,\qquad -c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y+\kappa=0,\]
where \(x,s,\tau,\kappa\ge0\) and \(y\) is free. The system is homogeneous. If \(\tau>0\) and \(\kappa=0\), division by \(\tau\) gives feasible primal-dual points with zero gap. If \(\tau=0\) and \(\kappa>0\), then \(b^{\mathsf T}y-c^{\mathsf T}x=-\kappa<0\), so at least one strict Farkas or recession signal is present according to the signs of the two terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous system encodes optimal solutions when its scaling variable is positive and infeasibility or recession signals when only its certificate variable is positive.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The primal is posed as a minimization problem in equality standard form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau>0,\kappa=0\) yields a zero-gap primal-dual solution after scaling; \(\tau=0,\kappa>0\) yields a strict certificate signal.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: With the displayed third equation, the case \(\tau=0\), \(\kappa>0\) gives \(b^{\mathsf T}y-c^{\mathsf T}x<0\), which does not imply the stated Farkas or improving-recession signals under the record's conventions. A source is needed to determine the intended sign convention and corresponding outcome statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Primal-Dual Solution Outcomes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scaling outcome of a homogeneous primal-dual embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x,y,s,\tau,\kappa)\) satisfy the homogeneous embedding equations with \(x,s,\tau,\kappa\ge0\). If \(\tau>0\) and \(\kappa=0\), define \(\bar x=x/\tau\), \(\bar y=y/\tau\), and \(\bar s=s/\tau\). Then \(A\bar x=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}\bar y+\bar s=c\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}\bar x=b^{\mathsf T}\bar y\). Hence \(\bar x\) and \((\bar y,\bar s)\) are respectively primal and dual feasible with zero duality gap, and therefore constitute complementary optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive embedding scale and zero certificate variable recover feasible primal-dual points with equal objectives, certifying optimality.

\(x,s,\tau,\kappa\ge0\), \(\tau>0\), and \(\kappa=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal-Solution Equivalence for the Artificial Primal–Dual Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of original optimizers from artificial start-embedding problems under sufficiently large penalty parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that the original primal and dual problems have optimal solutions \(x^*\) and \((p^*,s^*)\). If \[M_1\geq\max\{(b-Ae)^{\top}p^*,0\}+1\] and \[M_2\geq\max\{(e-c)^{\top}x^*,(e-c)^{\top}e,0\}+1,\] then: an artificial-primal feasible point \((\bar x,\bar x_{n+1},\bar x_{n+2})\) is optimal if and only if \(\bar x\) is optimal for the original primal and \(\bar x_{n+1}=0\); and an artificial-dual feasible point \((\bar p,\bar p_{m+1},\bar s,\bar s_{n+1},\bar s_{n+2})\) is optimal if and only if \((\bar p,\bar s)\) is optimal for the original dual and \(\bar p_{m+1}=0\).

children.title: Primal Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Embedding outcomes certifying that the primal constraint system has no feasible solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong Farkas certificate for infeasibility of an equality-form primal LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). For the primal feasibility system \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), any vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[A^{\mathsf T}y\le0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y>0\]
is a certificate that the primal feasible set is empty. The certificate is directly checked by matrix-vector multiplication, componentwise comparison, and one scalar inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplier whose transpose image is nonpositive and whose pairing with the right-hand side is positive certifies that the primal system has no feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
Primal nonnegativity and vector inequalities are interpreted componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity and sufficiency of the primal-infeasibility multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exactly one of the following systems is feasible: \[(i)\quad Ax=b,\quad x\ge0,\] \[(ii)\quad A^{\mathsf T}y\le0,\quad b^{\mathsf T}y>0.\] Therefore the equality-form primal feasible set is empty if and only if a multiplier satisfying the second system exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal system is infeasible exactly when a strictly separating Farkas multiplier exists.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
Vector inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=\varnothing\iff\exists y:\ A^{\mathsf T}y\le0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y>0.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong recession certificate for infeasibility of the equality-form LP dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). For the dual feasibility system \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(s\ge0\), any vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying
\[d\ge0,\qquad Ad=0,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}d<0\]
is a certificate that the dual feasible set is empty. These conditions are directly verifiable from \(A\), \(c\), and \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative null direction with negative cost certifies that the dual system has no feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
Dual slack nonnegativity and vector inequalities are interpreted componentwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(y,s)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous Infeasibility Signals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint strong certificates showing that both primal and dual feasible sets are empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the standard-form primal-dual pair, vectors \(y_I\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(d_I\in\mathbb R^n\) form simultaneous infeasibility signals if
\[A^{\mathsf T}y_I\le0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y_I>0,\]
\[d_I\ge0,\qquad Ad_I=0,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}d_I<0.\]
The first line is a Farkas certificate excluding primal feasibility; the second excludes dual feasibility. These conditions may hold simultaneously because primal and dual feasibility are not logical complements when neither side is assumed feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two independent strict certificates can simultaneously establish that both the primal and dual feasible regions are empty.
assumptions_latex: The primal is \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\).
The dual is \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(s\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal feasible set and the dual feasible set are both empty.

children.title: Certificate Normalization Regimes
