knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Normalization Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive rescaling conventions for strict homogeneous infeasibility certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal certificate conditions \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le0\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y>0\) and the dual certificate conditions \(d\ge0\), \(Ad=0\), \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) are positively homogeneous. Consequently one may impose \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\) by replacing \(y\) with \(y/(b^{\mathsf T}y)\), and impose \(c^{\mathsf T}d=-1\) by replacing \(d\) with \(d/(-c^{\mathsf T}d)\). Norm normalizations such as \(\|y\|=1\) or \(\|d\|=1\) are also valid for nonzero certificates, but they do not fix the strict separating margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict homogeneous certificates may be rescaled to unit right-hand-side or unit negative-cost margins without changing what they certify.
assumptions_latex: The certificate has a strictly signed scalar margin.
Only multiplication by a positive scalar is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every strong certificate has an equivalent normalization with \(b^{\mathsf T}y=1\) or \(c^{\mathsf T}d=-1\), respectively.

children.title: Weak-Certificate Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Near-zero or unstable embedding outcomes that do not support a robust infeasibility classification.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Certificate Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of non-strict homogeneous inequalities to certify infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing the strict margin in a Farkas certificate by a weak inequality destroys its certifying force. In particular, \(y=0\) always satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\), while \(d=0\) always satisfies \(d\ge0\), \(Ad=0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d\le0\), regardless of feasibility. More generally, a nonzero vector with zero margin, \(b^{\mathsf T}y=0\) or \(c^{\mathsf T}d=0\), provides no contradiction to a feasible point. A strong infeasibility conclusion therefore requires a strictly positive or strictly negative margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-strict certificate tests admit zero and zero-margin vectors even for feasible problems, so strict separation is essential for an infeasibility conclusion.
assumptions_latex: Certificate conditions are homogeneous.
The strict scalar margin is replaced by a non-strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak conditions with \(b^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) or \(c^{\mathsf T}d\le0\) do not, by themselves, certify infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical failure caused by testing homogeneous certificate residuals without fixing scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\ne0\) be a candidate for a homogeneous certificate system, with positively homogeneous residuals and decisive margin. For \(z_\alpha=\alpha z\), \(\alpha>0\), every absolute residual and the absolute margin tends to zero as \(\alpha\downarrow0\). Thus residual upper bounds that do not fix scale cannot validate a certificate: an invalid or zero-margin candidate can be made arbitrarily small without acquiring a strict margin. Approximate validation must normalize the candidate and require that the normalized strict margin dominate the normalized violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogeneous residuals shrink under scaling, so small unnormalized absolute residuals alone cannot validate an approximate certificate.
assumptions_latex: The certificate equations, sign violations, and margin are positively homogeneous.
The residual acceptance rule does not fix certificate scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\mapsto\alpha z\text{ can make every absolute residual arbitrarily small without creating a strict certificate.}
knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Free Absolute Tolerances Are Unsound

children.title: Primal Recession Certificates
children.top_down_role: Embedding outcomes exposing feasible recession structure in the primal problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Recession Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable recession directions for the equality-form primal feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), a vector \(d\) is a primal recession certificate exactly when
\[Ad=0,\qquad d\ge0.\]
If \(x\in P\), then \(x+\alpha d\in P\) for every \(\alpha\ge0\). For the minimization objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\), the additional condition \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) makes the ray objective-improving and, provided \(P\ne\varnothing\), certifies that the primal optimal value is \(-\infty\). If \(c^{\mathsf T}d=0\), the ray preserves objective value and does not certify unbounded improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative null direction is a primal recession direction; negative cost makes it an unboundedness certificate when a feasible base point exists.
assumptions_latex: \(P\ne\varnothing\) is required for an actual feasible ray.
The primal objective is minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ad=0\) and \(d\ge0\) certify recession; adding \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) certifies primal unboundedness from any feasible base point.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Recession Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Verifiable recession directions for the equality-form dual feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(D=\{(y,s):A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), a pair \((h,k)\) is a dual recession certificate exactly when
\[A^{\mathsf T}h+k=0,\qquad k\ge0.\]
If \((y,s)\in D\), then \((y+\alpha h,s+\alpha k)\in D\) for every \(\alpha\ge0\). For the maximization objective \(b^{\mathsf T}y\), the additional condition \(b^{\mathsf T}h>0\) makes the ray objective-improving and, provided \(D\ne\varnothing\), certifies that the dual optimal value is \(+\infty\). A zero objective slope describes recession without unbounded improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction preserving the dual equality and slack nonnegativity is recessionary; positive dual objective slope certifies unboundedness from a feasible base point.
assumptions_latex: \(D\ne\varnothing\) is required for an actual feasible ray.
The dual objective is maximized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{\mathsf T}h+k=0\) and \(k\ge0\) certify dual recession; adding \(b^{\mathsf T}h>0\) certifies dual unboundedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Improving Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form minimization certificate of primal unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal linear program \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), a feasible point \(\bar x\) together with a vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) is an objective-improving ray certificate. The feasible ray \(\{\bar x+td:t\ge0\}\) has objective values tending to \(-\infty\), so the primal optimal value is \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point and a nonnegative null-space direction of strictly negative cost form a checkable certificate that the primal objective is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: The primal linear program is \(\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
A point \(\bar x\) satisfies \(A\bar x=b\) and \(\bar x\ge0\).
A vector \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(Ad=0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The primal optimal value is \(-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity complementing the seed's sufficient certificate for a feasible standard-form minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\ne\varnothing\). Then \(\inf_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\) if and only if there exists \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(Ad=0\), \(d\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). For every \(\bar x\in F\), the ray \(\bar x+td\), \(t\ge0\), realizes the unbounded decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible standard-form minimization LP is unbounded below exactly when it has a negative-cost nonnegative null direction.
assumptions_latex: F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\iff\exists d\ge0:\ Ad=0,\ c^{\mathsf T}d<0.
knowledge_statements.title: Improving-Ray Necessity for Standard-Form Unboundedness

children.title: Finite-Value Recession Structure
children.top_down_role: Recession directions present without a corresponding objective-unboundedness conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Value Recession Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession geometry of a feasible standard-form LP with finite value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) be nonempty. Then \(\operatorname{rec}(F)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:Ad=0,\ d\ge0\}\). If \(\inf_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is finite, then \(c^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\) for every \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(F)\). If the optimal set \(F^*=\{x\in F:c^{\mathsf T}x=v^*\}\) is nonempty, then \(\operatorname{rec}(F^*)=\{d\in\operatorname{rec}(F):c^{\mathsf T}d=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite value excludes negative-cost recession directions, and when the optimum is attained, the recession directions of the full optimal set are exactly the zero-cost recession directions of the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and is nonempty.
The infimum of \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(F\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(F)\) satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\); if \(F^*\ne\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{rec}(F^*)=\{d\in\operatorname{rec}(F):c^{\mathsf T}d=0\}\).

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the feasible set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absence of Improving Rays Characterizes Finite Attained Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse recession characterization for a nonempty standard-form feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\ne\varnothing\). Then \(\inf_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is finite if and only if \(c^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\) for every \(d\) satisfying \(Ad=0\) and \(d\ge0\). In that case the minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty standard-form polyhedron, absence of a negative-cost recession direction is equivalent to a finite attained minimum.
assumptions_latex: F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x> -\infty\iff c^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\ \forall d\ge0\text{ with }Ad=0,\quad\text{and then }\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Absence of Improving Rays Characterizes Finite Attained Value

children.title: Ambiguous Recession Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Embedding limits where numerical or geometric ambiguity obstructs a stable recession certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguous Recession Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between improving-ray certificates and value-preserving recession.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), let \(x\in F\), and let \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(F)\setminus\{0\}\) satisfy \(c^{\mathsf T}d=0\). Then \(x+td\in F\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}(x+td)=c^{\mathsf T}x\) for every \(t\ge0\). This ray can establish an unbounded constant-objective level set, but it certifies neither objective unboundedness nor infeasibility. Without a feasible base point, the direction alone also does not certify primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero zero-cost recession direction can establish an unbounded constant-objective level set, but it proves neither unbounded objective value nor infeasibility, and without a base point it does not prove feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The primal feasible set is \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
A point \(x\) belongs to \(F\).
A nonzero direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(F)\) satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}d=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ray \(\{x+td:t\ge0\}\) has constant objective value and certifies neither objective unboundedness nor infeasibility.

source_refs.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Certified Sign Test for an Approximate Recession Slope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Error threshold separating a certified improving ray from an ambiguous near-zero slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\hat d\) approximate an exact primal recession direction \(d\), with \(\|d-\hat d\|\le\varepsilon\) in a norm having dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\). Then \(|c^{\mathsf T}d-c^{\mathsf T}\hat d|\le\|c\|_*\varepsilon\). Hence \(c^{\mathsf T}\hat d+\|c\|_*\varepsilon<0\) certifies \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). If \(|c^{\mathsf T}\hat d|\le\|c\|_*\varepsilon\), the error bound permits negative, zero, or positive exact slope, so no slope classification follows from \(\hat d\) alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate recession direction has a certified objective-slope sign only when its computed slope exceeds the error bound in magnitude.
assumptions_latex: An exact recession direction \(d\) lies within distance \(\varepsilon\) of \(\hat d\).
\(\|\cdot\|_*\) is dual to the direction-error norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^{\mathsf T}\hat d+\|c\|_*\varepsilon<0\Rightarrow c^{\mathsf T}d<0;\quad |c^{\mathsf T}\hat d|\le\|c\|_*\varepsilon\Rightarrow\text{the slope sign is uncertified}.
knowledge_statements.title: Certified Sign Test for an Approximate Recession Slope

children.title: Indeterminate Ill-Posed Outcome Family

children.title: Indeterminate Embedding Status
children.top_down_role: Embedding outcomes lacking a decisive optimality or infeasibility classification.

assumptions_latex: A homogeneous self-dual LP embedding produces a nonzero limiting vector with nonnegative status scalars \(\tau\) and \(\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary case \(\tau=\kappa=0\) has indeterminate embedding status under the usual ratio-based extraction rules.

notation.meaning: Embedding normalization scalar used to recover finite primal-dual variables.
Embedding certificate scalar associated with infeasibility or unboundedness extraction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous self-dual embedding boundary where neither standard extraction scalar is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An embedding limit has indeterminate status when \(\tau=0\) and \(\kappa=0\), while the complete homogeneous limit vector is nonzero. Because \(\tau=0\), normalized primal-dual candidates obtained by division by \(\tau\) are undefined. Because \(\kappa=0\), certificate vectors whose validity is established by normalization with \(\kappa\) are likewise unavailable. Consequently the limit, without additional rank, facial, or perturbation information, yields neither a finite primal-dual solution nor a strict infeasibility or objective-unboundedness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If both embedding status scalars vanish at a nonzero limit, the usual normalizations recover neither a solution nor a strict status certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Indeterminate Embedding Status

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The meaning and extraction roles of the embedding scalars depend on the precise homogeneous self-dual formulation. An authoritative source with a specific definition or theorem locator is required before the boundary claim can be assessed reliably.

children.title: Primal Ill-Posedness
children.top_down_role: Primal instances lying near transitions between feasible or infeasible status.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit primal-feasibility boundary example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m=n=1\), take \(A=0\) and \(b=0\). The equation \(0x=0\) has nonnegative solutions. For every \(\varepsilon>0\), replacing \(b\) by \(\varepsilon\) while retaining \(A=0\) makes the equation infeasible, whereas the unperturbed data remain feasible. Hence \((A,b)=(0,0)\) lies on the primal-feasibility boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At A=0 and b=0, the primal system is feasible, but an arbitrarily small nonzero right-hand side makes it infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(A=0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (A,b)=(0,0)\in\partial\mathcal F_P.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Primal Boundary Family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological boundary definition for standard-form primal feasibility in a fixed finite-dimensional data space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(m,n\) and \(\mathcal D=\mathbb R^{m\times n}\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\), equipped with any norm. Let \(\mathcal F_P=\{(A,b,c)\in\mathcal D:\exists x\ge0,\ Ax=b\}\). Data \(d\) are primal ill-posed exactly when \(d\in\partial\mathcal F_P\), equivalently every neighborhood of \(d\) contains both primal-feasible and primal-infeasible data. The qualitative boundary is independent of the chosen norm in fixed finite dimensions, while numerical distances to it depend on the norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal ill-posed data lie on the boundary between feasible and infeasible primal systems; the boundary topology is norm independent in fixed finite dimensions, although its measured distance is not.
assumptions_latex: The dimensions \(m,n\) and perturbed components \((A,b,c)\) are fixed.
Primal feasibility means \(Ax=b\) with \(x\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\text{ is primal ill-posed}\iff d\in\partial\mathcal F_P.

notation.meaning: Set of data whose primal system is feasible.
Boundary in the fixed finite-dimensional data space.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Feasibility Ill-Posedness

assumptions_latex: LP data are triples \(d=(A,b,c)\) in a finite-dimensional normed data space.
Primal feasibility means existence of \(x\ge0\) satisfying \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal ill-posedness is characterized by \(d\in\partial\mathcal F_P\), equivalently \(\operatorname{dist}(d,\partial\mathcal F_P)=0\).

notation.meaning: Set of data having a feasible primal system.
Topological boundary in the chosen data norm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Data-space boundary definition for standard-form primal feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_P=\{(A,b,c):\exists x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). The data \(d=(A,b,c)\) are primal ill-posed when \(d\in\partial\mathcal F_P\), where the boundary is taken in the specified norm on the data space. Equivalently, every neighborhood of \(d\) contains a data triple with a feasible primal system and a data triple with an infeasible primal system. The primal distance to ill-posedness is \(\rho_P(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,\partial\mathcal F_P)\), so ill-posedness is \(\rho_P(d)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal data are ill-posed when they lie on the boundary between feasible and infeasible primal systems in the chosen perturbation norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Ill-Posedness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary definition is plausible, but the admissible perturbations, data-space dimensions, topology, and norm must be fixed and supported by an authoritative locator. The current record has no citation.

children.title: Dual Ill-Posedness
children.top_down_role: Dual instances lying near transitions between feasible or infeasible status.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit dual-feasibility boundary example.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m=n=1\), take \(A=0\) and \(c=0\). The dual equation is \(s=0\), so it is feasible. Replacing \(c\) by \(\varepsilon>0\) remains feasible with \(s=\varepsilon\), whereas replacing it by \(-\varepsilon\) is infeasible because it would require \(s=-\varepsilon<0\). Hence \((A,c)=(0,0)\) lies on the dual-feasibility boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At A=0 and c=0, arbitrarily small positive cost perturbations are dual feasible and negative ones are dual infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(A=0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (A,c)=(0,0)\in\partial\mathcal F_D.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Dual Boundary Family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological boundary definition for the standard-form dual feasibility system in a fixed finite-dimensional data space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(m,n\) and the data space \(\mathcal D=\mathbb R^{m\times n}\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\), equipped with any norm. Let \(\mathcal F_D=\{(A,b,c)\in\mathcal D:\exists(y,s),\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\). Data \(d\) are dual ill-posed exactly when \(d\in\partial\mathcal F_D\), equivalently every neighborhood of \(d\) contains both dual-feasible and dual-infeasible data. The qualitative boundary is independent of the chosen norm because \(\mathcal D\) is finite dimensional; numerical distances to it are norm dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual ill-posed data lie on the boundary between feasible and infeasible dual systems; the boundary topology is norm independent in fixed finite dimensions, although its measured distance is not.
assumptions_latex: The dimensions \(m,n\) and the perturbed data components \((A,b,c)\) are fixed.
Dual feasibility means \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\) with \(s\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\text{ is dual ill-posed}\iff d\in\partial\mathcal F_D.

notation.meaning: Set of data whose dual system is feasible.
Boundary in the fixed finite-dimensional data space.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Feasibility Ill-Posedness

assumptions_latex: LP data are triples \(d=(A,b,c)\) in a finite-dimensional normed data space.
Dual feasibility means existence of \((y,s)\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\) and \(s\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual ill-posedness is characterized by \(d\in\partial\mathcal F_D\), equivalently \(\operatorname{dist}(d,\partial\mathcal F_D)=0\).

notation.meaning: Set of data having a feasible dual system.
Topological boundary in the chosen data norm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Data-space boundary definition for standard-form dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_D=\{(A,b,c):\exists(y,s),\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\). The data \(d=(A,b,c)\) are dual ill-posed when \(d\in\partial\mathcal F_D\), where the boundary is taken in the specified norm on the data space. Equivalently, every neighborhood of \(d\) contains a data triple with a feasible dual system and a data triple with an infeasible dual system. The dual distance to ill-posedness is \(\rho_D(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,\partial\mathcal F_D)\), so ill-posedness is \(\rho_D(d)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual data are ill-posed when they lie on the boundary between feasible and infeasible dual systems in the chosen perturbation norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Ill-Posedness

children.title: Weak Status Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificate outcomes too small or unstable to support reliable interpretation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrarily Small Feasibility Residual Without Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why a small residual is only a weak status witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the scalar system \(0x=\delta,\ x\ge0\) with \(\delta>0\), the candidate \(x=0\) has residual \(|0x-\delta|=\delta\), which can be arbitrarily small, but the system is infeasible for every \(\delta>0\). Therefore no positive absolute residual tolerance by itself converts approximate primal feasibility into exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible scalar system can have an arbitrarily small feasibility residual, so residual size alone cannot establish exact status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\ge0}|0x-\delta|=\delta\to0\quad\text{while the system remains infeasible for every }\delta>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrarily Small Feasibility Residual Without Feasibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-formed approximate feasibility and alternative-system predicates for a standard-form primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal system \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\) and dual system \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\), tolerance-weakened witnesses may be tested by declared norms and tolerances as follows: approximate primal feasibility requires \(\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_p\) and \(\|x_-\|\le\varepsilon_p\); an approximate primal-infeasibility witness uses \(\|y\|=1\), \(\|(A^{\mathsf T}y)_-\|\le\varepsilon_I\), and \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le-\gamma\); an approximate dual-infeasibility direction uses \(\|d\|=1\), \(\|Ad\|\le\varepsilon_I\), \(\|d_-\|\le\varepsilon_I\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d\le-\gamma\), where \(\gamma>0\). With positive residual tolerances these are reproducible approximate-status tests, but they are not exact Farkas or recession certificates unless error bounds show that an exact witness with the required signs exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized witnesses with small residuals and a strict objective or separation margin support tolerance-based status, but positive residual tolerances alone do not prove exact LP status.
assumptions_latex: Norms, normalizations, tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_I\ge0\), and margin \(\gamma>0\) are declared.
\(z_-\) denotes the componentwise negative part.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon_p>0\text{ or }\varepsilon_I>0\Longrightarrow\text{the displayed predicates are approximate evidence, not automatically exact certificates}.

notation.meaning: Declared strict separation or improving-slope margin.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Weakened Status Witnesses

assumptions_latex: The primal system is \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\), and norms and tolerances \(\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_c>0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities certify only approximate, tolerance-dependent status and do not imply an exact alternative.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-dependent evidence near an embedding or feasibility-status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A weak primal-feasibility certificate is a vector \(x\ge0\) satisfying \(\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon_f\). A weak primal-infeasibility certificate is a vector \(y\) satisfying \(\|A^{\mathsf T}yrbracket_-\le\varepsilon_c\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y
e0\), and a prescribed normalization such as \(|b^{\mathsf T}y|=1\), where \(\|z\rrbracket_-\) denotes the norm of the negative part of \(z\). With nonzero tolerances these predicates are numerically verifiable but do not establish the exact feasibility alternative unless residual-error bounds and conditioning margins are also supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small feasibility or certificate residuals provide checkable approximate status, but without conditioning margins they do not prove an exact LP status.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Status Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed infeasibility predicate lacks the sign condition required by the relevant Farkas alternative, and the expression using \(\rrbracket\) is malformed LaTeX. The norm, negative-part notation, normalization, and residual-to-exact-status conditions require an authoritative source before a reliable replacement can be made.

children.title: Perturbation-Sensitive Outcomes
children.top_down_role: Status classifications that change under small changes to problem data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discontinuity of a Fixed Status Map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General topological definition for sensitivity of a declared discrete LP-status classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite-dimensional normed data space \(\mathcal D\), a discrete status set \(\Sigma\), and a declared status map \(S:\mathcal D\to\Sigma\). The outcome at \(d\) is perturbation-sensitive when, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), some \(d'\) satisfies \(\|d'-d\|<\varepsilon\) and \(S(d')\ne S(d)\). Equivalently, the status-preservation radius \(r_S(d)=\sup\{r\ge0:S(d')=S(d)\text{ whenever }\|d'-d\|<r\}\) is zero. If \(r_S(d)>0\), the status is locally stable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A declared LP status is perturbation-sensitive exactly when its largest status-preserving neighborhood has radius zero.
assumptions_latex: The data space, admissible perturbations, norm, status set, and treatment of boundary cases are fixed through the declared map \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\text{ is perturbation-sensitive}\iff r_S(d)=0.

notation.meaning: Largest open-ball radius on which the status at d is unchanged.

knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuity of a Fixed Status Map

assumptions_latex: LP data vary in a fixed normed data space, and \(S(d)\) denotes a discrete status such as primal feasibility or dual feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Status is perturbation-sensitive at \(d\) exactly when every neighborhood of \(d\) contains data with a different status.

notation.meaning: Open norm ball of radius \(\varepsilon\) about the data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological criterion for status instability under arbitrarily small data perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The outcome at data \(d\) is perturbation-sensitive for a specified status map \(S\) when, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(d'\in B_\varepsilon(d)\) such that \(S(d')\ne S(d)\). If \(S\) is the primal-feasibility indicator, this condition is equivalent to \(d\in\partial\mathcal F_P\); for the dual-feasibility indicator it is equivalent to \(d\in\partial\mathcal F_D\). A positive distance from the relevant boundary instead gives a neighborhood on which that status is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP outcome is perturbation-sensitive when arbitrarily small changes to the data can change the selected feasibility or solution status.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Sensitive Outcomes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The topological condition is plausible for a fixed binary feasibility indicator, but the status partition, treatment of boundary data, admissible perturbations, and norm are not fixed or cited. These choices materially affect the claimed equivalences.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Method Global Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic global consequence shared by feasible primal-dual interior-point methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\) be strictly primal-dual feasible for every \(k\), and define \(\mu_k=(x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k/n\). If \(\mu_k\to0\) and the primal and dual optimal sets are nonempty, then \(c^{\mathsf T}x^k-b^{\mathsf T}y^k=n\mu_k\to0\), \(c^{\mathsf T}x^k\to v^*\), and \(b^{\mathsf T}y^k\to v^*\), where \(v^*\) is the common optimal value. Every accumulation point of \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\) is primal-dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For strictly feasible primal-dual iterates, vanishing complementarity forces the duality gap and both objective errors to vanish, and every accumulation point is optimal.
assumptions_latex: Each iterate \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\) is strictly primal-dual feasible: \(Ax^k=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y^k+s^k=c\), and \(x^k,s^k>0\).
The complementarity measure \(\mu_k=(x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k/n\) tends to zero.
The primal and dual optimal sets are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The duality gaps tend to zero, both objective sequences tend to the common optimum \(v^*\), and every accumulation point is primal-dual optimal.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible-Method Global Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based global convergence statement for bounded infeasible interior-point sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\) be a bounded sequence with \(x^k,s^k\ge0\). Define \(r_p^k=Ax^k-b\) and \(r_d^k=A^{\mathsf T}y^k+s^k-c\). If \(r_p^k\to0\), \(r_d^k\to0\), and \((x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k\to0\), and the primal and dual LPs have a common finite optimal value \(v^*\), then every accumulation point is primal-dual optimal and \(c^{\mathsf T}x^k\to v^*\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y^k\to v^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded nonnegative primal-dual sequence, vanishing feasibility residuals and complementarity make every accumulation point optimal and force both objective sequences to converge to the common optimum.
assumptions_latex: Iterates satisfy \(x^k,s^k\ge0\), with residuals \(r_p^k=Ax^k-b\) and \(r_d^k=A^{\mathsf T}y^k+s^k-c\).
The sequence \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\) is bounded, \(r_p^k\to0\), \(r_d^k\to0\), and \((x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k\to0\).
The primal and dual LPs have a common finite optimal value \(v^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accumulation point is primal-dual optimal, and \(c^{\mathsf T}x^k\to v^*\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y^k\to v^*\).

children.title: Sequence Convergence Taxonomy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions only; no subsequential or full-sequence convergence is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathbf{x}^k)_{k\geq 1}\) be a sequence, and let \(k_1<k_2<\cdots\) be positive integers. Then \((\mathbf{x}^{k_j})_{j\geq 1}\) is a subsequence of \((\mathbf{x}^k)_{k\geq 1}\). If \(\mathbf{x}^{k_j}\to\bar{\mathbf{x}}\), then \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\) is a limit point of the original sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Terms selected using strictly increasing indices form a subsequence. A limit of any convergent subsequence is a limit point of the original sequence.

k_1<k_2<\cdots,\quad k_j\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \((x^{k_j},y^{k_j},s^{k_j})\to(\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)\), where \(x^{k_j},s^{k_j}\ge0\), \(Ax^{k_j}-b\to0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y^{k_j}+s^{k_j}-c\to0\), and \((x^{k_j})^{\mathsf T}s^{k_j}\to0\). Then \(A\bar x=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}\bar y+\bar s=c\), \(\bar x,\bar s\ge0\), and \(\bar x^{\mathsf T}\bar s=0\). Consequently, \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)\) is primal-dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent primal-dual subsequence whose feasibility residuals and complementarity vanish has a primal-dual optimal limit.
assumptions_latex: A subsequence \((x^{k_j},y^{k_j},s^{k_j})\) converges to \((\bar x,\bar y,\bar s)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic Partition Bounds and Strict-Complementarity Recovery for IPF
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-specific limit-point structure for an infeasible primal-dual interior-point iteration, using the IPF partition notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{(x^k,\lambda^k,s^k)\}\) be generated by Algorithm IPF. There exists a constant \(C_3>0\) such that, for all sufficiently large \(k\), \(0<x_i^k\leq \mu_k/C_3\) for \(i\in\mathcal N\), \(0<s_i^k\leq \mu_k/C_3\) for \(i\in\mathcal B\), \(s_i^k\geq C_3\gamma\) for \(i\in\mathcal N\), and \(x_i^k\geq C_3\gamma\) for \(i\in\mathcal B\). Hence, any limit point of \(\{(x^k,s^k)\}\) can be used to construct a strictly complementary solution of the associated primal and dual linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For sufficiently late IPF iterates, the basic and nonbasic partition components satisfy the stated barrier-parameter upper bounds and uniform lower bounds. Any limit point of the primal-slack sequence can then be used to construct a strictly complementary solution.
assumptions_latex: \{(x^k,\lambda^k,s^k)\}\text{ is generated by Algorithm IPF}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists C_3>0\;\exists K\;\forall k\geq K:\;\left(0<x_i^k\leq \mu_k/C_3\ \forall i\in\mathcal N\right)\land\left(0<s_i^k\leq \mu_k/C_3\ \forall i\in\mathcal B\right)\land\left(s_i^k\geq C_3\gamma\ \forall i\in\mathcal N\right)\land\left(x_i^k\geq C_3\gamma\ \forall i\in\mathcal B\right);\text{ any limit point of }\{(x^k,s^k)\}\text{ can be used to construct a strictly complementary solution}.

children.title: Primal-Dual Sequence Convergence
children.top_down_role: Joint convergence behavior of primal variables, dual variables, plus slacks.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Sequence Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form finite-dimensional LP; the result distinguishes optimality of accumulation points from convergence of the entire primal-dual sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and consider the primal LP \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\). Let \(\{(x^k,y^k,s^k)\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\) be bounded, with \(x^k\ge0\) and \(s^k\ge0\) for every \(k\). If \(Ax^k-b\to0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y^k+s^k-c\to0\), and \((x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k\to0\), then every accumulation point is primal feasible, dual feasible, and complementary, and hence is a primal-dual optimal triple. If the primal-dual optimal triple is unique, the full sequence converges to it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded nonnegative primal-dual sequence, vanishing primal residual, dual residual, and complementarity gap make every accumulation point primal-dual optimal. If the optimal triple is unique, the full sequence converges to it.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
The sequence \(\{(x^k,y^k,s^k)\}\subset\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\) is bounded and satisfies \(x^k\ge0\) and \(s^k\ge0\) for every \(k\).
The residuals satisfy \(Ax^k-b\to0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y^k+s^k-c\to0\), and the complementarity gap satisfies \((x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accumulation point is a primal-dual optimal triple; if that triple is unique, then \((x^k,y^k,s^k)\) converges to it.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two Interior Accumulation Points on an Optimal Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-level counterexample showing that strict feasibility and exact objective optimality do not force full-sequence convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{0:0\le x_1\le1,\ 0\le x_2\le1\}\). For \(j\ge1\), define \[x^{2j}=\left(\frac14+\frac1{20(j+1)},\frac12\right),\qquad x^{2j+1}=\left(\frac34-\frac1{20(j+1)},\frac12\right).\] Every iterate is strictly feasible and optimal, but \(x^{2j}\to(1/4,1/2)\) and \(x^{2j+1}\to(3/4,1/2)\). Hence the sequence has two distinct optimal accumulation points and does not converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded strictly feasible sequence can remain exactly optimal while alternating between neighborhoods of two distinct optimal points.
assumptions_latex: The LP has constant zero objective on the unit square.
The sequence is defined by the displayed even and odd subsequences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{acc}(x^k)=\{(1/4,1/2),(3/4,1/2)\},\qquad x^k\text{ does not converge}.

notation.meaning: set of accumulation points of the sequence

review_flags: This is a sequence-taxonomy counterexample, not a claim that a specified interior-point update generates the sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Two Interior Accumulation Points on an Optimal Face

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective convergence and feasibility do not imply a unique limit point or full-sequence convergence.

notation.meaning: A strictly feasible sequence with alternating endpoint limits.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary showing that feasibility and objective convergence alone cannot establish convergence of iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{0:x_1+x_2=1,\ x_1,x_2\ge0\}\). Define strictly feasible iterates by \(x^{2j}=(1-1/(j+2),1/(j+2))\) and \(x^{2j+1}=(1/(j+2),1-1/(j+2))\) for \(j\ge0\). Every iterate is feasible and has the optimal objective value \(0\), while \[x^{2j}\to(1,0),\qquad x^{2j+1}\to(0,1).\] Thus the sequence has two optimal accumulation points and does not converge. Full-sequence convergence therefore requires an additional mechanism, such as uniqueness or convergence to a selected center of the optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly feasible optimal sequence can alternate toward two endpoints of an optimal face, so residual and objective convergence do not guarantee iterate convergence.

children.title: Path-Following Complexity Architecture
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood preservation and central-parameter progress as a general complexity framework.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Following Complexity Architecture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic short-step path-following architecture; constants depend on the chosen central-path neighborhood, and the stated end-to-end consequence concerns arithmetic complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge1\), let \(0<\varepsilon<\mu_0\), and define \(\mu_k=(x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k/n\). Suppose a path-following iteration preserves a fixed central-path neighborhood and satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-\delta/\sqrt n)\mu_k\) for a dimension-independent constant \(\delta\in(0,1)\). Then \[\mu_k\le \exp(-\delta k/\sqrt n)\mu_0.\] Consequently, \[k\ge\left\lceil\frac{\sqrt n}{\delta}\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil\] suffices to obtain \(\mu_k\le\varepsilon\). If each iteration uses a polynomially bounded number of real-arithmetic operations, this iteration estimate yields a polynomial total arithmetic-operation bound in the declared dimension and accuracy parameters; a bit-complexity conclusion requires separate precision and encoding bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preserving a central neighborhood while reducing complementarity by a constant over square-root dimension yields a square-root-dimension logarithmic iteration bound. Polynomial per-iteration arithmetic cost then gives polynomial arithmetic complexity, while bit complexity requires additional precision control.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge1\), \(0<\varepsilon<\mu_0\), and \(\mu_k=(x^k)^{\mathsf T}s^k/n\).
Each iterate remains in a fixed central-path neighborhood.
For some dimension-independent \(\delta\in(0,1)\), every iteration satisfies \(\mu_{k+1}\le(1-\delta/\sqrt n)\mu_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At most \(\left\lceil(\sqrt n/\delta)\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon)\right\rceil\) iterations are sufficient to obtain \(\mu_k\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Number of complementary primal-dual variable pairs.

children.title: Potential-Reduction Complexity Architecture
children.top_down_role: Uniform potential progress as a global polynomiality framework.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Reduction Complexity Architecture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract potential-reduction template separating iteration and arithmetic-operation bounds from bit-complexity requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi_k\) be a primal-dual potential such that \(\Phi_k\le\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}\) implies the prescribed residual and duality-gap accuracy. Suppose every nonterminal iteration satisfies \(\Phi_{k+1}\le\Phi_k-\delta\) for a constant \(\delta>0\). Then the target is reached after at most \[N=\max\left\{0,\left\lceil\frac{\Phi_0-\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}}{\delta}\right\rceil\right\}\] iterations. If this bound and the real-arithmetic cost of each iteration are polynomially bounded in the declared dimension, input-length, and encoded accuracy parameters, then the total arithmetic-operation count is polynomially bounded. A polynomial bit-complexity conclusion additionally requires control of precision and intermediate operand lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform potential decrease bounds the iteration count by the initial potential range divided by the guaranteed decrease. Polynomial per-iteration arithmetic cost gives polynomial arithmetic complexity, but bit complexity needs separate precision and operand-length bounds.
assumptions_latex: Reaching \(\Phi_k\le\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}\) implies the prescribed target accuracy.
Every nonterminal iteration satisfies \(\Phi_{k+1}\le\Phi_k-\delta\) for a constant \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target is reached after at most \(\max\{0,\lceil(\Phi_0-\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}})/\delta\rceil\}\) iterations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Architecture-level statement; exact homogeneous self-dual equations and decoding conventions vary among formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a homogeneous self-dual feasibility system whose variables include primal-dual variables and nonnegative scalars \(\tau\) and \(\kappa\), with a known interior start. Apply a polynomial path-following method until the embedding complementarity \(\mu\) is sufficiently small. If the terminal point has \(\tau>0\), scaling the primal-dual variables by \(1/\tau\) yields an approximate solution of the original primal-dual pair. If instead \(\kappa>0\) with the corresponding embedding residual conditions, scaling the appropriate variables yields a verifiable primal- or dual-infeasibility certificate. The embedding thereby unifies optimization and status detection within one complexity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous self-dual embedding supplies a known start and lets one path-following run decode either an approximate solution or an infeasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational LP with binary input length \(L\), the bit complexity \(T_{\mathrm{bit}}(L,\varepsilon)\) is the total number of Boolean operations used to return an exact certified answer or an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate answer under a specified encoding of \(\varepsilon\). The count includes arithmetic on finite binary strings, comparisons, rounding or exact rational operations, and growth of intermediate operand lengths. A bit-polynomial guarantee requires \(T_{\mathrm{bit}}(L,\varepsilon)\) to be polynomial in \(L\) and in the encoded accuracy requirement, commonly \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bit complexity counts Boolean work on finite encodings, including intermediate precision growth; polynomiality is measured in input length and encoded accuracy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unit-cost real-arithmetic model, each addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and comparison of represented real quantities costs one operation, independently of operand magnitude or precision. For an LP with \(m\) constraints and \(n\) variables, \(T_{\mathrm{arith}}(m,n,\varepsilon)\) is the total such operation count required to meet the stated accuracy \(\varepsilon\). This model measures algebraic work but does not itself control coefficient encoding, intermediate bit lengths, rounding error, or the Boolean cost of realizing an arithmetic operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arithmetic complexity counts real-number operations at unit cost, exposing algebraic work while ignoring operand length and implementation precision.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an interior-point update rule and a termination predicate expressing the required residual, duality-gap, or complementarity accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\). Its worst-case iteration complexity \(N(m,n,\varepsilon)\) is the smallest bound such that every admissible LP instance of dimensions \((m,n)\), from every allowed initialization, satisfies the predicate within at most \(N(m,n,\varepsilon)\) updates. The count treats each update as one iteration and therefore does not include the arithmetic, bit, or sparse-linear-algebra cost of computing that update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration complexity counts updates needed to reach a precise accuracy predicate, without asserting that every update has equal computational cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Algebra Cost Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-iteration implementation model covering dense or sparse direct solves and any explicitly specified factorization reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose iteration \(k\) forms a linear system with coefficient matrix \(M_k\), incurs formation and update cost \(U_k\), factors the matrix at charged cost \(F_k\), and performs \(q_k\) triangular or equivalent solves at charged cost \(S_k\) per solve. Over \(N\) iterations, the declared linear-algebra cost model is \[T_{\mathrm{LA}}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(U_k+F_k+q_kS_k\bigr).\] The quantities \(F_k\) and \(S_k\) must be evaluated under the specified dense or sparse representation, ordering, factorization, and reuse policy. In particular, an iteration bound alone does not determine \(T_{\mathrm{LA}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-algebra cost model sums system formation and updates, charged factorizations, and repeated solves across iterations under a specified dense or sparse implementation and reuse policy.
assumptions_latex: The method performs \(N\) iterations indexed by \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\).
At iteration \(k\), the system representation, ordering, factorization method, and factorization-reuse policy are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The modeled cost is \(T_{\mathrm{LA}}=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(U_k+F_k+q_kS_k)\).

Consequently, \[T_{\mathrm{LA}}=O\!\left(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(U_k+r_k^3+q_kr_k^2)\right).\] If \(r_k\le r\), \(U_k=O(r^3)\), and \(q_k=O(1)\), then \(T_{\mathrm{LA}}=O(Nr^3)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar sparse Cholesky accounting under a fixed ordering; supernodal implementations may use a more detailed block model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sparse positive-definite system factored as \(LL^{\mathsf T}\) under a fixed ordering, let \(\ell_j\) be the number of stored entries in column \(j\) of \(L\). In the scalar sparse-Cholesky model, factor storage and one triangular solve cost \(\Theta(\sum_j\ell_j)\), while numerical factorization costs \(\Theta(\sum_j\ell_j^2)\). Hence the nonzero count of the original matrix alone does not determine sparse work: the ordering and resulting filled factor must be specified.

children.title: Cross-Model Complexity Gaps
children.top_down_role: Situations where iteration bounds do not directly yield arithmetic or bit guarantees.

assumptions_latex: An interior-point method has a polynomial iteration bound in the declared dimension and accuracy parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: That iteration bound alone implies neither polynomial bit complexity nor a specific end-to-end arithmetic or linear-algebra bound.

notation.meaning: Maximum intermediate operand length in bits.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation among iteration, arithmetic, linear-algebra, and Turing bit-complexity guarantees.

source_refs.locator: Complexity of Simplex, Ellipsoid, and Interior-Point Methods p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound \(N\le p(m,n,\log(1/\varepsilon))\) controls only the number of iterations. End-to-end arithmetic work additionally requires a bound on \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}C_k\), including the cost of each linear solve. Bit complexity further requires polynomial control of the precision and operand lengths \(B_k\) and of the Boolean cost of operations on those operands. Hence polynomial iteration complexity does not, without these additional bounds, imply polynomial arithmetic complexity, polynomial bit complexity, or an implementation-independent wall-clock guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomially many iterations need not mean polynomial total work: per-step linear algebra, numerical precision, and intermediate bit lengths require separate bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A weakly polynomial LP guarantee may depend polynomially on the binary input length \(L\) and, for approximation, on \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\). A strongly polynomial algorithm would instead use a number of arithmetic operations bounded by a polynomial in \(m+n\), independent of coefficient magnitudes and \(L\), while keeping intermediate encodings polynomially bounded. Classical path-following, potential-reduction, and embedding analyses establish weak polynomiality through input-length or accuracy dependence; these analyses do not supply the coefficient-independent operation bound required for strong polynomiality of general linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical interior-point methods are polynomial in encoded input size or accuracy, but their analyses do not meet the coefficient-independent requirements of strong polynomiality.

knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear Predictor-Corrector Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local result for feasible primal-dual predictor-corrector iterates near a regular strictly complementary LP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a primal-dual LP with complementarity measure \(\mu_k=x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k/n\). Suppose feasible positive iterates remain in a fixed central-path neighborhood and converge to a strictly complementary solution at which the reduced primal-dual Jacobian is nonsingular. If the predictor-corrector parameters satisfy \(\sigma_k\to0\), the linear-system residual is \(o(\mu_k)\), and the accepted step lengths satisfy \(\alpha_k\to1\), then
\[
\frac{\mu_{k+1}}{\mu_k}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Under the associated local error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(z_k,\mathcal S_*)\le C\mu_k\), the iterates also converge superlinearly to the locally isolated solution: \(\|z_{k+1}-z_*\|/\|z_k-z_*\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing centering, increasingly accurate Newton solves, and asymptotically full steps yield superlinear complementarity reduction and, under a local error bound, superlinear iterate convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k>0,\ s_k>0\), with primal-dual feasibility and membership in a fixed central neighborhood.
The limiting solution is strictly complementary and its reduced primal-dual Jacobian is nonsingular.
\(\sigma_k\to0\), the solve residual is \(o(\mu_k)\), and \(\alpha_k\to1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_{k+1}/\mu_k\to0\), and the local error bound implies \(\|z_{k+1}-z_*\|/\|z_k-z_*\|\to0\).

children.title: Quadratic Local Convergence
children.top_down_role: Local regimes exhibiting quadratic-type reduction near a regular solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Local Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Q-quadratic convergence of primal-dual iterates to a locally isolated LP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(z_k\in V\) converge to \(z_*\in V\), and define \(e_k=\lVert z_k-z_*\rVert\). The convergence is locally Q-quadratic if there exist \(C>0\) and \(k_0\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
e_{k+1}\le C e_k^2\qquad\text{for every }k\ge k_0.
\]
For primal-dual LP iterates \(z_k=(x_k,y_k,s_k)\), define \(\mu_k=x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k/n\), where \(n\) is the number of complementary pairs. If positive constants \(c_1,c_2\) satisfy \(c_1\mu_k\le e_k\le c_2\mu_k\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), then Q-quadratic convergence is equivalent, up to changed constants, to \(\mu_{k+1}=O(\mu_k^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic local convergence means that every sufficiently late iterate error is at most a constant times the square of the preceding error; finite termination is allowed. Under a two-sided comparison between iterate error and complementarity, this is equivalent to quadratic complementarity reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(z_k\to z_*\) in a finite-dimensional normed space.
For the complementarity characterization, \(c_1,c_2>0\) and \(c_1\mu_k\le\lVert z_k-z_*\rVert\le c_2\mu_k\) eventually.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert z_{k+1}-z_*\rVert\le C\lVert z_k-z_*\rVert^2\) eventually; under the two-sided error bound, this is equivalent to \(\mu_{k+1}=O(\mu_k^2)\).

notation.meaning: iterate error relative to the limit

children.title: Nearly Quadratic Local Convergence
children.top_down_role: Local regimes approaching but not attaining a fully quadratic rate.

knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Quadratic Local Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convergence whose Q-order can be made arbitrarily close to two from below.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_k\to z_*\) and let \(e_k=\|z_k-z_*\|\). A parameterized local method is nearly Q-quadratic if, for every fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), its admissible parameters can be chosen so that constants \(C_\delta>0\) and \(k_\delta\) exist with
\[
e_{k+1}\le C_\delta e_k^{\,2-\delta}\qquad(k\ge k_\delta).
\]
Thus every order strictly below two is attainable, although a uniform estimate \(e_{k+1}\le C e_k^2\) need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearly quadratic family attains every fixed convergence order below two, while its assumptions or constants may not support a uniform quadratic estimate.
assumptions_latex: For each \(\delta\in(0,1)\), the method parameters may depend on \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^{2-\delta})\) for every fixed admissible \(\delta>0\), without necessarily having \(e_{k+1}=O(e_k^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Predictor-Corrector Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient local regime for quadratic complementarity reduction by a primal-dual predictor-corrector step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let positive feasible iterates converge to a regular strictly complementary primal-dual solution while remaining in a central neighborhood. Suppose the corrector uses \(\sigma_k=O(\mu_k)\), the combined predictor-corrector equation has residual norm \(O(\mu_k^2)\), and a full step is eventually admissible. If the local Newton remainder is bounded quadratically, then a constant \(C>0\) exists such that
\[
\mu_{k+1}\le C\mu_k^2
\]
for all sufficiently large \(k\). When \(\|z_k-z_*\|=\Theta(\mu_k)\), the primal-dual iterates converge Q-quadratically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular predictor-corrector method becomes quadratically convergent when centering and solve errors are second order and full steps are eventually accepted.
assumptions_latex: The limiting solution is strictly complementary and the local primal-dual Jacobian is nonsingular.
\(\sigma_k=O(\mu_k)\) and the combined equation residual is \(O(\mu_k^2)\).
Full steps are eventually accepted and the Newton remainder is quadratically bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_{k+1}=O(\mu_k^2)\); if \(\|z_k-z_*\|=\Theta(\mu_k)\), then \(z_k\to z_*\) Q-quadratically.

children.title: Central-Path Regularity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Path geometry supporting quadratic-type local behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Path Regularity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsingularity condition supporting smooth central-path derivatives and fast local Newton convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the primal-dual LP equations \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(x\ge0\), and \(s\ge0\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank. For \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{Diag}(s)\), and the all-ones vector \(e\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
F(x,y,s;\mu)=(Ax-b,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c,\ Xs-\mu e).
\]
A complementary primal-dual solution \(z_*=(x_*,y_*,s_*)\) is central-path regular when
\[
J_*=
\begin{pmatrix}
A&0&0\\
0&A^{\mathsf T}&I\\
S_*&0&X_*
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is nonsingular, where \(X_*=\operatorname{Diag}(x_*)\) and \(S_*=\operatorname{Diag}(s_*)\). Under this condition, there is a locally unique smooth branch \(z(\mu)\) satisfying \(F(z(\mu);\mu)=0\) for all sufficiently small \(\mu>0\). In standard LP terminology, strict complementarity together with primal and dual nondegeneracy is a sufficient regime for this nonsingularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Central-path regularity is nonsingularity of the limiting primal-dual Jacobian. It yields a locally unique smooth central-path branch; strict complementarity with primal and dual nondegeneracy is a standard sufficient regime.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank after redundant equality constraints are removed.
\(z_*=(x_*,y_*,s_*)\) is a complementary primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(J_*\) is nonsingular, then a locally unique smooth branch \(z(\mu)\) satisfies \(F(z(\mu);\mu)=0\) for all sufficiently small \(\mu>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Endpoint Derivative Equation for a Regular Central Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order endpoint expansion of the locally smooth central-path branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under endpoint regularity, the smooth branch satisfies
\[
z(\mu)=z_*+\mu\dot z_*+O(\mu^2),
\qquad
J_*\dot z_*=(0,0,e).
\]
Consequently \(\|z(\mu)-z_*\|=O(\mu)\). If \(\dot z_*\ne0\), then \(\|z(\mu)-z_*\|\) is also bounded below by a positive constant times \(\mu\) for all sufficiently small positive \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular central path has a first-order endpoint expansion obtained from one limiting Jacobian system.
assumptions_latex: The accepted seed's limiting Jacobian \(J_*\) is nonsingular.
The central-path branch is the local branch supplied by the endpoint implicit-function theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J_*\dot z_*=(0,0,e),\qquad z(\mu)-z_*=\mu\dot z_*+O(\mu^2).

notation.meaning: right derivative of the central path at zero

children.title: Quadratic-Rate Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degeneracy, weak correction, or irregular path geometry that degrades the local rate.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic-Rate Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate optimal faces can prevent central-path convergence to a prescribed solution and invalidate quadratic iterate-rate conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\min\ 0\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1+x_2=1,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.
\]
Every feasible point is optimal. At the optimal endpoint \(x_*=(1,0)\), take \(y_*=0\) and \(s_*=(0,0)\); then the second component has \(x_{*,2}=s_{*,2}=0\), and the limiting complementarity Jacobian is singular. The logarithmic-barrier central point is \(x(\mu)=(1/2,1/2)\) for every \(\mu>0\), so it does not converge to \(x_*\). Consequently, complementarity reduction alone cannot imply quadratic convergence of iterates to this prescribed degenerate optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a constant objective on a simplex, the central path stays at the analytic center and cannot converge quadratically to a chosen degenerate endpoint.
assumptions_latex: The target is the endpoint \(x_*=(1,0)\) of the displayed optimal face.
The central point is defined by the logarithmic barrier on \(x_1+x_2=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The central path does not approach \(x_*\), so no estimate \(\|x(\mu_{k+1})-x_*\|=O(\|x(\mu_k)-x_*\|^2)\) is possible.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step-length boundary for quadratic convergence of a regular primal-dual Newton iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be the local primal-dual KKT residual mapping, with \(F(z_*)=0\), nonsingular \(F'(z_*)\), and locally Lipschitz derivative. For the exact Newton direction \(p_k=-F'(z_k)^{-1}F(z_k)\) and damped update \(z_{k+1}=z_k+\alpha_kp_k\), writing \(e_k=z_k-z_*\) gives
\[
e_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)e_k+O(\lVert e_k\rVert^2).
\]
Hence the standard quadratic estimate is ensured by this expansion when \(1-\alpha_k=O(\lVert e_k\rVert)\). If \(\alpha_k\le 1-\eta\) infinitely often for some \(\eta>0\), a first-order term persists and regularity of the Newton direction alone does not guarantee quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular primal-dual Newton direction does not by itself guarantee quadratic convergence when accepted steps remain persistently damped.
assumptions_latex: \(F(z_*)=0\), \(F'(z_*)\) is nonsingular, and \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_{k+1}=(1-\alpha_k)e_k+O(\lVert e_k\rVert^2)\); persistent damping therefore prevents the usual regular-Newton quadratic guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Persistent Damping Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local solve-accuracy boundary for quadratic convergence of a regular primal-dual KKT iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) denote the local primal-dual KKT residual mapping, with \(F(z_*)=0\), nonsingular \(F'(z_*)\), and locally Lipschitz derivative. If a full inexact Newton step satisfies
\[
F'(z_k)p_k=-F(z_k)+r_k,\qquad z_{k+1}=z_k+p_k,
\]
then
\[
\lVert z_{k+1}-z_*\rVert=O(\lVert z_k-z_*\rVert^2)+O(\lVert r_k\rVert).
\]
Thus \(\lVert r_k\rVert=O(\lVert z_k-z_*\rVert^2)\) preserves the standard quadratic estimate, whereas the weaker condition \(\lVert r_k\rVert=O(\lVert z_k-z_*\rVert)\) alone does not guarantee it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a regular primal-dual KKT system, second-order linear-solve residuals preserve the quadratic Newton estimate; first-order residual control alone does not guarantee that rate.
assumptions_latex: \(F(z_*)=0\), \(F'(z_*)\) is nonsingular, and \(F'\) is locally Lipschitz.
\(z_k\to z_*\), the displayed inexact primal-dual Newton equation holds, and full steps are taken.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert z_{k+1}-z_*\rVert=O(\lVert z_k-z_*\rVert^2)+O(\lVert r_k\rVert)\); consequently a merely first-order residual bound does not imply Q-quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Primal-Dual Newton Residual Boundary

children.title: Degenerate Local-Convergence Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rate Transfer Under Degenerate Error Comparability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional condition under which a complementarity-parameter rate transfers to convergence toward a selected solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_k\to z_*\) and \(\mu_k\downarrow0\). Suppose that for some \(\alpha\in(0,1]\) and constants \(0<c\le C\),
\[
c\mu_k^{\alpha}\le \|z_k-z_*\|\le C\mu_k^{\alpha}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(k\). If \(\mu_{k+1}=O(\mu_k^p)\) for \(p>1\), then
\[
\|z_{k+1}-z_*\|=O(\|z_k-z_*\|^p).
\]
Without convergence to a selected point and a two-sided comparison of this kind, a parameter rate need not determine a selected-point rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy does not prevent fast convergence to a selected solution when a two-sided local comparison between point error and the path parameter is available.
assumptions_latex: \(z_k\) converges to the selected solution \(z_*\).
Iterate error and \(\mu_k^{\alpha}\) are locally comparable from both sides.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_{k+1}=O(\mu_k^p)\Longrightarrow \|z_{k+1}-z_*\|=O(\|z_k-z_*\|^p).
knowledge_statements.title: Rate Transfer Under Degenerate Error Comparability
Degenerate Local-Convergence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of fast iterate convergence when the optimal set is nonisolated or the limiting complementarity Jacobian is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_k\) be interior-point iterates with \(\mu_k\to0\) and accumulation set contained in the primal-dual solution set \(\mathcal S_*\). If the selected limit is nonisolated or the limiting complementarity Jacobian is singular, a local error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(z,\mathcal S_*)\le C\|F(z;0)\|\) need not hold. Hence even \(\mu_{k+1}=O(\mu_k^p)\) with \(p>1\) does not by itself imply the same Q-order for \(\|z_k-z_*\|\). Fast iterate convergence requires an additional regularity, identification, or error-bound condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At degenerate optima, fast complementarity reduction need not translate into fast convergence to a particular solution unless an error bound or identification property is restored.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu_k\to0\) and all accumulation points are primal-dual optimal.
The candidate limit is nonisolated or its limiting complementarity Jacobian is singular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A superlinear or quadratic rate for \(\mu_k\) alone does not guarantee that rate for \(\|z_k-z_*\|\).

children.top_down_role: Methods using curvature information from the central trajectory.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cubic Residual of the Quadratic Path Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local consistency of the second-order Taylor model of a regular primal-dual central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z(\mu)=(x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) be twice differentiable and satisfy \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x\circ s=\mu e\). Define \(\widehat z(h)=z+h z'+\tfrac12h^2z''\). Then the affine feasibility equations hold exactly at \(\widehat z(h)\), and
\[
\widehat x(h)\circ\widehat s(h)-(\mu+h)e
=\frac{h^3}{2}(x'\circ s''+x''\circ s')+\frac{h^4}{4}x''\circ s''=O(h^3).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quadratic trajectory model preserves affine feasibility exactly and matches complementarity through second order, leaving a cubic residual.
assumptions_latex: \(z(\mu)\) is twice differentiable near the current positive parameter.
\(z'\) and \(z''\) are the exact first and second central-path derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\widehat x(h)=b,\quad A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y(h)+\widehat s(h)=c,\quad \widehat x(h)\circ\widehat s(h)=(\mu+h)e+O(h^3).
knowledge_statements.title: Cubic Residual of the Quadratic Path Model

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Path Consistency Does Not Certify a Proposed Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates local Taylor consistency from quantitative positivity, neighborhood preservation, and repeated progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat z(h)=z+h z'+\tfrac12h^2z''\) be a quadratic central-path model at a point with \(x,s>0\), and suppose its complementarity residual is \(O(|h|^3)\). Positivity holds for all sufficiently small \(|h|\) by continuity, but the residual estimate alone neither certifies positivity for a proposed finite \(h\), nor proves membership in a prescribed central neighborhood, nor supplies a uniform nonzero parameter reduction over repeated iterations. Those conclusions require componentwise step bounds and a neighborhood-preservation estimate with explicit constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cubic complementarity residual gives local consistency, but does not by itself certify a particular finite step or uniform repeated progress.
assumptions_latex: \(z'\) and \(z''\) are exact derivatives of a positive central-path branch at the current parameter.
Only an asymptotic \(O(|h|^3)\) complementarity-residual estimate is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\widehat x(h)\circ\widehat s(h)-(\mu+h)e\|=O(|h|^3)\centernot\Longrightarrow\text{acceptability of a prescribed }h\text{ or a uniform repeated reduction}.

notation.meaning: quadratic Taylor model of the central trajectory

review_flags: The statement preserves the local positivity consequence of continuity while rejecting unsupported quantitative step guarantees.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Path Consistency Does Not Certify a Proposed Step

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directly checks a supplied quadratic trajectory step without asserting a uniform admissible reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=(x,y,s)\) be primal-dual feasible at parameter \(\mu>0\), let \(h\in(-\mu,0)\), and set \(\widehat z(h)=z+h z'+\tfrac12h^2z''\) and \(\widehat\mu=\mu+h\). For \(0\le\theta<1\), define \(\mathcal N_\infty(\theta,\widehat\mu)=\{(u,v,w):Au=b,\ A^{\mathsf T}v+w=c,\ u,w>0,\ \|u\circ w/\widehat\mu-e\|_\infty\le\theta\}\). If \(z'\) and \(z''\) satisfy the differentiated affine-feasibility equations, then the trial belongs to this neighborhood exactly when \(\widehat x>0\), \(\widehat s>0\), and \(\|\widehat x\circ\widehat s/\widehat\mu-e\|_\infty\le\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accept a quadratic trajectory trial only after checking a positive new parameter, positive primal and dual coordinates, and membership in the declared central neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(z'\) and \(z''\) satisfy the exact differentiated primal- and dual-feasibility equations.
\(h\in(-\mu,0)\) and \(0\le\theta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat z(h)\in\mathcal N_\infty(\theta,\mu+h)\iff \widehat x>0,\ \widehat s>0,\ \left\|\widehat x\circ\widehat s/(\mu+h)-e\right\|_\infty\le\theta.

notation.meaning: componentwise central neighborhood at the trial parameter

review_flags: This acceptance predicate gives no uniform lower bound on parameter reduction.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Step Quadratic-Trajectory Acceptance Predicate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the first two parameter derivatives used by quadratic trajectory models at a regular positive central point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank and let \((x(\mu),y(\mu),s(\mu))\) satisfy \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(x\circ s=\mu e\), with \(x,s>0\). At every parameter where the central-path Jacobian is nonsingular, the tangent and curvature are the unique solutions of \[Ax'=0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y'+s'=0,\quad Sx'+Xs'=e,\] \[Ax''=0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y''+s''=0,\quad Sx''+Xs''=-2(x'\circ s').\] Both systems have the same coefficient matrix and different complementarity right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The central-path tangent and curvature solve two linear systems with one common Jacobian; the curvature right-hand side is negative twice the componentwise product of the tangent components.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank.
\(x,s>0\) and the primal-dual central equations hold.
The central-path Jacobian is nonsingular at the current positive parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x',y',s')\text{ and }(x'',y'',s'')\text{ are uniquely determined by the displayed common-Jacobian systems}.

notation.meaning: diagonal matrices formed from x and s

review_flags: Defines exact derivatives only at a regular central point; it does not establish a repeated-step complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Tangent-and-Curvature Central-Path System
Second-Order Trajectory Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A curvature-corrected step obtained from first and second derivatives of the primal-dual central path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a central point \((x,y,s)\) at parameter \(\mu>0\), solve
\[
Ax'=0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y'+s'=0,\quad Sx'+Xs'=e,
\]
then solve with the same Jacobian
\[
Ax''=0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y''+s''=0,\quad Sx''+Xs''=-2X's'.
\]
Choose \(h<0\) by backtracking so that \(x+h x'+h^2x''/2>0\), \(s+h s'+h^2s''/2>0\), and the trial point lies in the prescribed central neighborhood. Accept the quadratic trajectory approximation, set \(\mu\leftarrow\mu+h\), and stop when the new complementarity measure is at most the requested tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute tangent and curvature directions from two systems sharing one Jacobian, then take a positivity-preserving quadratic approximation to the central trajectory.
assumptions_latex: The current point satisfies \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(Xs=\mu e\) with \(x,s>0\).
The central-path Jacobian is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted point is the second-order Taylor approximation to the central path and remains positive in the chosen neighborhood.

notation.meaning: diagonal matrix of the primal tangent

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Direction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive central-path derivative directions of order greater than two using a shared primal-dual Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a regular central point, initialize \(z^{(0)}=(x,y,s)\). For \(r=1,\ldots,q\), solve with the current central-path Jacobian
\[
Ax^{(r)}=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y^{(r)}+s^{(r)}=0,
\]
\[
Sx^{(r)}+Xs^{(r)}=\mathbf 1_{\{r=1\}}e-\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}{r\choose j}X^{(j)}s^{(r-j)}.
\]
Form \(z(h)=\sum_{r=0}^{q}h^r z^{(r)}/r!\). Choose \(h<0\) so that the trial primal and slack vectors are positive and satisfy the prescribed neighborhood test; accept the trial point and stop when its complementarity is below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order methods recursively compute central-path derivatives with one Jacobian and use a truncated Taylor trajectory subject to positivity and neighborhood tests.
assumptions_latex: The current point lies on a regular primal-dual central path.
The requested derivative order satisfies \(q\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trial curve matches the central path through derivative order \(q\) at the current parameter.

notation.meaning: r-th derivative of the primal-dual path
