Indeterminate Status Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status boundary when no validated solution or certificate supports a definitive LP status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an interior-point run stops because of an iteration, time, memory, numerical-factorization, or stagnation limit, and the reconstructed output satisfies neither the approximate optimality predicate nor a validated infeasibility or unboundedness certificate, the solver must return an indeterminate status. It may attach the best iterate \((x,y,s)\), residuals, objective values, and the stopping reason, but it must not relabel the outcome optimal, infeasible, or unbounded. Likewise, simultaneous approximate evidence for incompatible statuses, or failure of original-space postsolve validation, requires indeterminate handling until tighter validation resolves the conflict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resource limits, numerical failure, conflicting evidence, or failed postsolve validation require an indeterminate status unless a definitive termination predicate is validated.
assumptions_latex: Termination statuses are assigned only through explicit predicates and original-space validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absence of a validated definitive predicate forces an indeterminate rather than optimal, infeasible, or unbounded status.

children.title: Crossover Procedures
children.top_down_role: Procedures converting an interior solution toward a vertex representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic simplex-style conversion of an interior-point output into a basic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), select \(m\) linearly independent columns \(B\), put \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B\), and compute \(x_N=0\), \(A_Bx_B=b\), \(A_B^\top y=c_B\), and \(r_N=c_N-A_N^\top y\). If \(x_B\ge0\), primal-simplex pivots may retain primal feasibility while repairing negative reduced costs; if \(r_N\ge0\), dual-simplex pivots may retain dual feasibility while repairing negative basic values. If neither side is feasible, a phase-I or other crash-repair procedure is required. Accept an output only after independent basis validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossover forms an independent candidate basis and uses primal, dual, or phase-I simplex repair according to which feasibility conditions initially hold.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
The selected set \(B\) has \(m\) indices and \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a candidate basic solution for validation or reports that the selected repair procedure did not produce one.

notation.meaning: Basic and nonbasic column index sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Output Need Not Be Basic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary motivating crossover as a separate solver-lifecycle operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible point in the relative interior of a positive-dimensional optimal face need not be a vertex or a basic feasible solution. In particular, a strictly positive feasible point for a full-row-rank standard-form system with \(m<n\) has more than \(m\) positive components and cannot be basic. Thus convergence to such an interior optimum does not itself identify or output a basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior optimum on a positive-dimensional face can be nonbasic, so optimization convergence alone does not perform crossover.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m<n\).
The returned optimum is strictly positive or lies in the relative interior of a positive-dimensional optimal face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A separate selection and repair operation is needed to obtain a basic representation.

Crossover Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual crossover from an interior iterate to a basic LP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a near-optimal primal-dual point \((x,y,s)\) for \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\). Select an index set \(B\) of \(m\) linearly independent columns, set \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B\), and compute \(x_N=0\), \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(y_B=A_B^{-T}c_B\), and \(s_N=c_N-A_N^Ty_B\), with \(s_B=0\). If primal or dual signs fail, perform primal or dual simplex pivots initialized from this basis until feasibility and the requested optimality tolerance hold or failure is declared. Output the validated basis and associated basic primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossover selects an independent basis near the interior solution, reconstructs its basic primal-dual point, and repairs sign violations by simplex pivots.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\).
The input iterate is sufficiently accurate to guide basis selection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a validated basic primal-dual solution and basis, or an explicit crossover failure.

children.title: Basis Identification
children.top_down_role: Selection of candidate basic and nonbasic variable classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic identification of a candidate basis without prescribing a solver-specific score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} with \operatorname{rank}(A)=m, form any priority ordering of columns from the approximate primal values and dual slacks, favoring indices with comparatively large x_j and small s_j. Scan that ordering and retain a column exactly when it increases the rank of the retained set; continue until m columns have been retained. The resulting set B has |B|=m and A_B nonsingular. This construction produces only a candidate basis: it does not certify primal feasibility, reduced-cost optimality, or numerical conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use complementarity information only to order columns, then greedily retain independent columns until a candidate basis is obtained.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n} has full row rank.
Rank decisions are exact; numerical implementations require a separate rank tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scan terminates with |B|=m and nonsingular A_B, but optimality and numerical acceptability remain unverified.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementarity-Prioritized Rank Completion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite identification of a nondegenerate optimal basis from a convergent primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\} with A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c and s\geq0. Suppose an optimal pair has B\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}, |B|=m, A_B nonsingular, x_B^*>0, x_N^*=0, s_B^*=0, and s_N^*>0. Let \gamma=\min\{\min_{j\in B}x_j^*,\min_{j\in N}s_j^*\}>0. If \|x-x^*\|_\infty<\gamma/3 and \|s-s^*\|_\infty<\gamma/3, then B=\{j:x_j>2\gamma/3\}=\{j:s_j<\gamma/3\}. Consequently, any primal-dual sequence converging to this pair identifies B after finitely many iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly separated nondegenerate optimal basis is recovered exactly once primal and dual variables are sufficiently close to their limits.
assumptions_latex: A_B is nonsingular and |B|=m.
The approximate pair lies within \gamma/3 in both infinity norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The thresholded primal-positive and dual-zero sets both equal B, giving finite identification along every convergent sequence.

notation.meaning: Indices of the nondegenerate optimal basis.
Minimum positive primal or dual separation at the optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Identification Under Strict Separation
Basis Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementarity-guided identification of a nonsingular candidate basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), an interior pair \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and threshold \(\tau>0\), assign each column the score \(q_j=\log(x_j+\tau)-\log(s_j+\tau)\). Process indices in nonincreasing \(q_j\), adding index \(j\) whenever its column increases the rank of the selected columns, until \(m\) indices have been accepted. The resulting set \(B\) is a candidate basis; if fewer than \(m\) columns are obtained, basis identification fails. Before crossover, explicitly factor \(A_B\) and reject or repair \(B\) when its numerical rank or conditioning violates the solver threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Columns favored by large primal values and small dual slacks are greedily selected subject to independence, then checked numerically as a candidate basis.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\).
The score threshold \(\tau\) and numerical-rank tolerance are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful selection produces \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\) and numerically nonsingular \(A_B\).

children.title: Degeneracy-Aware Crossover
children.top_down_role: Crossover behavior when several bases represent the same solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bland and lexicographic variants for degenerate simplex-style crossover repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: During exact-arithmetic primal or dual simplex repair, zero-length pivots may be taken. Bland's rule chooses the smallest-index eligible entering variable and the smallest-index eligible leaving variable among minimum-ratio ties. Alternatively, a lexicographic ratio test selects the lexicographically first admissible normalized comparison vector. When the corresponding standard simplex eligibility rules are used consistently, either rule prevents cycling and yields finite termination over the finite set of bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bland or lexicographic pivoting permits degenerate pivots while preventing cycling in exact arithmetic.
assumptions_latex: Eligibility, ratio tests, and tie-breaking are evaluated exactly.
The relevant primal or dual simplex method uses its standard termination alternatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The repair sequence does not cycle and terminates after finitely many basis changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Anti-Cycling Crossover Rules

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on transferring exact anti-cycling conclusions to numerical crossover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact noncycling conclusions for Bland or lexicographic rules do not follow merely from approximate feasibility, eligibility, and tie tests. Inconsistent tolerance decisions can make a previously visited basis eligible again. A floating-point implementation needs a consistently implemented perturbation or lexicographic scheme, an explicit repeated-basis safeguard, or another separately justified numerical anti-cycling mechanism before finite termination can be claimed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact anti-cycling theorems do not automatically survive inconsistent floating-point tolerance tests.
assumptions_latex: Pivot eligibility or ties are decided using nonzero numerical tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite numerical termination requires an additional consistent anti-cycling mechanism.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Anti-Cycling Boundary
Degeneracy-Aware Crossover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anti-cycling crossover for bases admitting zero-length or tied pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: During simplex repair of a crossover basis, permit zero-length pivots but apply Bland's rule to every ambiguity: choose the smallest-index eligible entering variable, and among all leaving variables attaining the minimum ratio choose the smallest-index one. Recompute or update the basis factorization after each pivot and validate rank before accepting the new basis. In exact arithmetic, if the standard primal or dual simplex eligibility conditions are used consistently, this index rule prevents repetition of a basis and hence prevents cycling despite degeneracy. Stop with a validated basic solution, a definitive certificate, or an explicit numerical crossover failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degenerate crossover permits zero steps but uses smallest-index entering and leaving choices to prevent basis cycling, with rank validation after every pivot.
assumptions_latex: Simplex repair uses exact eligibility and ratio tests, or numerically consistent tolerance variants.
The LP has finitely many candidate bases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: In exact arithmetic, Bland tie-breaking prevents cycling and the crossover pivot sequence terminates finitely.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validation certificate for a candidate optimal basis in standard-form minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\). For \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\) and complement \(N\), compute \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(x_N=0\), \(y=A_B^{-\top}c_B\), and \(r_N=c_N-A_N^\top y\). The data \((B,x,y,r_N)\) validate an optimal basis when \(A_B\) is nonsingular, \(x_B\ge0\), and \(r_N\ge0\). Indeed, the associated primal and dual solutions are feasible and satisfy \(c^\top x=b^\top y\); zero basic variables or zero reduced costs indicate degeneracy or alternative optimal bases but do not invalidate the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular basis is validated by nonnegative basic values and nonnegative nonbasic reduced costs; their primal and dual objectives then agree.

\(A_B\) is square and nonsingular
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_B\ge0\) and \(r_N\ge0\) certify primal-dual optimality of the basis solution.

Passing nonzero tolerances certifies only compliance with those tests; it is not an exact optimality certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Form Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slack and barrier representation of finite lower and upper row bounds, with equality rows handled separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\ell\le Gx\le u\), where \(G\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\) and components of \(\ell\) and \(u\) may be infinite. If \(\ell_i=u_i\in\mathbb R\), row \(i\) is the equality \(G_i x=\ell_i\) and receives no logarithmic-barrier term. Otherwise, define \(t_i=G_i x-\ell_i\ge0\) for every finite lower bound and \(s_i=u_i-G_i x\ge0\) for every finite upper bound. A logarithmic-barrier realization adds \(-\mu\sum_i\log t_i-\mu\sum_i\log s_i\), with each sum taken only over the defined inequality slacks, and requires those slacks to be positive. Infinite bounds contribute neither a slack inequality nor a barrier term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite inequality sides receive nonnegative slacks and logarithmic-barrier terms; equality rows are imposed directly, and infinite bounds are omitted.
assumptions_latex: \(G\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\)
\(\ell_i\le u_i\) whenever both bounds are finite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The row system is equivalent to its equality rows together with nonnegativity of every defined inequality slack.

notation.meaning: Slack for a finite lower inequality bound.
Slack for a finite upper inequality bound.

source_refs.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hessian contributions of finite lower and upper row sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_\ell=\{i:\ell_i> -\infty,\ \ell_i<u_i\}\) and \(I_u=\{i:u_i<+\infty,\ \ell_i<u_i\}\). On the strict interior set \(t_i=G_ix-\ell_i>0\) and \(s_i=u_i-G_ix>0\), and define \(\phi(x)=-\sum_{i\in I_\ell}\log t_i-\sum_{i\in I_u}\log s_i\). Then \(\nabla^2\phi(x)=G^{\mathsf T}WG\), where \(W\) is diagonal with \(W_{ii}=\mathbf 1_{i\in I_\ell}t_i^{-2}+\mathbf 1_{i\in I_u}s_i^{-2}\). Thus a one-sided row contributes one positive rank-one weight, a proper ranged row contributes two, an equality row is excluded from the barrier, and an infinite side contributes zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each finite inequality side contributes inverse-square row curvature; a proper ranged row receives contributions from both sides.
assumptions_latex: Every included slack is strictly positive.
Rows with equal finite bounds are imposed as equalities rather than barrier inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla^2\phi(x)=G^{\mathsf T}WG,\qquad W_{ii}=\mathbf 1_{i\in I_\ell}t_i^{-2}+\mathbf 1_{i\in I_u}s_i^{-2}.

notation.meaning: indices having proper finite lower and upper inequality sides

children.title: Lower-Bound Handling
children.top_down_role: Representation choices for finite variable lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of finite variable lower bounds to nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the minimization problem \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge\ell\}\) with finite \(\ell\in\mathbb R^n\), set \(z=x-\ell\). Then \(z\ge0\), \(Az=b-A\ell\), and \(c^\top x=c^\top z+c^\top\ell\). Thus translation gives a bijection between feasible points and preserves minimizers after adding the constant \(c^\top\ell\). In a barrier method the lower-bound distance is exactly \(z_i=x_i-\ell_i\), so strict bound feasibility is \(z_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translate each finite lower bound to zero; feasibility and minimizers are preserved, with only the right-hand side and objective constant changed.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\in\mathbb R^n\) is finite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto z=x-\ell\) bijects the original feasible set with \(\{z:Az=b-A\ell,\ z\ge0\}\).

children.title: Upper-Bound Handling
children.top_down_role: Representation choices for finite variable upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement transformation of finite variable upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\le u\}\) with finite \(u\in\mathbb R^n\), define \(z=u-x\). Then \(z\ge0\), \(Az=Au-b\), and \(c^\top x=c^\top u-c^\top z\). The substitution is bijective and converts upper bounds to nonnegativity while negating the corresponding objective coefficients. Direct substitution gives \(-Az=b-Au\); multiplying this equality by \(-1\) gives the displayed form. Strict upper-bound feasibility is equivalent to \(z_i=u_i-x_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace an upper-bounded variable by its distance from the upper bound; the substitution is bijective and negates its objective coefficient, with an equivalent sign choice for the transformed equality.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) is finite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto z=u-x\) bijects the original feasible set with \(\{z:Az=Au-b,\ z\ge0\}\).

children.title: Fixed-Variable Handling
children.top_down_role: Treatment of variables whose lower and upper limits coincide.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Variable Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination of variables whose lower and upper bounds coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the variables as \(x=(x_F,x_R)\) and suppose \(x_F=f\) is fixed by coincident bounds. In \(Ax=b\) and objective \(c^\top x\), eliminate \(x_F\) to obtain \(A_Rx_R=b-A_Ff\) and objective \(c_R^\top x_R+c_F^\top f\). The reduced problem has a one-to-one correspondence with feasible and optimal solutions of the original problem after restoring \(x_F=f\). Elimination avoids assigning a logarithmic barrier to a variable having no strictly feasible interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Remove fixed variables, shift their column contributions into the right-hand side, and restore their fixed values after solving.
assumptions_latex: \(x_F=f\) is imposed exactly
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reduced and original LPs have corresponding feasible points and identical objective ordering.

children.title: Bound-Transformation Effects
children.top_down_role: Size, sparsity, and conditioning consequences of transformed bound representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Transformation Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence and numerical non-invariance under affine variable transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=q+Dz\), where \(D\) is nonsingular and chosen to normalize or complement variable bounds. Then \(Ax=b\) becomes \(ADz=b-Aq\), while \(c^\top x=(D^\top c)^\top z+c^\top q\). Hence the transformation preserves feasibility and objective ordering bijectively. Numerical geometry is not invariant: a local quadratic metric \(H\) transforms to \(D^\top H D\), and generally \(\kappa_2(D^\top H D)\ne\kappa_2(H)\). Bound transformations can therefore improve or worsen scaling and the conditioning of interior-point linear systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible bound transformations preserve the LP mathematically but can substantially change scaling and linear-system conditioning.
assumptions_latex: \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular
\(H\) is symmetric positive definite
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Affine equivalence preserves solutions but does not preserve the spectral condition number of the local metric.

children.title: Free-Variable Representations
children.top_down_role: Alternative representations and their dimensional and conditioning effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Free-Variable Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Native and split-variable representations of an unrestricted LP variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unrestricted scalar variable \(x_j\in\mathbb R\) may remain native, in which case it receives no one-sided logarithmic barrier, or be replaced by \(x_j=p_j-q_j\) with \(p_j,q_j\ge0\). The split representation preserves all attainable values and replaces a constraint column \(a_j\) by \((a_j,-a_j)\), but increases dimension by one. It is not injective because \((p_j,q_j)\) and \((p_j+t,q_j+t)\) represent the same value for every admissible \(t\). This redundant direction can affect scaling, conditioning, and crossover identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A free variable may remain unrestricted or be split into two nonnegative variables; splitting adds dimension and a redundant representation direction.
assumptions_latex: \(x_j\) has no finite lower or upper bound
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_j=p_j-q_j\) is surjective onto \(\mathbb R\) but is not one-to-one on \(\mathbb R_+^2\).

notation.meaning: Constraint-matrix column of the free variable.

source_refs.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Background: Linear Programming and Interior-Point Methods p. 21

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the ordinary nonnegative-variable logarithmic barrier on an unrestricted split representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace a free variable \(x\) by \(x=p-q\) with \(p,q>0\). Every inherited constraint and objective term depends on \((p,q)\) only through \(p-q\), so \((p,q)\mapsto(p+t,q+t)\) preserves them for \(t\ge0\). The ordinary barrier contribution \(-\mu(\log p+\log q)\) tends to \(-\infty\) along this ray. For example, \(\min\{0:x\in\mathbb R\}\) becomes the barrier problem \(\inf_{p,q>0}-\mu(\log p+\log q)=-\infty\). Thus an unmodified split lift need not possess a barrier minimizer or central path even though the original LP has optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The redundant common-positive ray of a split free variable can make its ordinary logarithmic-barrier subproblem unbounded.
assumptions_latex: No additional constraint bounds the redundant direction \((p,q)\mapsto(p+t,q+t)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{t\ge0}-\mu[\log(p+t)+\log(q+t)]=-\infty.

notation.meaning: displacement along the redundant common ray

children.title: Geometric Robustness Boundaries

children.title: Empty or Thin Primal-Dual Interiors
children.top_down_role: Failure of strict-interiority regimes and the need for reformulation, embedding, or facial reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty or Thin Primal-Dual Interiors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for strictly feasible primal-dual central-path equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^\top y:A^\top y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), a strictly feasible central-path point at \(\mu>0\) satisfies primal and dual feasibility together with \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and \(XSe=\mu e\). If either feasible set has no point satisfying its strict inequalities, these equations have no solution. Forced zero variables or slacks make the ambient interior empty even when a relative interior exists; direct strict-interiority path following then requires elimination, reformulation, embedding, or facial reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If primal or dual strict feasibility is absent, the usual positive central path cannot exist, even though feasible relative-interior points may remain.
assumptions_latex: The LP is expressed in standard primal-dual form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absence of primal or dual strict feasibility implies nonexistence of a strictly feasible central-path point.

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrices formed from primal variables and dual slacks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal Coordinate-Face Reduction for Thin Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduction of a nonempty standard-form feasible set with forced-zero coordinates to its minimal coordinate face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\ne\varnothing\), define \(B=\{i:\exists x\in P\text{ with }x_i>0\}\), and let \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B\). Then every \(x\in P\) satisfies \(x_N=0\), and there exists \(\bar x\in P\) with \(\bar x_B>0\). Hence \(P\) lies in the coordinate face \(\{x\ge0:x_N=0\}\) and has nonempty relative interior within that face. Eliminating the forced-zero variables \(x_N\) converts ambient thinness into strict positivity on the surviving coordinates. The same construction applies to a nonempty dual-slack set by replacing \(x\) with \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All coordinates that can never be positive are forced to zero; after deleting them, a feasible point exists that is positive in every surviving coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) is nonempty.
\(B\) and \(N\) are defined by coordinatewise attainability of strict positivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_N=0\) for all \(x\in P\) and \(\exists\bar x\in P\) such that \(\bar x_B>0\).

notation.meaning: Coordinates positive at some feasible point
Coordinates forced to zero throughout the feasible set
A relative-interior feasible point positive on all surviving coordinates

children.title: Degenerate Optimal Faces
children.top_down_role: Optimal-face structures exhibiting degeneracy.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Optimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis-degeneracy sense for an optimal face of a standard-form LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), and let \(F^*=\{x\in P:c^\top x=v^*\}\) be the optimal face. An optimal basic feasible point \(x\in F^*\) is degenerate when fewer than \(m\) components of \(x\) are positive, equivalently when at least one variable in an associated basis is zero. In the local basis-degeneracy sense, \(F^*\) is called degenerate when it contains such a point. A degenerate point can correspond to several bases, so the point alone need not identify a unique active-set representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal face is basis-degenerate here when it contains an optimal basic feasible point with a zero basic variable.
assumptions_latex: \(P\ne\varnothing\)
\(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\)
The optimal value \(v^*\) is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy means an optimal basic feasible point has fewer than \(m\) positive components.

children.title: Multiple Optimal Faces
children.top_down_role: Optimal sets with nonunique face or solution representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Many Optimal Proper Faces Within One Optimizer Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes faces composed entirely of optimizers from multiple disjoint complete optimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[0,1]^2\) and \(c=0\). Then \(F^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=P\). Its four vertices and four edges are distinct nonempty proper faces composed entirely of optimal points, while the complete optimizer set is the single maximal face \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a constant objective on a square, every edge and vertex is optimal, while the complete optimizer set remains one maximal face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^*=P\text{ is one maximal optimizer face containing eight distinct nonempty proper faces of optimal points.}
review_flags: Proper subfaces consist of optimal points but are not separate complete argmin sets for the fixed objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Many Optimal Proper Faces Within One Optimizer Face

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Tests for Multiple Optimal Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes multiplicity of optimizers without asserting basis degeneracy or selecting a representative optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron and suppose \(F^*=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is nonempty. The following are equivalent: \(F^*\) contains two distinct points; \(F^*\) contains a nontrivial line segment; and \(\dim(F^*)\ge1\). Every convex combination of optimal points is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained LP has multiple optimal solutions exactly when its optimizer face has positive dimension, equivalently when it contains a nontrivial optimal segment.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron.
The finite minimum is attained, so \(F^*\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |F^*|>1\iff \exists x^1\ne x^2:\ [x^1,x^2]\subseteq F^*\iff\dim(F^*)\ge1.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Tests for Multiple Optimal Solutions
Multiple Optimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarifies uniqueness of the maximal optimal face and multiplicity of its subfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polyhedron \(P\) and an attained finite minimum \(v^*=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\), the complete solution set \(F^*=\{x\in P:c^\top x=v^*\}\) is one uniquely determined exposed face of \(P\). Thus a fixed linear objective cannot have several disjoint maximal optimal faces. However, every nonempty face contained in \(F^*\) is also composed entirely of optimal points, so \(F^*\) may contain multiple optimal vertices, edges, and other proper subfaces, each admitting different active sets or bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full optimizer set is one exposed face, but it may contain many optimal proper faces, vertices, and basis representations.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron
\(v^*\) is finite and attained
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*=P\cap\{x:c^\top x=v^*\}\) is the unique maximal optimal face.

children.title: Convergence-Rate Degradation
children.top_down_role: Rate deterioration associated with degenerate or nonunique optimal geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence-Rate Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of nonsingular-Newton guarantees at degenerate primal-dual solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the primal-dual KKT residual \(F(x,y,s)=(Ax-b,\ A^\top y+s-c,\ Xs)\). At a solution \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\), its Jacobian is \[J^*=\begin{pmatrix}A&0&0\\0&A^\top&I\\S^*&0&X^*\end{pmatrix}.\] If degeneracy or failure of strict complementarity makes \(J^*\) singular, the standard nonsingular-Jacobian hypotheses used to obtain local quadratic Newton convergence are absent. Consequently, quadratic or superlinear convergence and stable identification of the optimal face cannot be inferred from that theory; steps may instead be governed by regularization, neighborhood restrictions, or higher-order error terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular limiting KKT Jacobian removes the usual local quadratic-convergence guarantee and can make face identification and steps less stable.
assumptions_latex: \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) satisfies the primal-dual KKT equations
\(J^*\) is singular
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Standard nonsingular-Newton theory supplies no quadratic local convergence guarantee at the solution.

notation.meaning: KKT Jacobian at the limiting solution.

children.title: Solution-Recovery Ambiguity

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Recovery Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-variable LP whose interior limit does not determine a unique optimal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min 0\) subject to \(x_1+x_2=1\) and \(x_1,x_2\ge0\). Every feasible point is optimal, while the logarithmic-barrier minimizer of \(-\mu(\log x_1+\log x_2)\) is \(x(\mu)=(1/2,1/2)\) for every \(\mu>0\). Crossover may recover either optimal vertex \((1,0)\) or \((0,1)\), corresponding respectively to bases \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\). Hence the interior solution and objective value do not determine a unique basic optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The analytic center of an optimal segment is unique, yet crossover can legitimately return either endpoint and either associated basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interior-point limit \((1/2,1/2)\) does not identify a unique optimal vertex or basis.

children.title: Failure of Strict Complementarity
children.top_down_role: Non-strict complementary regimes affecting endpoint and local-rate geometry.

assumptions_latex: The primal-dual pair is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\ge 0\}\).
The triple \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) is primal-dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) is not strictly complementary if and only if \(x_i^*=s_i^*=0\) for at least one \(i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard-form primal-dual pair, complementarity gives \(x_i^*s_i^*=0\) for every \(i\). The optimal triple \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) is strictly complementary when \(x_i^*+s_i^*>0\) for every \(i\). Consequently, strict complementarity fails at this triple precisely when the transition set \(T:=\{i:x_i^*=s_i^*=0\}\) is nonempty. Such a pair does not induce the disjoint positive-support partition \(\{i:x_i^*>0\}\cup\{i:s_i^*>0\}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), even though another optimal pair may be strictly complementary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal pair fails strict complementarity when at least one variable and its complementary dual slack are both zero.

children.title: Feasibility-Boundary Ill-Posedness
children.top_down_role: Instability near feasibility-status boundaries.

children.title: Near-Infeasible Instances
children.top_down_role: Models lying close to a change in feasibility status.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-qualified regime under a fixed data norm; the tolerance and scaling convention are part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a norm \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal D}\) and an absolute data tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). Let \(\mathcal I\) be the infeasible-data set for \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\), and let \(\rho(d)=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal D}(d,\mathcal I)\). A feasible datum \(d\) is \(\varepsilon\)-near-infeasible when \(0<\rho(d)\le\varepsilon\). The strict lower inequality distinguishes this regime from feasibility-ill-posed boundary data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed norm and tolerance, a feasible instance is near-infeasible when its positive distance to infeasible data is no greater than the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The data space and norm \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal D}\) are fixed.
\(\varepsilon>0\) is a declared absolute data tolerance.
The datum \(d\) is feasible for \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-near-infeasible}\Longleftrightarrow 0<\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal D}(d,\mathcal I)\le\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Infeasible Feasible Data

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-infeasibility is not invariant under an arbitrary nonisometric reparameterization of the data unless the norm or tolerance is transformed with it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be an invertible reparameterization of the data that maps feasible data to feasible data and infeasible data to infeasible data. In general, \(\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal D}(Td,T\mathcal I)\neq\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal D}(d,\mathcal I)\). Consequently, with the same numerical tolerance \(\varepsilon\), the classifications \(0<\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal D}(d,\mathcal I)\le\varepsilon\) and \(0<\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal D}(Td,T\mathcal I)\le\varepsilon\) need not agree. They are guaranteed to agree under this convention when \(T\) is an isometry of the selected data norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed absolute near-infeasibility threshold can change under equivalent but nonisometric scaling of the model data.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is invertible and preserves feasibility status.
The same data norm and numerical tolerance are used before and after reparameterization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ nonisometric}\Longrightarrow\text{near-infeasibility classification need not be invariant}.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling Dependence of Near-Infeasibility Classification

assumptions_latex: Data are \(d=(A,b)\) for the feasibility system \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\).
A norm \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal D}\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) are fixed on the data space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible datum is \(\varepsilon\)-near-infeasible when \(0<\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal D}(d,\mathcal I)\le\varepsilon\|d\|_{\mathcal D}\).

notation.meaning: Distance induced by the selected data norm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A norm-relative definition for primal standard-form feasibility; numerical thresholds depend on data scaling.

source_refs.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F:=\{(A,b):\exists x\ge0,\ Ax=b\}\) and \(\mathcal I:=\mathcal D\setminus\mathcal F\). A datum \(d=(A,b)\in\mathcal F\) is \(\varepsilon\)-near-infeasible, relative to \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal D}\), when its relative distance to infeasibility satisfies \[0<\frac{\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal D}(d,\mathcal I)}{\|d\|_{\mathcal D}}\le\varepsilon.\] Thus a perturbation whose norm is comparable to \(\varepsilon\|d\|_{\mathcal D}\) can approach or cross the feasibility boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible LP is near-infeasible when its distance to infeasible data is positive but small relative to the chosen data norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) denote the infeasible-data set and define \(\rho(d):=\inf_{q\in\mathcal I}\|d-q\|_{\mathcal D}\). knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instability concerns persistence of a fixed normalized Farkas certificate and degeneration of its margins under data perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\) be a normalized Farkas certificate satisfying \(\|y\|_2=1\), \(A^Ty\ge 0\), and \(b^Ty<0\). Define \(m_A(y):=\min_i(A^Ty)_i\) and \(m_b(y):=-b^Ty\). If \(m_A(y)=0\), arbitrarily small perturbations of an active column of \(A\) can make the same vector \(y\) violate \((A+\Delta A)^Ty\ge0\). For perturbations of \(b\), the fixed certificate remains strict whenever \(\|\Delta b\|_2<m_b(y)\); consequently, along a family of certificates with \(m_b(y)\downarrow0\), the guaranteed perturbation radius for preserving strict separation vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed Farkas certificate is unstable to matrix perturbations when its cone margin is zero, while a family whose positive separation margins approach zero has a vanishing robustness radius for right-hand-side perturbations.
assumptions_latex: The system is \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\).
The vector \(y\) satisfies \(\|y\|_2=1\), \(A^Ty\ge0\), and \(b^Ty<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A zero cone margin permits arbitrarily small perturbations of \(A\) to invalidate the fixed certificate, and separation margins tending to zero imply vanishing robustness to perturbations of \(b\).

notation.meaning: Smallest cone-membership margin of the certificate

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Normal Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic singularity of the positive-diagonal primal-dual normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be diagonal with \(D\succ0\), and define \(N:=ADA^T\). Then \(\ker(N)=\ker(A^T)\). Consequently, \(N\) is singular if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive diagonal scaling, the normal-equations matrix has the same null space as the transpose of the constraint matrix and is singular exactly when the constraints lack full row rank.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compatibility and Solutions of Singular Normal Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact solvability and nonuniqueness boundary for the seed's normal-equations matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=ADA^T\) with \(D\succ0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<m\). The equation \(Ny=g\) is solvable if and only if \(g\in\operatorname{range}(A)\), equivalently \(z^Tg=0\) for every \(z\in\ker(A^T)\). If solvable, all solutions are \(y=N^\dagger g+z\) with \(z\in\ker(A^T)\), and \(N^\dagger g\) is the unique minimum-norm solution.

\(\operatorname{rank}(A)<m\).

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Augmented Systems

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compatibility and Nonuniqueness of a Singular Augmented System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact solvability boundary for the singular augmented matrix in the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\begin{bmatrix}-D^{-1}&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\) with \(D\succ0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<m\). The system \(K\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r_d\\r_p\end{bmatrix}\) is solvable if and only if \(z^Tr_p=0\) for every \(z\in\ker(A^T)\). When solvable, \(u\) is unique and the multiplier solutions are exactly \(v_0+\ker(A^T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular augmented system is solvable exactly when its constraint-block right-hand side respects every row dependency; only its multiplier component is then nonunique.

\(\operatorname{rank}(A)<m\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h\in\ker(A)\), then \(A(\Delta x+h)=A\Delta x\), so the equality equations alone cannot distinguish primal Newton directions differing by \(h\). If \(z\in\ker(A^T)\), then \(A^T(\Delta y+z)=A^T\Delta y\), so the dual equations cannot distinguish multiplier directions differing by \(z\). In particular, row-rank deficiency creates nonuniqueness in \(\Delta y\), whereas a nontrivial \(\ker(A)\) supplies homogeneous primal feasible directions whose eventual admissibility is restricted by nonnegativity and complementarity equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Right-null directions preserve primal equalities, while left-null directions are invisible in dual equations and create multiplier nonuniqueness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical resolution of the seed's nonuniqueness without altering the underlying equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A\Delta x=r_p\) is consistent and \(\Delta x_0\) is one solution, every solution is \(\Delta x_0+h\) with \(h\in\ker(A)\); exactly one lies in \(\operatorname{range}(A^T)\), and it is the minimum-Euclidean-norm solution. Likewise, all \(\Delta y\) satisfying \(A^T\Delta y=q\) form \(\Delta y_0+\ker(A^T)\), with a unique minimum-norm representative in \(\operatorname{range}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each affine class created by a null space has a unique orthogonal minimum-norm representative.
assumptions_latex: The displayed linear equations are consistent.

children.title: Small-Pivot Instability
children.top_down_role: Reliability loss caused by pivots near numerical resolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Small-Pivot Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary is stated through unbounded elimination multipliers; quantitative rounding-error conclusions require a separate floating-point model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At elimination step \(k\), let \(p_k\ne0\) be the pivot and let \(a_{ik}^{(k)}\) be an entry eliminated with multiplier \(\ell_{ik}:=a_{ik}^{(k)}/p_k\). For any family satisfying \(|p_k|/|a_{ik}^{(k)}|\to0\), one has \(|\ell_{ik}|\to\infty\). Thus pivots that vanish relative to their elimination-column entries produce unbounded multiplier and update amplification in unpivoted elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivot that becomes tiny relative to an entry it must eliminate produces an unbounded elimination multiplier and unbounded algebraic update amplification.
assumptions_latex: At step \(k\), elimination uses a nonzero pivot \(p_k\) and an entry \(a_{ik}^{(k)}\) below it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|p_k|/|a_{ik}^{(k)}|\to0\), then \(|\ell_{ik}|=|a_{ik}^{(k)}/p_k|\to\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Column Partial Pivoting Bounds Local Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local mitigation of small-pivot amplification; cumulative element growth belongs to the pivot-growth sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At elimination step \(k\), suppose partial pivoting selects \(p_k=a_{rk}^{(k)}\) with \(|p_k|=\max_{i\ge k}|a_{ik}^{(k)}|>0\). Then every multiplier used in that column satisfies \(|\ell_{ik}|=|a_{ik}^{(k)}/p_k|\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing the largest available entry in the elimination column bounds every local elimination multiplier by one.
assumptions_latex: Partial pivoting selects a nonzero entry of maximum magnitude in the active elimination column.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\ell_{ik}|\le1\quad\text{for every eliminated row }i.
knowledge_statements.title: Column Partial Pivoting Bounds Local Multipliers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Small Pivot Can Be an Ordering Artifact
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates a small initial pivot from singularity or intrinsic ill-conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A_\varepsilon=\begin{bmatrix}\varepsilon&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(0<\varepsilon<1\), unpivoted elimination has \(p_1=\varepsilon\), \(\ell_{21}=1/\varepsilon\), and \(u_{22}=1-1/\varepsilon\). Thus \(|\ell_{21}|\to\infty\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), although \(A_\varepsilon\to\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\), whose determinant is \(-1\). Interchanging the rows gives first pivot \(1\) and multiplier \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly nonsingular matrix family can have an arbitrarily small unpivoted pivot, while a row interchange removes the local pathology.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell_{21}=\varepsilon^{-1}\to\infty\text{ without pivoting, whereas the row-pivoted multiplier is }\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: A Small Pivot Can Be an Ordering Artifact

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite-Factorization Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional counterexample isolates the need for block pivoting in scalar indefinite symmetric factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The matrix \(K:=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) is nonsingular and symmetric indefinite, but scalar unpivoted \(LDL^T\) factorization encounters the zero first pivot \(d_1=K_{11}=0\). Both diagonal entries of \(K\) are zero, so a symmetric permutation alone cannot provide a nonzero scalar leading pivot; a \(2\times2\) pivot block handles this matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular symmetric indefinite matrix can have no usable scalar diagonal pivot, causing scalar LDL-transpose factorization to break down and requiring a two-by-two pivot block.

children.title: Pivot-Growth Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Numerical regimes in which pivot growth undermines factor accuracy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Element growth is defined for the intermediate matrices produced by one fixed elimination and pivoting algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\neq0\) be processed by a fixed elimination algorithm, and let \(K^{(0)}=K,K^{(1)},\ldots,K^{(r)}\) be the active or updated matrices whose entries the algorithm monitors. Its element-growth factor is \[\rho(K)=\frac{\max_{0\le j\le r}\|K^{(j)}\|_{\max}}{\|K\|_{\max}}.\] The matrix sequence is part of the definition; growth factors formed from Schur complements, stored factors, or other intermediates need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The element-growth factor is the largest monitored intermediate entry divided by the largest original entry, for a fixed factorization algorithm.
assumptions_latex: The factorization algorithm and monitored sequence of intermediate matrices are fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Algorithm-Relative Element-Growth Factor

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The numerical boundary is conditional on the proven backward-error estimate of the selected factorization algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a fixed floating-point factorization algorithm satisfies \(\|E\|_{\max}\le C(n)u\rho(K)\|K\|_{\max}\), where \(u\) is unit roundoff and \(C(n)\) is the algorithm's stated dimension factor. For a prescribed relative backward-error budget \(\eta>0\), the estimate guarantees \(\|E\|_{\max}\le\eta\|K\|_{\max}\) only when \(C(n)u\rho(K)\le\eta\). If \(C(n)u\rho(K)>\eta\), that guarantee is lost, although actual failure does not follow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pivot growth crosses the stated stability boundary when its algorithm-specific backward-error bound exceeds the allowed error budget.
assumptions_latex: The selected algorithm has the displayed growth-dependent backward-error estimate.
Floating-point arithmetic has unit roundoff \(u\).
\(\eta>0\) is the declared relative backward-error budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C(n)u\rho(K)>\eta\Longrightarrow\text{the displayed backward-error guarantee does not establish the requested budget}.

notation.meaning: Backward perturbation represented by the computed factors

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Growth-Dependent Backward-Error Boundary
Pivot-Growth Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnostic boundary for finite-precision pivoted factorization of an interior-point Newton matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be factorized by a fixed pivoting algorithm, and let \(K^{(j)}\) denote its successive active matrices. Define \(\rho=\max_j\|K^{(j)}\|_{\max}/\|K\|_{\max}\). If the algorithm admits a backward-error estimate \(\|E\|_{\max}\le c n u\rho\|K\|_{\max}\), where \(u\) is unit roundoff, then a prescribed relative error budget \(\eta\) is no longer guaranteed when \(c n u\rho>\eta\). This inequality is the pivot-growth stability boundary; crossing it does not prove failure, but removes the stated backward-stability guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pivot growth crosses its stability boundary when the factorization’s growth-dependent backward-error bound exceeds the prescribed relative error budget.
assumptions_latex: \(K\ne0\) is an interior-point Newton or KKT matrix.
The chosen pivoting algorithm has the displayed backward-error estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c n u\rho>\eta\) removes the backward-error guarantee \(\|E\|_{\max}\le\eta\|K\|_{\max}\).
