children.title: Factorization Breakdown
children.top_down_role: Conditions preventing completion or reliable use of a factorization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and numerical breakdown are defined relative to a fixed pivoted scalar- or block-factorization scheme and its declared acceptance test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a pivoted elimination scheme. At step \(j\), let \(\mathcal P_j\) be the pivot blocks admissible under that scheme. Exact breakdown occurs when every \(P\in\mathcal P_j\) is singular, so the prescribed elimination has no invertible next pivot. If the scheme additionally accepts a pivot only when a declared quality test \(q(P,K^{(j)})>\tau\) holds, numerical breakdown occurs when no admissible pivot passes that test. Continuing then requires changing the permitted pivot, delaying elimination, regularizing the matrix, or changing the factorization strategy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factorization breakdown means that no pivot allowed by the fixed scheme is algebraically invertible or numerically acceptable, so that scheme cannot continue unchanged.
assumptions_latex: A scalar- or block-pivot elimination scheme and its admissible pivot set are fixed.
For numerical breakdown, a pivot-quality functional \(q\) and threshold \(\tau\) are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall P\in\mathcal P_j,\ P\text{ singular}\bigr)\ \text{or}\ \bigl(\forall P\in\mathcal P_j,\ q(P,K^{(j)})\le\tau\bigr)\Longrightarrow\text{the prescribed scheme cannot continue unchanged}.

notation.meaning: Active matrix at elimination step j
Pivot blocks admissible under the fixed scheme
Declared pivot-quality test and acceptance threshold

knowledge_statements.title: Scheme-Relative Factorization Breakdown
Factorization Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic and threshold breakdown during pivoted block factorization of a Newton or KKT matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a pivoted block factorization \(P K P^{T}=L D L^{T}\). At elimination step \(j\), let \(D_j\) be the selected scalar or block pivot. Exact factorization breaks down if every admissible \(D_j\) is singular. With numerical pivot threshold \(\tau>0\), numerical breakdown is declared if every admissible pivot satisfies \(\sigma_{\min}(D_j)\le\tau\|K^{(j)}\|_2\). In either case the prescribed elimination cannot form the required inverse pivot and therefore cannot return the requested factors without regularization, delayed pivots, or a changed factorization strategy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factorization breaks down when no admissible nonsingular, sufficiently large pivot remains, so the prescribed elimination cannot continue without modifying its strategy.
assumptions_latex: \(K\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is processed by a specified pivoted block-elimination scheme.
\(\tau>0\) is the scheme's numerical pivot threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No admissible invertible pivot exists under the exact or threshold criterion, so the prescribed factorization cannot continue.

notation.meaning: active matrix at elimination step j

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local scope are appropriate, but admissible pivots and numerical-breakdown thresholds are factorization-specific. A source identifying the block-factorization scheme and supporting the singular-value threshold criterion is required.

children.title: Sparse Factorization Resource Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of sparse efficiency through unfavorable ordering or dense structure.

children.title: Fill-In Explosion
children.top_down_role: Excessive new nonzeros generated during elimination.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit linearly sparse family exhibiting strong fill under a specified ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge3\), let \(K_n\) have diagonal entries \((K_n)_{11}=n\), \((K_n)_{ii}=2\) for \(i>1\), entries \((K_n)_{1i}=(K_n)_{i1}=1\) for \(i>1\), and all other entries zero. Then \(K_n\) is symmetric positive definite and \(\operatorname{nnz}(K_n)=3n-2\). Eliminating vertex \(1\), the center of its star graph, first makes its \(n-1\) later neighbors a clique, so the symbolic Cholesky factor satisfies \(\operatorname{nnz}(L_n)=n+\binom n2=\Theta(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating the center of a sparse star first turns the leaves into a clique, producing quadratic factor fill from a linear-size input.
assumptions_latex: Symbolic Cholesky fill is measured without numerical cancellation.
The star center is first in the elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{nnz}(K_n)=\Theta(n),\qquad \operatorname{nnz}(L_n)=\Theta(n^2).

notation.meaning: Symbolic Cholesky factor under center-first elimination.

knowledge_statements.title: Star Elimination Produces Quadratic Fill

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic symbolic-factor growth under a fixed family of matrices and elimination orderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For structurally symmetric matrices \(K_n\) and symmetric elimination permutations \(P_n\), let \(L_n\) denote the symbolic triangular factor of \(P_nK_nP_n^{\mathsf T}\), ignoring numerical cancellation. The family has fill-in explosion under \((P_n)\) when \[\frac{\operatorname{nnz}(L_n)}{\operatorname{nnz}(K_n)}\longrightarrow\infty.\] It has strong fill-in explosion when \(\operatorname{nnz}(K_n)=O(n)\) while \(\operatorname{nnz}(L_n)=\Theta(n^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fill-in explodes when symbolic factor nonzeros grow without bound relative to input nonzeros; the strong regime converts linear input sparsity into quadratic factor size.
assumptions_latex: \((K_n)\) is a family of structurally symmetric matrices.
A symmetric elimination ordering \(P_n\) is fixed for each member.
Symbolic nonzeros are counted without numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{nnz}(L_n)/\operatorname{nnz}(K_n)\to\infty,\quad\text{with strong explosion if }\operatorname{nnz}(K_n)=O(n),\ \operatorname{nnz}(L_n)=\Theta(n^2).

notation.meaning: symbolic triangular factor under the selected ordering

review_flags: The definition is ordering-relative and does not itself establish memory exhaustion.
knowledge_statements.title: Fill-In Explosion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General graph representation of symbolic Cholesky fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed symmetric elimination ordering, eliminating each vertex completes its later neighbors into a clique. The resulting filled graph is chordal, and, absent numerical cancellation, its edges encode the off-diagonal structural nonzeros of the Cholesky factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph elimination represents symbolic Cholesky fill as an ordering-induced chordal completion.
assumptions_latex: The matrix is symmetric positive definite after symmetric permutation.
Numerical cancellation is ignored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{nnz}(L)=n+|E(G_P^+)|.
knowledge_statements.title: Elimination-Graph Representation of Symbolic Fill

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally accepted inventory is the explicit star family realizing strong fill explosion. The defining asymptotic criterion remains a core gap, so expansion is required. General symbolic-fill representation, factor-memory capacity failure, dense-input effects, and ordering-quality diagnosis were excluded as adjacent or external scopes.

children.title: Factor-Memory Exhaustion
children.top_down_role: Storage failure caused by oversized factors or workspace requirements.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fill Ratio Alone Does Not Determine Memory Exhaustion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates a relative sparsity diagnostic from the absolute capacity predicate owned by this leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a fixed factorization require \(B>0\) bytes in total. With memory budget \(M_1>B\) it fits, whereas with \(M_2<B\) it does not, although the matrix, factors, nonzero counts, and fill ratio are identical. Conversely, a smaller fill ratio can still exhaust memory when the absolute dimensions and factor nonzero count are sufficiently large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same fill ratio can fit one memory budget and exceed another; exhaustion depends on absolute storage and capacity.
assumptions_latex: Total factorization storage is a finite positive quantity \(B\).
Exhaustion means that the required in-memory representation exceeds the available budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{fillratio}\text{ alone does not determine whether }B\le M.

notation.meaning: total bytes required by the selected factorization

knowledge_statements.title: Fill Ratio Alone Does Not Determine Memory Exhaustion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementation-independent sufficient exhaustion certificate using mandatory numerical factor values; it is not a complete fit test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an in-memory factorization must retain \(N_f\) numerical factor values simultaneously and each stored value occupies at least \(w>0\) bytes. If \(wN_f>M\), where \(M\) is available memory, the factorization cannot fit regardless of index compression or workspace management. If \(wN_f\le M\), no fit conclusion follows because indices, pointers, permutations, metadata, temporary fronts, and work arrays may require additional storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mandatory factor values certify exhaustion when their byte count exceeds capacity, but fitting those values alone does not certify that the whole factorization fits.
assumptions_latex: All \(N_f\) numerical factor values must coexist in memory.
Each numerical value requires at least \(w\) bytes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: wN_f>M\Longrightarrow\text{factor-memory exhaustion},\qquad wN_f\le M\centernot\Longrightarrow\text{factorization fits}.

notation.meaning: number of simultaneously stored numerical factor values

review_flags: This is a sufficient lower-bound certificate, not a complete implementation storage model.
knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Value Storage Lower-Bound Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient fit certificate under explicit upper bounds for every simultaneously live storage component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a selected in-memory factorization have simultaneously live storage components indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,k\). Suppose \(B_i\) is a valid byte upper bound for component \(i\), including numerical values, indices, pointers, permutations, metadata, frontal storage, and work arrays, and let \(M\) be memory available to the factorization. If \(\sum_{i=1}^k B_i\le M\), then the declared factorization storage fits within \(M\). This certificate is invalid if a live component is omitted, an alleged \(B_i\) is not an upper bound, or bounds from incompatible execution phases are combined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid upper bounds for every simultaneously live factorization component certify a fit when their sum does not exceed usable memory.
assumptions_latex: \(B_i\) upper-bounds the bytes occupied by live component \(i\).
Every component that can be live simultaneously is included in the accounting.
\(M\) is the memory actually available to those components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^k B_i\le M\Longrightarrow\text{the declared in-memory representation fits within }M.

notation.meaning: valid byte upper bound for live storage component i

review_flags: Sufficient only under the declared execution and liveness model; it does not certify runtime allocation success or an adequate work budget.
knowledge_statements.title: Declared Peak-Memory Fit Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementation-parametric necessary-and-sufficient capacity predicate after all simultaneously live allocations are known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an execution of an in-memory factorization and let \(\mathcal L(t)\) be the allocations live at time \(t\), including numerical values, indices, pointers, permutations, metadata, fronts, and mandatory work arrays. If allocation \(a\) occupies \(B_a(t)\) bytes and \(M(t)\) bytes are usable by the factorization, define \(P(t)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal L(t)}B_a(t)\). The execution fits its declared memory budget exactly when \(P(t)\le M(t)\) for every \(t\); factor-memory exhaustion occurs exactly when \(P(t)>M(t)\) for some \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A realized factorization fits exactly when the total bytes of all simultaneously live allocations never exceed usable memory.
assumptions_latex: The execution, allocation sizes, lifetimes, and usable-memory function are completely specified.
Every mandatory simultaneously live allocation is included.
The predicate concerns capacity, excluding allocator fragmentation and unrelated external allocation failures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{fits}\iff\sup_t(P(t)-M(t))\le0,\qquad \text{exhaustion}\iff\exists t:\ P(t)>M(t).

notation.meaning: factorization allocations live at time t
usable factorization-memory capacity at time t

review_flags: This exact accounting predicate is retrospective or implementation-parametric; symbolic estimates may provide only bounds before execution.
knowledge_statements.title: Realized Peak Factor-Memory Predicate
Factor-Memory Exhaustion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hard memory boundary for storing sparse factors and factorization workspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M>0\) be available memory, let \(s_L\) and \(s_D\) be the bytes required per stored nonzero of factors \(L\) and \(D\), and let \(W\ge0\) be symbolic, frontal, and solver workspace. Factor-memory exhaustion occurs when \(s_L\operatorname{nnz}(L)+s_D\operatorname{nnz}(D)+W>M\). At this boundary the chosen in-memory factorization cannot simultaneously represent its factors and required workspace, irrespective of whether the linear system is mathematically nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor memory is exhausted when storage for factor entries plus required workspace exceeds available memory, even if the linear system is nonsingular.
assumptions_latex: The solver uses an in-memory sparse \(L D L^T\) factorization.
Memory accounting includes all mandatory factorization workspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_L\operatorname{nnz}(L)+s_D\operatorname{nnz}(D)+W>M\) makes the chosen in-memory factorization infeasible.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The memory inequality is coherent and matches the terminal failure container, but the accounting model for factor entries and mandatory workspace is implementation-dependent and uncited. A source for the stated in-memory resource model is required.

children.title: Dense-Structure Effects
children.top_down_role: Sparse-efficiency loss caused by dense rows, columns, or subblocks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact symbolic mechanism by which a broadly supported constraint-matrix column creates dense normal-equation coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\operatorname{Diag}(d)\succ0\) and \(H=ADA^{\mathsf T}\). If column \(a_j\) of \(A\) has support \(R=\{i:a_{ij}\ne0\}\) of size \(k\), its symbolic contribution \(d_ja_ja_j^{\mathsf T}\) contains every pair in \(R\times R\). Thus the column induces a \(k\)-vertex clique in the symbolic graph used to assemble \(H\), irrespective of sparsity outside \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A column touching k constraint rows creates all pairwise symbolic couplings among those rows in the normal-equation assembly.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is positive diagonal.
Sparsity is assessed symbolically, without accidental numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{supp}_{\mathrm{sym}}(H[R,R])\supseteq R\times R.

notation.meaning: row support of the selected column

review_flags: Symbolic clique formation does not alone determine eventual factor fill, ordering cost, or memory exhaustion.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Column Clique in Normal-Equation Structure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines formulation-relative structural density without attributing it to ordering or asserting memory exhaustion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a specified Newton-system formulation and symbolic assembly, a dense structural kernel of order \(q\) is an index set \(R\) with \(|R|=q\) for which the assembled Newton, frontal, or Schur-complement submatrix has \(\Theta(q^2)\) structurally present entries on \(R\times R\). Such a kernel can be induced by any input row, column, or subblock whose symbolic contribution couples \(\Theta(q^2)\) pairs of system indices, or it can arise during assembly or block elimination. It removes sparse-entry savings inside the kernel but does not alone determine external fill, ordering quality, or memory exhaustion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense structural kernel is a formulation-relative quadratic-size symbolic submatrix or clique that destroys local sparse-entry savings without itself proving fill or capacity failure.
assumptions_latex: A Newton-system formulation and symbolic assembly rule are fixed.
Accidental numerical cancellation is ignored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |R|=q\ \land\ \operatorname{nnz}_{\mathrm{sym}}(K[R,R])=\Theta(q^2)\Longrightarrow\text{no asymptotic entry-sparsity saving within }R.

notation.meaning: indices of the dense symbolic kernel
the fixed assembled Newton, frontal, or Schur-complement matrix

review_flags: Density is relative to the selected system formulation; a dense row or column is not asserted to create the same kernel in every formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Structural Kernel

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense Frontal-Block Storage and Conventional Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local direct-factorization cost of a structurally dense frontal block, without attributing its creation to a particular ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a sparse direct factorization forms and retains a structurally dense symmetric frontal block of order \(q\), then storing one triangular numerical part requires \(q(q+1)/2=\Theta(q^2)\) values. Conventional dense Cholesky or \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) elimination of the block performs \(\Theta(q^3)\) arithmetic operations. These local costs persist even when the remainder of the Newton system is sparse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense frontal block requires quadratic numerical storage and cubic conventional factorization work despite sparsity elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: A structurally dense symmetric frontal block of order \(q\) is explicitly formed and retained.
The block is factorized by a conventional dense Cholesky or \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) kernel.
Fast matrix multiplication and compressed low-rank structure are not used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{values}}\ge q(q+1)/2=\Theta(q^2),\qquad W_{\mathrm{factor}}=\Theta(q^3).

notation.meaning: order of the dense frontal block
arithmetic work for conventional dense block factorization

review_flags: Excludes metadata, workspace, pivoting overhead, low-rank compression, and fast matrix multiplication.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Frontal-Block Storage and Conventional Work

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget test for a declared conventional dense frontal kernel; overall factor-memory exhaustion remains a sibling scope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the declared dense-block model, let \(M_v\) be the number of numerical-value slots available for the frontal factor and let \(F\) be its arithmetic-work budget. A dense frontal kernel of order \(q\) is infeasible for that selected implementation if \(q(q+1)/2>M_v\) or if its declared conventional factorization work exceeds \(F\). Satisfying both inequalities does not certify that the complete sparse factorization fits, because other factors, indices, fronts, and workspace are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense kernel crosses its local resource boundary when its mandatory triangular values or conventional factorization work exceed the declared local budgets.
assumptions_latex: The dense frontal block must be explicitly stored and conventionally factorized.
\(M_v\) and \(F\) are budgets allocated to this block rather than the entire solve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q(q+1)/2>M_v\ \lor\ W_{\mathrm{factor}}(q)>F\Longrightarrow\text{the selected dense-kernel implementation is infeasible}.

notation.meaning: available numerical-value slots for the dense frontal factor
arithmetic-work budget allocated to the block

review_flags: This is a local kernel boundary, not a complete process-memory fit predicate.
knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Kernel Resource Boundary
Dense-Structure Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource boundary created by dense frontal blocks inside an otherwise sparse factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose multifrontal elimination produces a structurally dense frontal block of order \(q\). Storing its triangular factor requires at least \(q(q+1)/2\) numerical entries, and conventional dense elimination of that block requires \(\Theta(q^3)\) arithmetic operations. Consequently, for memory budget \(M\,\) entries and work budget \(F\), the selected factorization crosses a dense-structure resource boundary whenever \(q(q+1)/2>M\) or its block-factorization work exceeds \(F\). Sparsity elsewhere in the Newton matrix does not remove this local dense cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense frontal block imposes quadratic storage and cubic conventional factorization work, potentially exhausting resources despite sparsity elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: A sparse direct method forms a structurally dense frontal block of order \(q\).
The block is stored and factorized by conventional dense methods.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The block incurs \(\Omega(q^2)\) storage and \(\Theta(q^3)\) work, crossing the stated budget when either inequality holds.

notation.meaning: order of the dense frontal block

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected kind fits the resource-failure leaf, and the dense-block cost statement is mathematically plausible under the stated conventional method. However, the multifrontal storage and arithmetic claims require a specific sparse-direct-factorization citation.

children.title: Ordering-Induced Failure
children.top_down_role: Resource or sparsity failure attributable to unfavorable elimination ordering.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational obstruction to globally avoiding ordering-dependent fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The decision problem asking whether an undirected graph has an elimination ordering producing at most K fill edges is NP-complete. Consequently, unless \mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}, no polynomial-time algorithm finds a globally minimum-fill ordering for every graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum fill-in is NP-complete, so practical ordering heuristics cannot be guaranteed to minimize fill on every pattern.
assumptions_latex: The input is an undirected graph and an integer K.
Cost is the number of structural fill edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \textsc{Minimum Fill-In}\text{ is NP-complete}.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Fill Ordering Complexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit family isolating ordering as the source of fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the star G=K_{1,k}, eliminating every leaf before the center creates no fill, whereas eliminating the center first makes the k leaves a clique and creates \binom{k}{2} fill edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A star has zero fill under leaf-first elimination and quadratic fill under center-first elimination.
assumptions_latex: k\ge2.
Fill follows the standard graph-elimination rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(P_{\mathrm{leaf}})=0,\qquad f(P_{\mathrm{center}})=\binom{k}{2}.

notation.meaning: Star graph with one center and k leaves.
Number of fill edges produced by ordering P.

knowledge_statements.title: Star-Graph Ordering Separation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Avoidable resource failure attributable specifically to elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For one sparsity pattern, let r(P) be a consistently predicted resource requirement for admissible ordering P and let R be the available budget. Failure under the selected ordering P_s is ordering-induced when r(P_s)>R but r(P_a)\le R for some admissible ordering P_a.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource failure is ordering-induced when the selected ordering exceeds the budget although another valid ordering of the same pattern would fit.
assumptions_latex: P_s\text{ and }P_a\text{ are admissible orderings of the same sparsity pattern}.
r(P)\text{ is evaluated by one consistent symbolic memory or work model}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r(P_s)>R\ge r(P_a)

notation.meaning: Predicted factor-memory or factorization-work requirement under ordering P.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering-Induced Resource-Failure Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-elimination mechanism producing ordering-dependent factor patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In symbolic symmetric elimination, eliminating a vertex connects all of its remaining neighbors. Thus the filled graph G_P^+ and the structural nonzero counts of the factors may depend on the elimination ordering P, even though every ordering permutes the same original pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different elimination orders can produce different filled graphs and factor sizes for the same sparse pattern.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is the undirected graph used for symbolic elimination}.
Structural fill ignores numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G_{P_1}^+\text{ and }G_{P_2}^+\text{ may have different edge counts}.

notation.meaning: Filled graph produced under ordering P.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Dependence of Structural Fill
Ordering-Induced Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Avoidable sparse-factor resource failure attributable to the chosen elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For matrix pattern \(G\), let \(m(P)\) be the predicted memory required by a valid elimination ordering \(P\), and let \(M\) be available memory. Ordering-induced failure occurs when the selected ordering \(P_s\) satisfies \(m(P_s)>M\), while some valid ordering \(P_a\) satisfies \(m(P_a)\le M\). Hence failure is attributable to ordering-dependent fill rather than an unavoidable memory lower bound for every admissible ordering. The analogous work-budget boundary replaces \(m\) and \(M\) by predicted factorization work and its available budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure is ordering-induced when the selected ordering exceeds a resource budget although another valid ordering for the same sparsity pattern stays within it.
assumptions_latex: All compared orderings are valid for the same matrix sparsity pattern.
The same symbolic memory model is used for every ordering.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(P_s)>M\ge m(P_a)\) identifies an avoidable, ordering-dependent resource failure.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives a precise ordering-relative resource boundary and failure_boundary is appropriate. No source supports the ordering-dependent fill or predicted-resource model, so an inspectable sparse-ordering citation is required.

children.title: Finite-Precision Robustness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Floating-point departures from exact-arithmetic feasibility, positivity, and certificate conclusions.

children.title: Residual-Feasibility Drift Family
children.top_down_role: Accumulated departure from intended feasibility regimes.

children.title: Primal-Residual Drift
children.top_down_role: Accumulated numerical departure from primal constraint satisfaction.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Residual Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of the prescribed primal equality-residual tolerance along computed interior-point iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard-form constraint \(Ax=b\), define the scaled primal residual \(\eta_p^k=\|b-Ax^k\|_2/(1+\|b\|_2+\|A\|_2\|x^k\|_2)\). Given tolerance \(\tau_p>0\), primal-residual drift occurs at iteration \(k+1\) when \(\eta_p^k\le\tau_p\) but a residual recomputed from the stored iterate satisfies \(\eta_p^{k+1}>\tau_p\). Recomputing from \(x^{k+1}\), rather than relying only on a recursively updated residual, distinguishes actual feasibility drift from bookkeeping error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal-residual drift occurs when a recomputed scaled equality residual rises above tolerance after the preceding iterate satisfied that tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and stored iterates \(x^k\in\mathbb R^n\) are finite.
Residuals are recomputed using a specified working precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_p^k\le\tau_p<\eta_p^{k+1}\) is a primal-residual drift event.

notation.meaning: scaled primal equality residual at iteration k

source_refs.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

children.title: Dual-Residual Drift
children.top_down_role: Accumulated numerical departure from dual constraint satisfaction.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Residual Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of the prescribed dual equality-residual tolerance along computed primal-dual iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dual feasibility \(A^Ty+s=c\), define \(\eta_d^k=\|c-A^Ty^k-s^k\|_2/(1+\|c\|_2+\|A\|_2\|y^k\|_2+\|s^k\|_2)\). Given \(\tau_d>0\), dual-residual drift occurs at iteration \(k+1\) when \(\eta_d^k\le\tau_d\) but the residual recomputed from stored \(y^{k+1},s^{k+1}\) satisfies \(\eta_d^{k+1}>\tau_d\). Recalculation from the stored variables separates actual dual-feasibility loss from error in a recursively maintained residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual-residual drift occurs when a recomputed scaled dual-feasibility residual exceeds tolerance after the preceding iterate met that tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(c,s^k\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(y^k\in\mathbb R^m\) are finite.
Residuals are recomputed using a specified working precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_d^k\le\tau_d<\eta_d^{k+1}\) is a dual-residual drift event.

notation.meaning: scaled dual-feasibility residual at iteration k

source_refs.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Infeasible-Interior-Point Algorithms p. 107

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of the nominal dual-residual update from errors in stored variable updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_d^k=c-A^{\mathsf T}y^k-s^k\). Suppose \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\Delta y^k+e_y^k\) and \(s^{k+1}=s^k+\Delta s^k+e_s^k\), where \(e_y^k,e_s^k\) are stored-update errors. Direct recomputation gives \(r_d^{k+1}=r_d^k-A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y^k-\Delta s^k-A^{\mathsf T}e_y^k-e_s^k\). Thus the recomputed residual can grow or cross tolerance even when the nominal residual update is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The next recomputed dual residual equals the nominal residual update minus the stationarity error induced by stored multiplier and slack updates.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(c\) are fixed.
Residuals are directly recomputed from stored iterates.
\(e_y^k,e_s^k\) are the differences between stored and nominal updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_d^{k+1}=r_d^k-A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y^k-\Delta s^k-A^{\mathsf T}e_y^k-e_s^k.\)

notation.meaning: Dual stationarity residual at iteration k.
Stored multiplier and slack update errors.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Residual Drift Error Decomposition

children.title: Feasibility Drift
children.top_down_role: Movement outside intended feasibility tolerances during the solve.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined equality-feasibility drift for computed primal-dual interior-point iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\eta_p^k\) and \(\eta_d^k\) be scaled primal and dual residuals, and define \(\eta_f^k=\max\{\eta_p^k/\tau_p,\eta_d^k/\tau_d\}\) for positive tolerances \(\tau_p,\tau_d\). Feasibility drift occurs from iteration \(k\) to \(k+1\) when \(\eta_f^k\le1\) but \(\eta_f^{k+1}>1\), with both residuals recomputed from the stored variables. Thus at least one equality-feasibility requirement becomes violated after the preceding iterate met both requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combined feasibility drifts when both scaled residual tests previously passed but a recomputed primal or dual residual subsequently violates its tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Scaled residuals \(\eta_p^k,\eta_d^k\ge0\) are recomputed consistently.
Tolerances \(\tau_p,\tau_d\) are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_f^k\le1<\eta_f^{k+1}\) certifies combined feasibility drift.

children.title: Drift Detection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Residual-monitoring regimes used to recognize significant accumulated drift.

knowledge_statements.title: Drift Detection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute, relative, and persistence conditions for detecting residual-feasibility drift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r^k\) be a residual recomputed from iteration \(k\), let \(d>0\) be its scaling denominator, and fix \(\tau_{\mathrm{abs}},\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}>0\), growth factor \(\gamma>1\), and persistence length \(q\ge1\). Absolute detection declares drift when \(\|r^k\|_2>\tau_{\mathrm{abs}}\); relative detection declares it when \(\|r^k\|_2/d>\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\); persistent-growth detection declares it when \(\|r^{k-j}\|_2>\gamma\|r^{k-j-1}\|_2\) for every \(j=0,\ldots,q-1\). A monitoring regime must specify which predicate triggers intervention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Drift monitoring may trigger on an absolute residual, a scaled relative residual, or persistent geometric growth over a specified number of iterations.
assumptions_latex: Residuals are recomputed from stored iterates in a fixed precision.
All thresholds and the scaling denominator are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Drift is detected exactly when the selected absolute, relative, or persistent-growth predicate holds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detection of hidden residual-maintenance drift by comparing direct recomputation with a recursively maintained residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_{\mathrm{rec}}^k\) be a residual recomputed from the stored iterate and problem data, and let \(\widetilde r^k\) be the corresponding recursively maintained residual. For \(d_k>0\), define \(\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}^k=\|r_{\mathrm{rec}}^k-\widetilde r^k\|/d_k\). A declared discrepancy threshold \(\tau_{\mathrm{gap}}>0\) detects residual-maintenance drift when \(\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}^k>\tau_{\mathrm{gap}}\). Replacing \(\widetilde r^k\) by \(r_{\mathrm{rec}}^k\) removes the accumulated representation discrepancy but does not restore feasibility of the iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large scaled discrepancy between directly recomputed and maintained residuals detects bookkeeping drift; residual replacement does not repair the iterate.
assumptions_latex: The recomputed and maintained quantities represent the same exact residual.
\(d_k>0\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{gap}}>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}^k>\tau_{\mathrm{gap}}\Rightarrow\) residual-maintenance drift is detected.

children.title: Primal Positivity Loss
children.top_down_role: Numerical departure of primal variables from the intended interior.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Positivity Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-step boundary for preserving strict positivity of primal variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) and direction \(\Delta x\in\mathbb R^n\). Define \(\alpha_x^{\max}=\min_{i:\Delta x_i<0}(-x_i/\Delta x_i)\), with the minimum over an empty set equal to \(+\infty\). In exact arithmetic, \(x+\alpha\Delta x>0\) for every \(0\le\alpha<\alpha_x^{\max}\), while any finite \(\alpha>\alpha_x^{\max}\) makes at least one component negative. Primal positivity loss occurs whenever the stored update has \(\operatorname{fl}(x_i+\alpha\Delta x_i)\le0\) for some \(i\); finite precision can therefore cause loss even near the exact boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum positivity-preserving primal step is set by the first decreasing component to reach zero; a stored nonpositive component constitutes positivity loss.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
The step length satisfies \(\alpha\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact strict positivity requires \(\alpha<\alpha_x^{\max}\); a computed component at or below zero is primal positivity loss.

notation.meaning: largest exact step before a primal component reaches zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval validation of whether a computed primal update remains strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=x+\alpha\Delta x\), and suppose validated arithmetic gives \(z_i\in[\ell_i,u_i]\) for every \(i\). If \(\ell_i>0\) for all \(i\), strict positivity is certified. If \(u_i\leq0\) for some \(i\), positivity loss is certified. Otherwise at least one enclosure contains zero, so strict positivity is unresolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validated component intervals certify positivity when all lower bounds are positive, certify loss when some upper bound is nonpositive, and otherwise leave the sign unresolved.
assumptions_latex: \(x,\Delta x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha\geq0\).
\(x_i+\alpha\Delta x_i\in[\ell_i,u_i]\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_i\ell_i>0\Rightarrow z>0;\quad(\exists i)\ u_i\leq0\Rightarrow z\notin\mathbb R_{++}^n\).

children.title: Dual Positivity Loss

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Positivity Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-step boundary for preserving strict positivity of dual slack variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) and direction \(\Delta s\in\mathbb R^n\). Define \(\alpha_s^{\max}=\min_{i:\Delta s_i<0}(-s_i/\Delta s_i)\), with the minimum over an empty set equal to \(+\infty\). In exact arithmetic, \(s+\alpha\Delta s>0\) for every \(0\le\alpha<\alpha_s^{\max}\), while any finite \(\alpha>\alpha_s^{\max}\) makes at least one slack negative. Dual positivity loss occurs whenever the stored update has \(\operatorname{fl}(s_i+\alpha\Delta s_i)\le0\) for some \(i\); finite precision can therefore cause loss even near the exact boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum positivity-preserving dual step is set by the first decreasing slack to reach zero; a stored nonpositive slack constitutes positivity loss.
assumptions_latex: \(s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
The step length satisfies \(\alpha\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact strict positivity requires \(\alpha<\alpha_s^{\max}\); a computed slack at or below zero is dual positivity loss.

notation.meaning: largest exact step before a dual slack reaches zero

children.title: Central-Neighborhood Departure

knowledge_statements.title: Central-Neighborhood Departure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision loss of a standard Euclidean primal-dual central neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a strictly positive primal-dual iterate, define \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\) and \(N_2(\theta)=\{(x,s):\|XSe-\mu e\|_2\leq \theta\mu\}\), where \(0<\theta<1\). Central-neighborhood departure occurs when the computed update \((\widehat x^+,\widehat s^+)\) satisfies \(\|\widehat X^+\widehat S^+e-\widehat\mu^+e\|_2>\theta\widehat\mu^+\), even though the exact-arithmetic update was selected to remain in \(N_2(\theta)\). Consequently, the neighborhood hypothesis used by the path-following iteration is lost; positivity alone does not prevent this failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rounding error causes the computed iterate to violate the prescribed complementarity neighborhood, invalidating the path-following neighborhood invariant even if all components remain positive.
assumptions_latex: \(x,s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\widehat x^+,\widehat s^+)\notin N_2(\theta)\)

children.title: Step-Acceptance Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of acceptable interior steps following positivity or centrality degradation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-parameterized failure of every permitted trial step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq(0,1]\) be the declared set of permitted trial step lengths and let \(P:T\to\{\mathrm{true},\mathrm{false}\}\) be the algorithm's complete acceptance predicate, including exactly its prescribed interiority, neighborhood, progress, and numerical-evaluation rules. Step-acceptance failure is the condition \(\{\alpha\in T:P(\alpha)=\mathrm{true}\}=\varnothing\). If \(T\) is finite, evaluating \(P(\alpha)=\mathrm{false}\) for every \(\alpha\in T\) certifies failure. Failed evaluation at only finitely many points does not certify failure for an infinite \(T\) without an additional exhaustive rule or theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Step acceptance fails exactly when no permitted trial length passes the algorithm's declared acceptance predicate; finite trial sets can be certified by exhaustive rejection.
assumptions_latex: \(T\subseteq(0,1]\) is the declared permitted trial set.
\(P\) is fully specified under the declared numerical evaluation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Accept}(T,P)=\varnothing\), where \(\operatorname{Accept}(T,P)=\{\alpha\in T:P(\alpha)\}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Predicate-Relative Step-Acceptance Failure
Step-Acceptance Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure to find an admissible positive step satisfying neighborhood and progress tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given direction \((\Delta x,\Delta s)\), let \(x(\alpha)=x+\alpha\Delta x\), \(s(\alpha)=s+\alpha\Delta s\), and fix \(\alpha_{\min}>0\). A step-acceptance failure occurs when no \(\alpha\in[\alpha_{\min},1]\) simultaneously satisfies \(x(\alpha)>0\), \(s(\alpha)>0\), the prescribed central-neighborhood test, and the algorithm's residual or merit decrease test. It also occurs numerically when an accepted computed step violates any such condition under validated evaluation. In either case, the iteration cannot perform its specified admissible update without reducing the minimum permitted step or changing the direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No sufficiently large trial step simultaneously preserves positivity, centrality, and required progress, so the specified interior-point iteration cannot accept an update.
assumptions_latex: \(x,s\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\)
\(0<\alpha_{\min}\leq1\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\alpha\in[\alpha_{\min},1]:x(\alpha)>0,\ s(\alpha)>0,\ \text{centrality and progress tests hold}\}=\varnothing\)

notation.meaning: Computed primal and dual-slack search direction.

children.title: Optimal-Status Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Uncertain acceptance of optimality under finite numerical tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Status Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate residual and gap tests that do not certify exact LP optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\), suppose a computed triple passes \(\|Ax-b\|\leq\varepsilon_p\), \(\|A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\|\leq\varepsilon_d\), \(x,s\geq-\varepsilon_+e\), and \(|c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y|\leq\varepsilon_g\). Optimal status remains ambiguous unless validated bounds establish an exactly feasible primal-dual pair with zero gap, or a justified correction theorem converts these inequalities into such a pair. Small residuals and gap alone are not an exact optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Passing numerical feasibility and gap tolerances does not by itself certify exact optimality; validated correction or an exact feasible zero-gap pair is required.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ c\in\mathbb R^n\)
\(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_+,\varepsilon_g\geq0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{tolerance tests}\not\Rightarrow\text{exact optimality}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(\varepsilon>0\), consider \(\min\{x:\varepsilon x=\varepsilon,\ x\geq0\}\). Its unique optimum is \(x^*=1\). The computed triple \(\widehat x=0\), \(\widehat y=0\), \(\widehat s=1\) has primal residual \(\varepsilon\), exact dual feasibility \(\varepsilon\widehat y+\widehat s=1\), nonnegative variables, and computed gap \(\widehat x-\varepsilon\widehat y=0\), yet \(\widehat x\) is infeasible and not optimal.

children.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Ambiguity

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerically approximate Farkas vectors whose decisive inequalities are not validated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the system \(Ax=b\), \(x\geq0\), an exact Farkas certificate is a vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\geq0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\). Let \(\widehat y\in\mathbb R^m\) be normalized, and suppose validated evaluation provides componentwise lower bounds \(L_i\leq(A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y)_i\) and an upper bound \(U\geq b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\). The computed vector is a validated infeasibility certificate only if \(L_i\geq0\) for every \(i\) and \(U<0\). If either condition is not established, the numerical certificate is ambiguous and does not certify infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate Farkas vector is inconclusive unless validated lower bounds establish every dual component as nonnegative and a validated upper bound establishes a strictly negative separating value.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m\)
\(\widehat y\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(\|\widehat y\|=1\)
\(L_i\leq(A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y)_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), and \(U\geq b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl((\exists i)\ L_i<0\bigr)\lor U\geq0\Rightarrow\widehat y\text{ is not a validated infeasibility certificate}\)

notation.meaning: Validated lower bound for component i of the dual separating vector.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible one-variable systems can satisfy arbitrarily tight relaxed Farkas inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(\varepsilon>0\), consider \(\varepsilon x=\varepsilon\), \(x\geq0\). It is feasible at \(x=1\). With normalized multiplier \(\widehat y=-1\), \(A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y=-\varepsilon\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y=-\varepsilon<0\). Thus a test accepting \(A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y\geq-\varepsilon\) together with a negative right-hand-side pairing falsely reports infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily small relaxed sign violations can make a feasible system appear to possess a Farkas certificate.

The tolerance test permits transpose-image components as low as \(-\varepsilon\).

children.title: Unboundedness-Certificate Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Numerically inconclusive evidence for objective unboundedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness-Certificate Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate recession directions whose nullspace membership, nonnegativity, or descent is not validated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) with a feasible point, an exact unboundedness certificate is a nonzero direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(Ad=0\), \(d\geq0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Let \(\widehat d\in\mathbb R^n\) be normalized. Suppose validated evaluation gives \(\|A\widehat d\|\leq\delta_A\), lower component bounds \(\widehat d_i-\delta_+\leq d_i\), and the objective upper bound \(c^{\mathsf T}\widehat d+\delta_c\). These bounds validate the displayed exact certificate only if exact nullspace membership is separately established, \(\widehat d_i-\delta_+\geq0\) for every \(i\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}\widehat d+\delta_c<0\). In particular, a residual bound with \(\delta_A>0\) alone does not establish \(A\widehat d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computed recession direction is inconclusive unless validation establishes exact nullspace membership, nonnegativity with the required error margins, and strict objective descent.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ c\in\mathbb R^n\)
\(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\neq\varnothing\)
\(\widehat d\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\|\widehat d\|=1\)
\(\delta_A,\delta_+,\delta_c\geq0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{failure to validate }A\widehat d=0,\ \widehat d\geq0,\text{ or }c^{\mathsf T}\widehat d<0\Rightarrow\widehat d\text{ is not a validated unboundedness certificate}\)

notation.meaning: Validated residual, component, and objective error bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded LP can admit an arbitrarily accurate approximate improving null direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(\varepsilon>0\), consider \(\min\{-x:\varepsilon x=0,\ x\geq0\}\). Its feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so its optimum is finite. The normalized direction \(\widehat d=1\) satisfies \(\widehat d\geq0\), \(c^{\mathsf T}\widehat d=-1<0\), and \(\|A\widehat d\|=\varepsilon\), but it is not a recession direction because \(A\widehat d\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded one-variable LP can have a nonnegative, strictly improving direction with arbitrarily small but nonzero constraint residual.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
A residual test permits \(\|A\widehat d\|\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|A\widehat d\|=\varepsilon\), \(\widehat d\geq0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}\widehat d<0\) do not imply that \(\widehat d\) is an unboundedness ray.

children.title: Ill-Posedness Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Difficulty distinguishing ill-posed instances from nearby status classes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily small coefficient perturbations switch exact feasibility status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the family \(t x=1\), \(x\geq0\). For every \(t>0\) it is feasible with \(x=1/t\); for every \(t\leq0\) it is infeasible. Consequently, every uncertainty interval \(U=[-\delta,\delta]\) with \(\delta>0\) contains both feasible and infeasible instances, so status is not robustly determined at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the zero coefficient, arbitrarily close admissible instances of a one-variable LP are feasible on one side and infeasible on the other.
assumptions_latex: The uncertain coefficient satisfies \(t\in[-\delta,\delta]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{S(t):t\in[-\delta,\delta]\}\supseteq\{\mathrm{feasible},\mathrm{infeasible}\}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: One-Parameter Feasibility Status Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Status Ambiguity over a Validated Data Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust status determination for LP data known only to lie in a validated uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be a validated nonempty set of admissible LP data and let \(S(d)\) denote the exact status of instance \(d\) under a fixed status classification. The status is robustly determined on \(U\) exactly when \(S\) is constant on \(U\). Ill-posedness ambiguity occurs when \(\{S(d):d\in U\}\) contains at least two statuses. Merely computing one representative instance cannot resolve that ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LP status is robust over uncertain data only when every admissible instance has the same exact status; two attainable statuses make the result ambiguous.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a validated nonempty set of admissible LP data.
The exact status map \(S\) uses one fixed classification convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\{S(d):d\in U\}|=1\) certifies robust status, whereas \(|\{S(d):d\in U\}|\geq2\) is status ambiguity.

notation.meaning: Exact status of LP instance d.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status uncertainty when data lie within numerical uncertainty of a status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d=(A,b,c)\) denote LP data, let \(\Sigma\) be the boundary in data space between instances having different primal-dual status, and let \(\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)\) use the same norm as the data-error model. If the available data are known only within radius \(\delta\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)\leq\delta\), then the uncertainty ball may contain instances on different sides of \(\Sigma\). No status assertion based solely on the approximate data is robustly determined in that case; a stronger data enclosure, perturbation analysis, or explicit certificate is required.

\(\delta\geq0\) bounds data uncertainty

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise margin guaranteeing that a correction to a reused candidate remains interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x>0\), \(s>0\), \(\|\delta x\|_\infty<\min_i x_i\), and \(\|\delta s\|_\infty<\min_i s_i\), then \(x+\delta x>0\) and \(s+\delta s>0\). This guaranteed radius collapses when either minimum is zero.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residuals produced by reusing an old feasible primal-dual point after LP-data perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(Ax=b\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\). For \(A'=A+\Delta A\), \(b'=b+\Delta b\), and \(c'=c+\Delta c\), direct reuse of \((x,y,s)\) gives \(r'_p=A'x-b'=\Delta A\,x-\Delta b\) and \(r'_d=A'^{\mathsf T}y+s-c'=\Delta A^{\mathsf T}y-\Delta c\). Thus small data changes generally destroy exact feasibility, while unchanged strictly positive \(x,s\) remain positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model perturbations become explicit primal and dual residuals at a reused point, even though unchanged positive variables and slacks remain positive.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax=b\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\).
\(A'=A+\Delta A\), \(b'=b+\Delta b\), and \(c'=c+\Delta c\).

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Transport Under Direct Reuse
Warm-Start Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of strict interiority or centrality when reusing a near-boundary solution after perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an old primal-dual solution \((x,y,s)\) and perturbed data \((A+\Delta A,b+\Delta b,c+\Delta c)\). Direct reuse is an admissible path-following warm start only if the reused point satisfies the new residual requirements, \(x>0\), \(s>0\), and the chosen central-neighborhood condition. A near-boundary solution need not satisfy these requirements after arbitrarily small perturbations. For example, the solution \(x=0\) of \(\min\{x:x\geq0\}\) is not strictly interior and therefore cannot initialize a method requiring \(x>0\), despite being an exact optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A previous near-boundary optimum may violate new residual, positivity, or centrality requirements, so direct reuse is not generally a valid interior-point initialization.

children.title: Reformulation Conditioning Effects
children.top_down_role: Conditioning changes introduced by variable or constraint transformations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent equality recombination with arbitrarily poor conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Premultiplication of Ax=b by a nonsingular R preserves its solution set. With A=I_2 and R_t=\begin{bmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}, the equivalent equality matrix is R_t and \kappa_2(R_t)\to\infty as |t|\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular recombination of equalities preserves their solutions but can make the equality matrix arbitrarily ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: R_t\text{ is applied consistently to both sides of the equality system}.
Conditioning uses the Euclidean operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:I_2x=b\}=\{x:R_tx=R_tb\},\qquad \lim_{|t|\to\infty}\kappa_2(R_t)=\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Row-Recombination Conditioning Deterioration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A positivity-preserving standard-form transformation with arbitrarily poor conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under x=Dz with positive diagonal D, Ax=b becomes ADz=b and nonnegativity is preserved. For A=I_2 and D_t=\operatorname{diag}(1,t), t\ge1, \kappa_2(AD_t)=t, while \kappa_2((AD_t)(AD_t)^{\mathsf T})=t^2. Thus equivalent standard-form coordinates can make both the constraint matrix and its unweighted normal matrix arbitrarily ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal variable reformulation can worsen matrix conditioning by a factor t and normal-equation conditioning by t squared.
assumptions_latex: D_t\text{ is positive diagonal}.
Condition numbers use the Euclidean operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa_2(AD_t)=t,\qquad \kappa_2((AD_t)(AD_t)^{\mathsf T})=t^2\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Diagonal Reformulation Deterioration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp row-transformation class preserving Euclidean conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If Q is orthogonal, replacing Ax=b by QAx=Qb preserves the feasible set and every singular value of A. Consequently \kappa_2(QA)=\kappa_2(A); conditioning deterioration is not inevitable for all equivalent row transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orthogonal row transformations preserve both the equality solution set and the Euclidean condition number.
assumptions_latex: Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I.
A\text{ has the rank required for its finite nonzero-singular-value condition number}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_i(QA)=\sigma_i(A),\qquad \kappa_2(QA)=\kappa_2(A).

Reformulation Conditioning Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent variable transformations can arbitrarily worsen Newton-system conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the nonsingular diagonal change \(x=Dz\), the equality matrix becomes \(AD\). Algebraic equivalence does not preserve numerical conditioning: with \(A=I_2\) and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,t)\), \(t\geq1\), one has \(\kappa_2(AD)=t\). The associated unweighted normal matrix is \((AD)(AD)^{\mathsf T}=\operatorname{diag}(1,t^2)\), whose condition number is \(t^2\). Hence equivalent reformulations can make linear solves arbitrarily sensitive as \(t\to\infty\), even though the represented feasible set is related by an invertible coordinate transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible diagonal reformulation can make the constraint matrix condition number grow like t and the normal-equation condition number like t squared.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is nonsingular and diagonal
Condition numbers use the Euclidean operator norm

children.title: Scaling Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of numerical behavior on scaling choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-invariant replacement for a fixed absolute equality-residual test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \rho(a,b;x)=|a^{\mathsf T}x-b|/(|a|^{\mathsf T}|x|+|b|). Whenever the denominator is positive, consistent row scaling by \gamma>0 leaves \rho unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalizing by a homogeneous data-and-solution scale makes the row residual invariant under positive row scaling.
assumptions_latex: \gamma>0.
|a|^{\mathsf T}|x|+|b|>0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho(\gamma a,\gamma b;x)=\rho(a,b;x).
knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Relative-Residual Invariance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noninvariance of a fixed absolute feasibility test under equivalent row scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing a^{\mathsf T}x=b by \gamma a^{\mathsf T}x=\gamma b, \gamma>0, preserves the equality but multiplies the same point's absolute residual by \gamma. Hence a fixed test |a^{\mathsf T}x-b|\le\tau is not invariant under equivalent row scaling and can reverse its verdict whenever the unscaled residual is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent row scaling multiplies absolute residuals, so a fixed absolute tolerance can change its verdict solely because of scaling.
assumptions_latex: \gamma>0.
\tau>0\text{ is fixed and absolute}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\gamma a^{\mathsf T}x-\gamma b|=\gamma|a^{\mathsf T}x-b|.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noninvariance of absolute reduced-cost and objective-gap tests under equivalent objective scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed feasible region, replacing c by \alpha c with \alpha>0 preserves the primal minimizers. Under the corresponding dual scaling (y,s)\mapsto(\alpha y,\alpha s), reduced costs and the primal-dual objective gap are multiplied by \alpha. Fixed absolute reduced-cost and gap tests are therefore not invariant under positive objective scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive objective scaling preserves minimizers but rescales reduced costs and the duality gap, so fixed absolute optimality tests can change verdicts.
assumptions_latex: \alpha>0.
The feasible region is unchanged.
Dual multipliers and slacks are scaled consistently.
The tested thresholds are fixed absolute quantities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}(\alpha c)^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad \bar c'=\alpha\bar c,\qquad g'=\alpha g.

Scaling Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute numerical tests are not invariant under equivalent row or objective scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace an equality \(a^{\mathsf T}x=b\) by the equivalent equality \(\gamma a^{\mathsf T}x=\gamma b\), where \(\gamma>0\). For the same computed point, its absolute residual changes from \(|a^{\mathsf T}x-b|\) to \(\gamma|a^{\mathsf T}x-b|\). Analogous sensitivity affects linear-system conditioning and finite-precision search directions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic characterization for the transformed equality matrix; it does not assert preservation of the standard-form nonnegative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular. Every matrix \(A\) whose rows contain at most one nonzero has the same property after \(A\mapsto AT\) if and only if \(T=DP\), where \(D\) is nonsingular diagonal and \(P\) is a permutation matrix. If \(T\) is not monomial, some coordinate row \(e_i^{\mathsf T}\) is spread into at least two nonzeros by multiplication with \(T\).

assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular.
The claim concerns sparsity of the equality coefficient matrix, independently of the transformed variable domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[\forall A:\operatorname{rowsupp}(A)\le1\Rightarrow\operatorname{rowsupp}(AT)\le1\bigr]\iff T=DP\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent coordinate transformations may convert sparse constraint matrices into dense matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the invertible variable transformation \(x=Tz\), the equality matrix becomes \(AT\). Sparsity is not invariant under this equivalence. Consequently, an equivalent reformulation may increase factorization storage and arithmetic substantially, independently of any subsequent elimination fill-in.

children.title: Crossover Instability
children.top_down_role: Numerical instability during conversion from an interior solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discontinuous recovered-basis selection near a nonunique optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For x_1+x_2=1 and x\ge0, the zero objective makes every feasible point optimal. Under c_\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}x=\varepsilon(x_1-x_2), \varepsilon>0 uniquely selects (0,1), while \varepsilon<0 uniquely selects (1,0). Hence arbitrarily small objective perturbations can switch the uniquely selected basic optimum and basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a nonunique optimal face, an arbitrarily small objective perturbation can switch the selected basic optimum and basis.
assumptions_latex: c_\varepsilon=(\varepsilon,-\varepsilon).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon>0\Rightarrow x^*=(0,1),\qquad \varepsilon<0\Rightarrow x^*=(1,0).
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Perturbation Basis Switch

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical instability after selection of a poorly conditioned basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If crossover selects a nonsingular basis B and computes x_B=A_B^{-1}b, then for a fixed A_B and sufficiently small right-hand-side perturbations, \|\Delta x_B\|/\|x_B\| is bounded to first order by \kappa(A_B)\|\Delta b\|/\|b\|, and perturbation directions can attain amplification of this order. Thus no conditioning-independent stability guarantee exists; near-zero basic components may change reported feasibility or status under amplified error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ill-conditioned recovered basis can amplify small errors enough to change near-zero feasibility or status decisions.
assumptions_latex: A_B\text{ is nonsingular}.
b\ne0\text{ and }x_B\ne0.
Perturbations and }\kappa(A_B)\text{ use compatible norms}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\|\Delta x_B\|}{\|x_B\|}\lesssim\kappa(A_B)\frac{\|\Delta b\|}{\|b\|},\qquad \sup_B\kappa(A_B)=\infty\text{ over admissible instances}.

notation.meaning: Normwise condition number of the selected basis matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Recovered-Basis Instability
Crossover Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discontinuous basis selection near an optimal face with multiple optimal bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the LP with \(x_1+x_2=1\), \(x_1,x_2\geq0\). With zero objective, every feasible point is optimal, and the optimal basis is not uniquely determined. For the perturbed objective \(c_\varepsilon^{\mathsf T}x=\varepsilon(x_1-x_2)\), where \(c_\varepsilon=(\varepsilon,-\varepsilon)\), \(\varepsilon>0\) uniquely selects \((0,1)\), whereas \(\varepsilon<0\) uniquely selects \((1,0)\). Thus arbitrarily small objective perturbations can select different basic optima and bases. A crossover procedure near such a nonunique optimal face can therefore exhibit discontinuous basis recovery under continuous changes in the LP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near an optimal face with multiple optimal bases, an arbitrarily small objective change can switch the uniquely selected basic optimum and recovered basis.
assumptions_latex: \(c_\varepsilon=(\varepsilon,-\varepsilon)\) with \(\varepsilon\in\mathbb R\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\Rightarrow x^*=(0,1),\qquad \varepsilon<0\Rightarrow x^*=(1,0)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{i:x_i^*>0\}\). Every basis representing \(x^*\) contains \(S\), while \(|S|<m\) leaves \(m-|S|\) zero-valued basic positions to be completed. If distinct bases \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) both contain \(S\), have nonsingular basis matrices, and generate the same basic feasible solution \(x^*\), then neither \(x^*\) nor its support distinguishes \(B_1\) from \(B_2\). Consequently, convergence of approximate primal solutions \(\widehat x\to x^*\) supplies the limiting support but does not by itself specify which representing basis a crossover procedure should recover.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal B(x^*)=\{B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}:|B|=m,\ A_B\text{ is nonsingular},\ x(B)=x^*\}\). If \(|\mathcal B(x^*)|>1\), then the primal point \(x^*\) does not uniquely determine a member of \(\mathcal B(x^*)\). A crossover procedure that returns a basis must therefore use additional criteria, such as an ordering rule, admissibility tests, or deterministic tie-breaking. Different admissible selection rules can return different members of \(\mathcal B(x^*)\) while preserving the same primal optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When several nonsingular bases represent the same degenerate optimum, the primal point does not select one of them. A crossover procedure must use an additional selection rule, and different admissible rules may return different representing bases.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a threshold \(\tau>0\), let \(I_x(\tau)=\{i:\widehat x_i>\tau\}\) and \(I_s(\tau)=\{i:\widehat s_i\le\tau\}\). Basis recovery breaks down whenever the available candidate indices cannot produce a set \(B\) satisfying simultaneously \(|B|=m\), \(\det(A_B)\ne0\), \(A_B^{-1}b\ge0\), and nonnegative reduced costs for all nonbasic indices. This can occur when thresholding yields too few indices, too many indistinguishable indices, or only numerically dependent column sets. Without a positive separation margin between basic and nonbasic indicators and a lower conditioning bound for an optimal \(A_B\), convergence of primal-dual residuals and complementarity to zero does not preclude such breakdown.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossover can fail when thresholded candidates contain no well-conditioned, primal-feasible, dual-feasible basis; small residuals alone do not guarantee successful recovery.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited locators do not establish the stated universal failure boundary as written. The candidate never defines whether the available set is \(I_x(\tau)\), \(I_s(\tau)\), their union, their intersection, or another completion set. Moreover, for a fixed LP possessing an optimal nonsingular basis, that basis has a positive instance-specific smallest singular value, so the absence of an explicitly assumed conditioning bound does not by itself show that exact primal-dual convergence can never permit recovery. A support or rank threshold schedule, a precise recovery algorithm, and either a sourced theorem or a concrete counterexample are required before the conclusion can be assessed reliably. The failure_boundary kind is appropriate for the terminal container, but the mathematical formulation needs authoritative support.
